file: 1995/1995-02-07_twlecommuting_optional habits_hygiene_cow orkers_fading memeory_language skills_expect answers_gas mask_tarzan like pharses.gif
title: Telecommuting Turns Dilbert Feral

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Day two of telecommuting is going smoothly. I have eliminated all optional habits of hygiene.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My co-workers are a fading memory. I am losing language skills. I talk to my computer and expect answers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For reasons that are unclear, my dog wears a gas mask and shouts Tarzan-like phrases.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Kreegah! Bundalo!

situation: Dilbert sits at his home computer on his second day of telecommuting and narrates his rapid decline. He has stopped practicing hygiene, forgotten his co-workers, and started talking to his computer as if it will answer. His dog Dogbert appears in a gas mask shouting jungle-style phrases.
punchline: Working alone from home for just two days has reduced Dilbert to an unkempt, isolated, language-impaired state, so bizarre that he cannot even explain his dog's behavior, yet he insists it is going smoothly.
summary: A man working from home for two days cheerfully reports that he has abandoned grooming, lost touch with colleagues, and is surrounded by strange pet behavior.

file: 1995/1995-04-16_job interview_resume_impressive_biggest fault_work too hard_forget to eat_bathe_die as desk_bloted_stinking corpse_someone hungrier.gif
title: Biggest Fault: Dying at Desk

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Looks like somebody has a job interview.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shhh

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Your résumé is impressive. I only have one question.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: What do you consider your biggest fault?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I work too hard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) Good one.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Why is that a fault?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... uh... I work so hard that I forget to eat and bathe for days. Eventually I starve to death at my desk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I become a bloated, stinking corpse. Insects breed in my body. I spread disease to the entire company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How did it go?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They want somebody hungrier.

situation: Wally notices Dilbert is heading to a job interview. When asked for his biggest fault, Dilbert gives the cliché answer that he works too hard, then is pressed to explain why that is a fault. He spirals into a gruesome description of starving to death at his desk and infecting the company, and afterward reports that they want someone hungrier.
punchline: Dilbert's absurdly morbid explanation of his 'fault' backfires, and the interviewer's rejection that they want someone 'hungrier' is a pun on both his starvation story and the idea of a more ambitious candidate.
summary: A job candidate's rehearsed answer about overworking collapses into a grotesque tale of dying at his desk, earning him a pun-filled rejection.

file: 1995/1995-11-20_dogbert the consultant_reorganize_core comeptency_giving money_consultants.gif
title: Core Competency: Paying Consultants

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend that you reorganize to strengthen the core competency of your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As luck would have it, your core competency is "giving money to consultants."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think that's the ONLY thing we're good at.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It depends on if you count "whining."

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, sits at a conference table with the Boss and advises him to reorganize around the company's core competency. He then declares that the company's core competency is giving money to consultants. When the Boss objects that it isn't the only thing they do well, Dogbert adds that whining might also count.
punchline: Dogbert mocks the company by saying its only real skill is overpaying consultants like himself, and the only other candidate is complaining.
summary: A consultant dog tells a clueless manager that his firm's greatest strength is funnelling cash to advisors, with grumbling as the runner-up.

file: 1995/1995-02-10_make less_janitor_plunger_plumber_rascal_animal_alice loves job_boss_raise.gif
title: Janitor Earns More, Then Gets Raise

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When you consider the hours I work, I make less per hour than the janitor!

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Look what was blocking the pipes! It took me all morning to plunge the rascal out.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I love my job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm giving him a raise.

situation: Alice complains to the Boss that, given her long hours, she earns less per hour than the janitor. The janitor then appears holding a plunger with a dead animal stuck on it that he pulled from the clogged pipes. Alice says she loves her job, and the Boss announces he is giving the janitor a raise.
punchline: Faced with the janitor's disgusting work, Alice sarcastically declares she loves her job, but the Boss misses the point and rewards the janitor with a raise instead of her.
summary: After an overworked employee grumbles about being paid less than the custodian, the custodian displays the grisly creature he unclogged and ends up with the pay increase she wanted.

file: 1995/1995-03-31_bad mouthing_last guy_slimy_brain_files_fleas skull_alice_wally.gif
title: Traditional Bad-Mouthing of Previous Employee

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd like to kick-off the project with the traditional bad-mouthing of the guy who worked on this before.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He's so slimy that slugs pour salt on HIM. His brain would rattle in a flea's skull!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oh, and I'll need your files.

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: Fleas don't have "skulls"!!!

setting: Conference room during a project kickoff meeting
situation: Alice opens a project kickoff by insulting the predecessor who previously worked on the project, delivering an increasingly vicious tirade. She then calmly asks for the files. The bald man at the table turns out to be the former project owner and responds with a pedantic correction.
punchline: The man being insulted is the previous project guy himself, and rather than defend himself against the abuse, he only objects to the anatomical inaccuracy of the insult.
summary: A colleague cheerfully trashes the project's previous owner in front of him, and his only complaint is a petty biology correction.

file: 1995/1995-11-07_sign on coffee maker_stupid label guy_iso 900 requirement_no exceptions_label everything.gif
title: Stupid Label Guy Labels Coffee Maker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you putting a sign on the coffee maker?

transcript.speaker: Label Guy
transcript.text: It's an ISO 9000 requirement. Everything must be clearly labeled. There can be no exceptions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's stupid.

transcript.speaker: Label Guy
transcript.text: Believe me, I don't like it any more than you do.

setting: Office break area with a coffee maker on the counter
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker why he is attaching a sign reading 'Coffee Maker' to the coffee maker. The coworker explains that an ISO 9000 requirement demands everything be labeled with no exceptions. Dilbert calls it stupid, and the coworker agrees, turning to reveal a label on his own back reading 'Stupid Label Guy'.
punchline: The man enforcing the absurd labeling rule is himself labeled 'Stupid Label Guy', showing that compliance requirements apply to everyone, even to the point of ridiculousness, and that he is a reluctant enforcer.
summary: A coworker obsessively tagging objects for quality-standard compliance turns out to be wearing a tag of his own.

file: 1995/1995-01-06_ass six meetings_customer focus_micro management_egomaniacal mahifest_survival_paper towels_mens room.gif
title: Boss's Micromanaged Ego Gets Swatted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Change these dates... and add six more meetings. And use the phrase "customer focus."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... Your micro-management has caused my ego to manifest itself and beg for survival.

transcript.speaker: Ego
transcript.text: I'm shrinking!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Run and get me some paper towels... five of them... from the men's room.

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect
transcript.text: Whap!

situation: The Boss micromanages Dilbert's document, ordering date changes, extra meetings and buzzwords. Dilbert warns that the micromanagement has made his ego appear as a tiny shrinking creature on the desk. The Boss squashes it with a flyswatter and sends Dilbert off for paper towels to clean up.
punchline: The Boss literally swats and kills Dilbert's ego, then casually orders him to fetch paper towels to clean up the mess, showing he has no regard for his employee's self-worth.
summary: A micromanaging manager crushes his employee's literally tiny ego with a flyswatter and then assigns him the cleanup.

file: 1995/1995-12-24_happy airlines_vacation_data in computer_dogbert_gate 13_never saw luggage_misfits offended tantra_goddess of flight.gif
title: Airline Check-In Takes Forever

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Happy Airlines

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Vacation, here we come!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click click click click click click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do they have to enter so much stuff in the computer?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click click click click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They already have our reservation and seat assignment in there. What else do they need?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click click click click

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm developing a sudden fear of flying.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click click click click click click click click

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Step aside.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's going on up here??!!

transcript.speaker: Ticket Agent
transcript.text: Gate 13. Have a nice flight.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Ticket Agent
transcript.text: "They never saw their beloved luggage again. The misfits always regretted offending Tantra, the goddess of flight. The end."

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click click click click click

setting: Airline check-in counter at an airport
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert check in for a vacation flight while the ticket agent types endlessly on her computer. Dilbert grows annoyed that so much data entry is needed, so Dogbert steps up and confronts the agent, who then gets him checked in. In the last panel the agent is shown typing a story that says the misfits' luggage was lost forever as punishment for offending the goddess of flight.
punchline: Dogbert's confrontation with the check-in agent apparently got their luggage lost, as she types out a vengeful story about the misfits offending the goddess of flight and never seeing their luggage again.
summary: After Dogbert bullies a slow airline clerk into hurrying, she quietly gets revenge by typing a tale in which their baggage is lost forever.

file: 1995/1995-01-11_venture capital firm_watching people_moronic ideas_money_crimp the mirth_finance.gif
title: Dogbert's Venture Capital Entertainment Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting my own venture capital firm.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm attracted to the concept of watching people with moronic ideas beg for money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you actually finance anybody?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That would sort of crimp the mirth.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert lying on the couch
situation: Dogbert announces he is starting a venture capital firm and explains that he likes the idea of watching people with foolish ideas beg for money. Dilbert, lying on the couch, asks whether Dogbert will actually fund anyone. Dogbert admits that funding people would ruin the fun.
punchline: Dogbert's venture capital firm exists purely to enjoy the spectacle of desperate entrepreneurs pitching bad ideas, and actually giving anyone money would spoil the entertainment.
summary: A scheming dog plans an investment business whose real purpose is amusement at the expense of hopeful pitchers, never intending to hand over any cash.

file: 1995/1995-05-05_hobby geography_twirling wedgie_dinosaur.gif
title: Book Signing Ends in Twirling Wedgie

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: My hobby is geography. Would you sign my book to each of the continents by name?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that my book recommends a twirling wedgie for people who ask for too much?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: We find the line moves faster if I do this to the first customer.

setting: A bookstore signing table with a line of customers
situation: Dogbert is signing copies of his book while a line of customers waits. The first customer, who has a geography hobby, asks him to sign a copy to each of the continents, and Dogbert warns that his book prescribes a twirling wedgie for people who ask too much. A green dinosaur then lifts the customer into the air by the seat of his pants and spins him to speed up the line.
punchline: Dogbert's book advice about punishing overly demanding people is carried out literally and brutally by his dinosaur assistant, using violence as a line-management technique.
summary: A bookstore author turns a fan's fussy autograph request into an excuse for his dinosaur enforcer to hoist and spin the guy.

file: 1995/1995-08-20_new software interface_operating system_new hardware_anti gravity_packaging_reaction_perfromance review.gif
title: Boss Promises Impossible Deadlines, Punishes Pessimism

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't promise the product manager more than we can deliver.

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: We need a totally new software interface in one month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You got it!

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: And rewrite the operating system so we dominate the industry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Concurrent development.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Check.

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: Suddenly I feel omnipotent.

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: I want all new hardware, anti-gravity packaging, holographic agents...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yawn yawn.

transcript.speaker: Product Manager
transcript.text: Can your team really do that in a month?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me get their reaction.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: AAAGH!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pessimism will not look good on your performance review.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Twitch

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss not to over-promise to the product manager, but the Boss cheerfully agrees to every outlandish demand, including a new interface and a rewritten operating system in one month. When he finally checks with his engineer, the engineer screams in horror, and the Boss threatens him with a bad performance review for pessimism.
punchline: The Boss commits to impossible deliverables without consulting his team, then punishes the engineer for reacting realistically to them.
summary: A manager agrees to absurd product demands without asking anyone, then threatens the engineer who reacts with despair.

file: 1995/1995-11-29_network connection_technology have not_global economy_french fry_electronic mail_snork.gif
title: Technology Have-Nots and Electronic Mail

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Alice, did you hear that Dilbert's network connection isn't working?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He is what we call a technology "have not." His competitiveness in the global economy will last as long as this French fry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So sad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: After lunch, I'm going to use something called "electronic mail." You can watch if you promise not to touch anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Snork!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gulp.

setting: Office lunch table in a break room or cubicle area
situation: Wally and Alice eat lunch with Dilbert, and Wally talks about Dilbert as if he weren't there, mocking him as a technology 'have not' because his network connection is down. Wally then condescendingly offers to let Dilbert watch him use email, as long as he doesn't touch anything, while Dilbert sits quietly eating.
punchline: Wally, who is notoriously lazy and incompetent, smugly lords his barely-there technology skills over Dilbert, an actual engineer, treating a temporary network outage as a permanent social divide and email as a rare privilege.
summary: While a coworker's network is down, a smug colleague belittles him as a digital pauper and graciously offers a supervised demonstration of email.

file: 1995/1995-12-01_shipped new prodcut_tech support_trained_embarrasments_monk_training_material_real monk_pig latin.gif
title: Tech Support Trained on Rice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We just shipped our newest product. You folks in tech support will need to be trained so you can avoid any embarrassments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We had a monk write the training material on a grain of rice. We could only afford one, so you'll have to share it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To be honest, I'm not sure we had a real monk. He wrote everything in pig latin.

situation: The Boss tells a group of headset-wearing tech support staff that their training for a newly shipped product is a single grain of rice with text written by a monk. They must share it. In the last panel he admits the monk may have been fake since the text was in pig latin, while the staff have collapsed on the floor in a daze.
punchline: Tech support gets absurdly inadequate training, a single shared grain of rice written by a dubious monk in pig latin, showing management's contempt for supporting the product they just shipped.
summary: A manager hands his support staff a microscopic, possibly fraudulent training document to prepare them for a product that has already launched.

file: 1995/1995-08-28_tina_tech worter_documentation written_software done.gif
title: Documenting Software That Doesn't Exist

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, you'll have to have all the documentation written by next week so we can ship it when the software is done.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: How can I write instructions for something that doesn't exist yet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll have to make logical guesses.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: "If you press any key your computer will lock up. If you call our tech support we'll blame 'Microsoft.'"

situation: The Boss tells Tina, the technical writer, to finish the product documentation by next week so it can ship as soon as the software is done. Tina objects that she can't write instructions for software that doesn't exist yet, and he tells her to make logical guesses. She then types a deliberately cynical manual entry predicting crashes and blaming Microsoft.
punchline: Forced to guess at documentation, Tina writes what she assumes any buggy software manual will say: it crashes on any keypress and tech support blames Microsoft.
summary: Told to write a manual for unfinished software, a technical writer invents a sarcastic entry that assumes the product will be buggy and its makers will shift blame.

file: 1995/1995-01-28_great idea_first idea_tougest_urge goes away.gif
title: New Hire's First Idea Punished

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I've only worked here one day but I thought of a great idea.

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect
transcript.text: Zip

transcript.speaker: Sound Effect
transcript.text: Sploosh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first idea is always the toughest.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The urge eventually goes away.

situation: A cheerful new employee tells Dilbert and Wally he has a great idea after only one day on the job. In the next panel Dilbert, Wally and a suited Dogbert zip past and blast him with a hose. The new hire ends up slumped and soaked while Dilbert and Wally calmly explain that the urge to suggest ideas goes away eventually.
punchline: Coworkers discourage new hires from offering ideas by literally hosing them down, implying that the office breaks your enthusiasm until you stop suggesting improvements.
summary: A fresh recruit's eagerness to contribute gets drenched by veteran coworkers who have long since given up on ideas.

file: 1995/1995-06-08_team building exercise_paper dolls_blindfolded_cognitive dissonance_learned something_cry and hug.gif
title: Blindfolded Paper Dolls Team Building

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this team-building exercise you will make paper dolls while blindfolded.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This may seem absurd. But soon, cognitive dissonance will set in and you'll cry and hug and think you learned something.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you sure we'll cry and hug?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, hugging is iffy.

setting: Conference room around a large oval table
situation: Dogbert, acting as a facilitator, instructs the team to make paper dolls while blindfolded as a team-building exercise. He cheerfully admits it is absurd and says cognitive dissonance will make everyone cry, hug, and falsely believe they learned something. Dilbert asks if the hugging is guaranteed, and the Boss, blindfolded and cutting paper, says hugging is uncertain.
punchline: The facilitator openly admits that team-building exercises work only by tricking participants into believing they learned something, and even the promised emotional payoff is not guaranteed.
summary: A consultant explains that a ridiculous blindfolded craft session will manufacture fake enlightenment, while the participants worry about whether the emotional bonding will actually happen.

file: 1995/1995-05-07_habits of highly defective people_ignore signs_belittle people_newest team_all complainers fault_motivate me_therapist_controversial issues_barney as mascot_assembly line code_prejudices_crisp photo copy_cpmics_psychology.gif
title: Seven Habits of Defective Bosses

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The 7 habits of highly defective people

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ow!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 1. Ignore any signs of discomfort in others.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But hey, I've been doing all of the talking.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 2. Use humor to belittle people in public.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our newest team member has movie star looks. Specifically, Lassie.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 3. Treat all complaints as the complainer's fault.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't motivate me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should see a therapist.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 4. Show up late and raise controversial issues.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think we should license "Barney" as our mascot.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 5. Give advice on things you don't understand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try writing some assembly line code here.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 6. Use compliments to show your prejudices.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh, nice crisp photocopy, Alice. I don't think a man could have done it better!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: 7. Think the comics are not about you

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hee hee! Look at the hair on that guy!

situation: A list-style strip presents seven habits of 'highly defective people', with each numbered panel showing the Pointy-Haired Boss demonstrating a bad management behavior. He ignores a skeleton waiting at his desk, insults a new hire, blames Dilbert for being unmotivated, proposes a silly mascot, gives clueless coding advice, and gives Alice a sexist compliment. In the last panel he reads the comics and laughs at a character with hair like his own.
punchline: The Boss exhibits every defective habit and then fails to realize that the comic strip he is laughing at, featuring a man with his own hairstyle, is about him.
summary: A parody self-help list catalogs the worst management behaviors, all performed by the clueless boss, who ends by laughing at the very comic that mocks him.

file: 1995/1995-01-12_dogbert_venture capitalist_technical expertise_business stuff_special_decotrative_non equity stock_common stock_avoid tension_partners experince.gif
title: Dogbert Swindles Inventor With Worthless Stock

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Venture Capitalist

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: You'll use your technical expertise and I'll do the business stuff. Sign here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Since you're the inventor of the technology, you'll get 100% of the special decorative non-equity stock. I'll settle for all the common stock.

transcript.speaker: Inventor
transcript.text: I hope we can avoid the tension that some partners experience.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give me my pen, you miscreant.

setting: A conference table in a business meeting room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a venture capitalist, tells an inventor that the inventor will handle the technology while Dogbert does the business side, and has him sign a contract. The inventor, who is signing, discovers that he gets only worthless decorative non-equity stock while Dogbert keeps all the real common stock. The inventor then smugly hopes they can avoid the tension some partners have, and Dogbert simply demands his pen back.
punchline: The inventor signs away all real ownership in exchange for worthless stock, and Dogbert dismisses him with contempt, treating the partnership as a one-sided scam.
summary: A scheming dog financier tricks a naive inventor into signing away real ownership for worthless paper, then insults him and grabs back his pen.

file: 1995/1995-12-29_new software_installed_send registartion_modem_credit card_number_new products_virus_excellent marketing.gif
title: Virus or Excellent Marketing Software

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Your new software is successfully installed. Do you want to send your registration info by modem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: The software has found your credit card number and is placing orders for new products it thinks you need... Please wait.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh...

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Making room on your hard drive...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell if it's a virus or just excellent marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Either way...

setting: Dilbert's home or office with his desktop computer
situation: Dilbert installs new software and agrees to send his registration info by modem. The software then finds his credit card number and starts ordering products it decides he needs, and begins clearing space on his hard drive to store them. Dilbert wonders aloud whether it's a virus or great marketing, while Dogbert, who is holding a credit card, hints that it makes no difference.
punchline: Software that steals your credit card and orders things on its own behaves identically whether it is malware or aggressive marketing, and Dogbert, seen with a credit card himself, is profiting either way.
summary: Newly installed software goes on a shopping spree with a user's card, leaving him unable to distinguish malicious code from clever sales tactics.

file: 1995/1995-10-17_co worker_perfume is killing_gas mask_humor_woman_stank like hog_cluless_waiting compliments.gif
title: Dogbert Jokes About Smelly Perfume

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, your mission is to tell my co-worker that her perfume is killing us. Wear this gas mask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Use humor to ease the tension.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you hear the joke about the woman who stank like a hog rendering plant?

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Three times today...

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert to tell a co-worker that her heavy perfume is unbearable, handing him a gas mask to wear. Dogbert agrees to use humor to soften the message and tells her a joke about a woman who smells like a hog rendering plant. The co-worker replies that she has already heard this joke three times today.
punchline: The perfume-wearing co-worker is oblivious and thinks the insult joke is aimed at someone else, noting that she has already heard it several times that day, which implies that others have been hinting at her smell all along.
summary: A gas-masked dog tries to tactfully hint at a colleague's overpowering fragrance with a joke, but she is too clueless to realize it is about her.

file: 1995/1995-02-21_pathological liar_work_luck_phd in laitology_from mit_diploma.gif
title: Dogbert's Fake Liatology Degree

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, I need your help dealing with a pathological liar at work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're in luck. I happen to have a Ph.D. in liatology from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd love to see your diploma.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll mail it to you.

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, with Dogbert reclining on a couch
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for advice on handling a pathological liar at work. Dogbert claims to hold a Ph.D. in 'liatology' from MIT. When Dilbert asks to see the diploma, Dogbert gives the classic evasive answer that he'll mail it.
punchline: Dogbert's claimed credential and his vague promise to mail proof reveal that he is himself a liar, making him unqualified to advise on lying.
summary: A man seeking help with a chronic fibber is offered expertise by a dog whose credentials sound suspiciously invented.

file: 1995/1995-05-06_retiring_media_vast weath_property_agree to be puppet_kermit_muppet_lease_entertainment.gif
title: Dogbert's Real Estate Puppet Landlord Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm retiring from my media empire and putting my vast wealth into real estate.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My plan is to buy all the property on Earth and evict everybody who doesn't agree to be my puppet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I be Kermit?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a "muppet." It's all spelled out in your lease.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert reads a newspaper on the couch while Dogbert announces he is leaving his media empire to become a global landlord. His plan is to buy all property on Earth and evict anyone who won't be his puppet. Dilbert asks if he can be Kermit, and Dogbert corrects him that the term is 'muppet', noting it is written in the lease.
punchline: Dogbert's world-domination scheme works through lease terms, and he coolly treats Dilbert's Kermit joke as a contract detail, making tenants literal Muppets under his control.
summary: A scheming dog plans to own all land and turn every tenant into his puppet, and his roommate's puppet-themed question gets answered with fine print.

file: 1995/1995-08-25_bowels of accounting_dilbert trapped_head backwards_brain explode_paradigm shit.gif
title: Dogbert Rescues Dilbert With Backwards Cap

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert is trapped in the bowels of accounting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I understand you have Dilbert in there. Free him, or else...

transcript.speaker: Accounting Monster
transcript.text: Else what?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or else I will put this cap on my head backwards! Your little hardwired accounting brain will explode just looking at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was that popping sound?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A paradigm shifting without a clutch.

setting: A cave-like dungeon representing the accounting department's depths
situation: Dogbert confronts a green, spear-carrying monster guarding the accounting department, where Dilbert is being held captive. Dogbert threatens to put his cap on backwards, claiming it will blow the rigid accounting mind. Dilbert is then seen hanging upside down, freed or at least affected, and asks about the popping sound.
punchline: Accountants are so rigidly conventional that merely seeing a cap worn backwards is enough to break their brains, which Dogbert quips is a paradigm shifting without a clutch.
summary: Dogbert defeats a rule-bound accounting guardian by threatening it with the horror of an unconventionally worn hat.

file: 1995/1995-05-30_mandatory training_business ethics_save money_training_decorate offcie_taken training_common sense.gif
title: Skipping Ethics Training to Save Money

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you taken the mandatory training for business ethics?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. But if you say I did then you'll save some money on training which you can spend to decorate your office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Luckily, I haven't taken the training myself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear it's mostly common sense anyway.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he has completed the company's mandatory business ethics training. Dilbert admits he hasn't but suggests the Boss simply claim he did, so the company saves training money that the Boss could spend decorating his own office. The Boss cheerfully reveals he hasn't taken the training either, and Dilbert notes it's mostly common sense.
punchline: The Boss eagerly embraces a dishonest cost-saving scheme and admits he skipped the ethics training himself, proving he lacks the very common sense the training is said to teach.
summary: A manager is happy to fake compliance records for an ethics course, showing exactly why such courses are needed.

file: 1995/1995-12-16_conquer the world_secret handshake_identify people_new ruling class_stick out tongue_vinously slp_face_slap.gif
title: Secret Handshake for the Ruling Class

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When I conquer the world I'll have a secret handshake to identify the people who will be part of my new ruling class.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Cross your eyes and stick out your tongue. Good, now vigorously slap your face.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The people who aren't doing that will be identified as my new ruling class.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap!

setting: A living room, with Dogbert and Ratbert on a couch
situation: Dogbert tells Ratbert about the secret handshake he plans to use to identify his future ruling class. He then instructs Ratbert to cross his eyes, stick out his tongue and slap his own face. Ratbert obeys and gets knocked over by his own slap.
punchline: Dogbert tricks the obedient Ratbert into humiliating himself, then reveals that the true ruling class is whoever refuses to follow such a ridiculous order.
summary: A scheming dog fools his gullible companion into slapping himself, revealing that the people with the sense to refuse are the ones who will rule.

file: 1995/1995-07-28_bob procurement_duties are simple_assume employees lie_multimedia laptop_demo labeler_low cost substitutes_savings_accomplishments.gif
title: Procurement Bob Substitutes Cheap Labeler

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob works in procurement.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Your duties are simple. People will come to you and ask for things.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Assume all employees are lying, treasure-hunting thieves. Give them low-cost substitutes and claim the savings on your accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I asked for a multimedia laptop PC. This is a "Dymo" labeler.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Nice try, Paul, if that's your real name.

situation: The Boss trains Bob, a green dinosaur, for a procurement job. He tells him to treat every employee as a lying thief and hand out cheap substitutes to claim savings. An employee then comes to Bob after requesting a multimedia laptop and is given a Dymo label maker instead, and Bob accuses him of using a fake name.
punchline: Procurement is run on paranoia and fake savings, so employees get absurdly cheap substitutes for what they ask for and are accused of dishonesty for complaining.
summary: A newly hired purchasing clerk follows his boss's cynical advice and swaps a requested computer for a label maker.

file: 1995/1995-05-23_salary deonds_opinion_interest in understanding_dogcart relations_hype performance.gif
title: Dilbert Hires Dogbert for Hype

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My salary depends on your opinion of my work. But you have no interest in understanding what I do, so...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert public relations firm to hype my performance and get me a big raise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Press release: Engineer cures cancer while saving baby from burning building.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not in his objectives.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that since the Boss doesn't understand his work yet determines his salary, he has hired Dogbert's PR firm to promote his performance. Dogbert reads out an absurdly exaggerated press release about Dilbert's heroics. The Boss responds only by noting it isn't in Dilbert's objectives.
punchline: The Boss is so fixated on formal objectives that even a ridiculously heroic achievement, curing cancer and saving a baby, is dismissed because it isn't on the list.
summary: An engineer sends a publicist to inflate his accomplishments for a raise, but his supervisor only cares whether the feats match a checklist.

file: 1995/1995-11-26_evaluates prey_badge_important decision maker_low ranking employee_coffee stain_below stain_rank_make decsiosn_wally.gif
title: Salesman Hunts for Decision Maker

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Badge.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: The clever salesman evaluates his prey.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I hope he's an important decision-maker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Take any seat. I call the good chair.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Warning! Cubicle! Low-ranking employee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's our organization chart: President... Senior Vice President... Vice President...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, lift your foot. Do you see that coffee stain on the carpet?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: That's you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, that's my boss. I would be under the carpet.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Do I have any hope of talking to somebody who can make a decision?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me check.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, Wally. What's a "decision"?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It sounds like something our competitors do.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Sob.

setting: Office reception area and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: A salesman visits the company hoping to pitch to an important decision-maker. Dilbert, a low-ranking engineer, walks him through the org chart and jokes that his boss is the coffee stain on the carpet while he is beneath it. When the salesman asks if anyone can make a decision, Dilbert asks Wally what a decision is, and the salesman sobs in despair.
punchline: The company is so indecisive that even employees don't know what a decision is, leaving the salesman with no one to sell to.
summary: A hopeful salesman keeps descending the corporate hierarchy in search of someone with authority, only to find an organization that has never made a decision.

file: 1995/1995-05-08_signs on cubciles_be classy_cubicles_conference rooms_catch.gif
title: Cubicles Named Like Conference Rooms

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is everybody putting signs on their cubicles?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We thought it would be classy to name our cubicles the same way we name conference rooms.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know there's a catch... But what?

situation: The Boss notices that employees have put signs on their cubicles and asks why. Dilbert says they just wanted to name their cubicles the way conference rooms are named. The Boss suspects a trick but can't work it out, while the signs nearby read "Menendez Rooms" and "O.J. Room".
punchline: The employees have named their cubicles after notorious 1990s murder defendants (the Menendez brothers and O.J. Simpson), a joke the clueless Boss fails to catch even as he suspects something is off.
summary: Staff quietly mock the boss by labelling their cubicles with infamous murder-trial names, and he senses a prank without seeing it.

file: 1995/1995-01-29_lake_push people_need a hobby_pretty one_flopping around_lower form_big one_weigh.gif
title: Dogbert Turns the Tables on Angler

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be down at the lake, pushing people in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You need a new hobby, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a sport!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Having any luck today?

transcript.speaker: Fisherman
transcript.text: Yeah, I got me a pretty one. You should have seen it flopping around. Beautiful!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Beautiful?? Are you saying there's beauty in causing a lower form of life to suffer?

transcript.speaker: Fisherman
transcript.text: Only if it's a big one.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How much do you weigh?

transcript.speaker: Fisherman
transcript.text: Oh, about 210 pounds, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you mind flopping around some more?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's beautiful.

situation: Dogbert announces he's heading to the lake to push people in, calling it a sport. At the lake he chats with a fisherman who boasts about the beautiful fish flopping around on his line, and Dogbert gets him to say it's only beautiful if the catch is big. After learning the man weighs 210 pounds, Dogbert pushes him into the water and asks him to keep flopping.
punchline: Dogbert uses the fisherman's own logic that a big, flopping creature is beautiful to justify pushing him into the lake and enjoying his suffering.
summary: A scheming dog trips up an angler with his own words about the beauty of a struggling catch, then dunks him to enjoy the show.

file: 1995/1995-01-10_own cubicles_keep binders_shopping cart_strong interest_graffitti_express indviduality_could be worse_joining gang.gif
title: Cubicle-Less Wally Joins a Gang

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now that we don't have our own cubicles I have to keep my binders in this shopping cart.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I've developed a strong interest in graffiti as a way to express my individuality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... it could be worse.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm thinking of joining a gang.

situation: After the company eliminates personal cubicles, Wally pushes a shopping cart containing his binders around the office. He explains that he has taken up graffiti, spray-painting a door, to express his individuality. Dilbert says it could be worse, and Wally replies that he is thinking of joining a gang.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at reassurance backfires because Wally's descent into homeless-style vandalism is about to get even worse, showing how the loss of cubicles is pushing employees toward delinquency.
summary: With his workspace taken away, a cart-pushing Wally turns to vandalism and then casually floats the idea of joining a gang.

file: 1995/1995-09-14_nest paper towels_call 911_never know_would have worked.gif
title: Paper Trolls Eat Technician

transcript.speaker: Technician
transcript.text: Here's the problem. We've got a whole nest of paper trolls.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Aiiee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I call 911 now I'll never know if the lower paper tray would have worked.

setting: Office copy room beside a large photocopier
situation: A copier technician tells Dilbert that a nest of paper trolls is jamming the machine, then is dragged into the copier with a scream, leaving only his legs visible. Dilbert, holding a sheet of paper, considers calling 911 but worries he'll never learn whether the lower paper tray would have fixed his copying problem.
punchline: Dilbert is so fixated on getting his copy made that he cares more about testing the paper tray than about saving the technician who was just eaten by the copier.
summary: A repairman vanishes into a jammed copier and the only thing his bystander worries about is whether another paper tray would have done the trick.

file: 1995/1995-08-22_accounting dept_expense report_soul_soul check_tak a seat.gif
title: Checking Your Soul Before Accounting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it's okay, I'll hold onto my soul while I visit the accounting department.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Soul check

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I came to answer your questions about my expense report.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Take a seat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like the way this is starting.

setting: A cave-like hellish underworld housing the accounting department
situation: Dilbert walks through a cavern past a soul check booth and announces he will keep his soul while visiting accounting. He arrives at a green dinosaur-like accountant seated at a computer who tells him to take a seat to discuss his expense report. Dilbert, surrounded by stalagmites, grows uneasy about how the meeting is beginning.
punchline: The accounting department is depicted as a literal hell where souls are at risk, implying that expense report audits are a dreadful, soul-crushing ordeal.
summary: A nervous employee enters an infernal, cave-like accounting office to face questions about his expense report and quickly realizes he is in trouble.

file: 1995/1995-12-28_king dogbert_first ruler_internet_bow before me_internet is millons individuals_until now_dogbert fancies himself king_technology.gif
title: King Dogbert Rules the Internet

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I declare myself "King Dogbert," the first ruler of the Internet!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bow before me or be expelled from the kingdom forever!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that the Internet is comprised of millions of individuals and organizations that operate independently?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Until now!

situation: Dogbert sits at a computer and proclaims himself King Dogbert, the first ruler of the Internet, demanding that everyone bow or be banished. Dilbert, in a bathrobe holding a mug, points out that the Internet is made up of millions of independent individuals and organizations. Dogbert replies that this was true only until now.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd confidence means he treats the Internet's decentralized nature as a minor obstacle that his self-declared kingship has already ended.
summary: A scheming dog crowns himself monarch of the web and brushes aside a friend's reminder that nobody actually controls it.

file: 1995/1995-09-18_office equipment_garage sale_new slogan_selling stuff_keeping money.gif
title: Acting Like You Own It

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where are you taking all of that office equipment?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm having a garage sale.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our new company slogan is "Act like you own the company." So I've been selling the stuff that I don't use and keeping the money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that my new color monitor?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, I never used that thing.

setting: Company parking lot, beside an open car trunk
situation: Dilbert sees Wally loading office equipment into the trunk of his car and asks about it. Wally explains he is following the new company slogan by selling off supplies he doesn't use and pocketing the cash. Dilbert then recognizes his own new color monitor among the items.
punchline: Wally treats equipment that belongs to other people as stuff he doesn't use, so he happily sells Dilbert's new monitor for his own profit.
summary: Wally twists a corporate slogan into a license to flog company property from his car trunk, including a coworker's brand-new monitor.
keywords: act like you own the company

file: 1995/1995-09-23_found software_performance evaluations_same company_fortune cookies_buy new car_use pc.gif
title: Fortune Cookie Performance Review Software

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found software that helps managers write performance evaluations!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's made by the same company that makes fortune cookies for Canada!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That makes me feel better.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next day

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Don't buy a new car."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't think you knew how to use a PC.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My secretary wrote these.

situation: The Boss excitedly announces he has found software that writes performance evaluations for managers. Wally and Dilbert are alarmed, then Wally is reassured to learn it comes from a fortune cookie company. The next day Wally reads his review, which is a cryptic fortune-cookie-style line, and the Boss admits his secretary wrote them.
punchline: The software is no better than fortune cookie advice, and the Boss didn't even use it himself, since his secretary wrote the evaluations, showing the reviews are meaningless and he avoids doing the work.
summary: A manager brags about evaluation software from a fortune cookie maker, but the resulting review reads like a vague fortune and was actually written by his secretary.

file: 1995/1995-06-22_standardize_one type computer_mac user_deviant users_macintosh_unix_holy wars_gustav.gif
title: Computer Standardization Sparks Holy Wars

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend standardizing on one type of computer for the office.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We must identify and eliminate the deviant users of Macintosh, Unix and... God help us... OS/2 Warp.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The holy wars begin

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Don't lie to me, Gustav! You're a stinkin' Mac user!!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, recommends the office standardize on a single type of computer while The Boss listens. He then declares that users of rival platforms like Macintosh, Unix and OS/2 Warp must be found and eliminated. In the final panel an employee grabs a coworker named Gustav and accuses him of being a Mac user.
punchline: A reasonable-sounding IT standardization policy instantly turns into a violent witch hunt over platform loyalty.
summary: A consultant's call for uniform office computers quickly descends into coworkers hunting each other over their preferred operating systems.

file: 1995/1995-11-08_project status_yellow light_twelve seconds_interface_manual_pure fiction_need to do_dummies book.gif
title: Ship It and Hope for Dummies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The project status is "yellow light."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In user tests we found that the product locks up every twelve seconds. The interface is incomprehensible and the manual is pure fiction.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it's clear what we need to do...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ship it and hope somebody writes a "Dummies" book about it?

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: Dilbert reports to a meeting that the project status is "yellow light," then details the product's severe problems: it freezes every twelve seconds, the interface is incomprehensible, and the manual is fiction. The Boss concludes that the obvious course of action is to ship it anyway and hope a third party writes a "Dummies" book to explain it.
punchline: Faced with a product that is clearly broken and unusable, management's plan is to release it regardless and let outside authors fix the documentation problem, while the "yellow light" status wildly understates how bad things are.
summary: A badly flawed product gets a mild status rating, and the boss's solution is to release it and let someone else write the user guide.

file: 1995/1995-11-12_mister catbert_total compensation plan_salary alone_danger_balances out_employee benefits_lower blood pressure_rubbing soft belly_trick_health benefit.gif
title: Belly Rub Cuts Everyone's Salary

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mister Catbert will explain our new "Total Compensation Plan" for excellence.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We no longer view compensation in the narrow terms of salary alone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Danger! Danger!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If employee benefits go up, then salaries can go down and it all balances out.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For example, did you know you could lower your blood pressure by rubbing my soft, furry belly?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might be a trick!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!!! It's a health benefit! Now I'll cut everybody's salary!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that the more health benefits I get, the worse I feel.

setting: Conference room during a compensation meeting
situation: The Boss introduces Catbert, the evil human resources director, to explain a new 'Total Compensation Plan.' Catbert claims that better benefits justify lower salaries and offers a belly rub as a health benefit. When Wally rubs his belly, Catbert gleefully announces he will now cut everyone's salary.
punchline: Employees fall for a trivial 'benefit' that management then uses to justify pay cuts, so each perk they accept leaves them worse off.
summary: An evil HR cat lures employees into petting him, then treats it as a perk that justifies slashing everyone's pay.

file: 1995/1995-07-29_bob in procurement_approved equipment list_approved list_more work_alleged test_philosophy_bob the dinosaur.gif
title: Approved List Is a Philosophy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob in Procurement

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I'm afraid the equipment you want is not on the approved equipment list.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Let me think... If I add this to the approved list, that's more work for me... But if I say no, it's more work for you... Hmm... Think, think...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to see this alleged list.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Well, it's not so much a physical list as it is a philosophy.

situation: Bob the dinosaur, who works in Procurement, tells Dilbert that the equipment he requested is not on the approved list. Bob muses aloud that approving it means more work for himself while refusing means more work for Dilbert. When Dilbert asks to see the list, Bob admits it doesn't physically exist.
punchline: The approved equipment list is not a real document but a convenient excuse the procurement clerk invents to avoid doing work.
summary: A procurement clerk blocks a purchase request by citing a list that turns out to be nothing more than a vague attitude.

file: 1995/1995-09-30_mouse_eating food_takes outosde_prince_dumpster_ordinary mouse_turn into prince_dilbert.gif
title: Dilbert Dumps Punning Prince Mouse

transcript.speaker: Mouse
transcript.text: You're making a big mistake. I'm no ordinary mouse. If you kiss me I'll turn into a prince!!!

transcript.speaker: Mouse
transcript.text: Did I say "prince"? I meant I'd become the symbol for the performer formerly known as Prince. Ha ha ha!! Get it?

transcript.speaker: Mouse
transcript.text: You're immune to both romance and mirth. You must be a... a...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's right. I'm an engineer.

setting: Dilbert's office doorway and a trash bin outside
situation: Dilbert carries a mouse by the tail toward the door while it claims it will turn into a prince if kissed. When it follows up with a lame joke about the artist formerly known as Prince, Dilbert carries it outside and drops it into the trash. The mouse concludes that Dilbert is immune to romance and humor, and he cheerfully confirms he is an engineer.
punchline: Dilbert is so devoid of romance and humor that he proudly accepts the stereotype of the engineer while throwing the joking mouse in the trash.
summary: A talking mouse promises a prince and then cracks a pop-culture pun, but the unimpressed engineer holding it just bins it.

file: 1995/1995-02-08_3 days telecomuting_silent appreciation_being in office.gif
title: Telecommuting Day Three: Pen Games

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Day three of telecommuting: I spend the morning throwing my pen in the air.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The afternoon is spent in silent appreciation of how much better this is than being in the office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ahh

setting: Dilbert's home office, working from home in a bathrobe
situation: Dilbert, wearing a bathrobe at his home computer, spends his telecommuting morning tossing a pen in the air, and it eventually bounces off his forehead as he tips back in his chair. By the afternoon he has collapsed in a heap on the floor beside the toppled chair, content and relaxed.
punchline: Even a day of pointless pen-tossing and lying on the floor is preferable to being in the office, which implies how awful the office is.
summary: A man working from home in his robe fills his days with idle pen tricks and floor-lying bliss, finding it far better than the workplace he left behind.

file: 1995/1995-09-16_meets goal_quarter_save head_big imporvement_save money_haircut_double goal_less experinced_employees_business.gif
title: Boss Offers Head Shave Incentive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If the department meets its goal for the quarter you can shave my head!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be a big improvement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He's trying to save money on a haircut.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If we double our goal can we iron your shirt, too?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need some less experienced employees.

situation: The Boss promises his employees they can shave his head if the department meets its quarterly goal. Dilbert and Wally mock the offer, with Wally suggesting he just wants a free haircut, and Alice sarcastically asks whether doubling the goal would earn them the chance to iron his shirt. The Boss privately thinks he needs less experienced employees who wouldn't see through his cheap incentive.
punchline: The Boss's feeble reward is so transparently self-serving that his experienced staff ridicule it, leaving him wishing for naive workers who would be easier to manipulate.
summary: A manager dangles a silly personal favor as a reward for hitting targets, and his sharp-witted staff mock him until he longs for gullible underlings.

file: 1995/1995-10-06_captain dogbert_good news_bad news_hotting town early_actually hitting town_crash warning_corporate jet_ceo_dog_animals.gif
title: Captain Dogbert's Good News, Bad News

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Captain Dogbert with some good news and some bad news.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The good news is that we'll be hitting town ten minutes ahead of schedule...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The bad news is we'll be hitting town.

setting: Aboard and outside a passenger airplane in flight over hills
situation: Dogbert, acting as the pilot, makes a cheerful public-address announcement while the plane streaks toward a town. He first gives the good news of arriving early, then reveals the bad news is that the plane will literally hit the town. A lone passenger looks out a window as the plane approaches.
punchline: The pilot's 'hitting town' is a euphemism for arriving that turns out to mean crashing into it, making the early arrival a disaster.
summary: A dog piloting a plane gleefully announces an early arrival, then reveals the plane is about to slam into the town it is flying to.

file: 1995/1995-08-03_hired as temp_ratbert_cardboard box_main hallway_regular employees_status_security gurad_crud behind refrigerator_company car.gif
title: Ratbert's Temp Status Below Security Guard

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Congratulations on getting hired as a temp, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Where do I start?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your office is this cardboard box in the main hallway. The regular employees will not make eye contact or ask your name.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your status is roughly between the security guard and the crud behind the refrigerator.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Do I get a company car?

situation: Dilbert congratulates Ratbert on being hired as a temp, then explains the reality of the job. Ratbert's office is a cardboard box in the main hallway, and regular employees will ignore him. Dilbert ranks his status just above the crud behind the refrigerator, and Ratbert cheerfully asks whether he gets a company car.
punchline: Ratbert remains naively optimistic about perks like a company car even though he has just been told he ranks barely above filth in the office hierarchy.
summary: A newly hired temp learns his desk is a box and his standing is near the bottom, yet he hopes for executive perks.

file: 1995/1995-09-24_take a contract_please review_copies_original_cannot approve_obstruction of dogs_fits any situation_absurd logic.gif
title: Dogbert's Absurd Logic Contract Review

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to take a contract to our company lawyer. I need your help, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please review this contract. I need it today.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give me all of your copies plus the original. Then go away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't do it! He plans to lose them!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good dog!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dang!

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: I cannot approve this. Somebody might sue us for no good reason.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's true with any contract. Isn't he using absurd logic?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's find out.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Approve the contract now or I'll sue you for obstruction of dogs!!

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: Okay okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The great thing about absurd logic is that it fits any situation.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the company lawyer's office
situation: Dilbert needs a contract approved by the company lawyer the same day and enlists Dogbert as a reviewer. Dogbert demands all copies of the contract, which Dilbert fears he'll lose, then accompanies Dilbert to the lawyer. When the lawyer refuses to approve it on the flimsy grounds that someone might sue, Dogbert threatens to sue him for 'obstruction of dogs' and the lawyer immediately caves.
punchline: The lawyer's absurd reason for refusing is defeated by an even more absurd legal threat, proving that absurd logic works in any situation.
summary: A lawyer's ridiculous excuse for blocking a contract is beaten by Dogbert's even sillier lawsuit threat.

file: 1995/1995-11-09_saint dogbert_land of cubicles_demons_computer guru_data base concepts_monster_dispatched_actual code.gif
title: Saint Dogbert Slays the Guru

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Saint Dogbert enters the land of cubicles searching for the demons of stupidity.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Suddenly he finds an over-promoted computer guru spouting useless database concepts.

transcript.speaker: Computer Guru
transcript.text: You'd be fools to ignore the Boolean anti-binary least-square approach.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The monster is dispatched to the dark world by the sight of its most feared object.

transcript.speaker: Saint Dogbert
transcript.text: Look! Actual code!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cool!

setting: Office cubicle area and a conference room
situation: Dogbert, dressed as a saint with a gold mitre and wand, wanders the cubicle farm hunting for demons of stupidity. He finds a bearded, over-promoted computer guru in a meeting who is spouting nonsense database jargon. Dogbert holds up a sheet of actual code and the guru melts away, smoking, while an engineer reacts with delight.
punchline: The guru who deals only in meaningless buzzwords is destroyed by the one thing he fears: real, working code, which exposes that he has no practical skills.
summary: A saintly Dogbert vanquishes a jargon-spewing tech guru by waving a page of real programming in his face.

file: 1995/1995-11-11_undefined acronyms_lower opinion_communication skills_complex pictures.gif
title: Dilbert Admits Loving Complex Pictures

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This next transparency is an incomprehensible jumble of complexity and undefined acronyms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might wonder why I'm going to show it to you since the only possible result is to lower your opinion of my communication skills.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Frankly, it's because I like making complex pictures more than I like you.

setting: Conference room during a presentation using an overhead projector
situation: Dilbert is giving a presentation with an overhead projector and warns his audience that the next transparency is an incomprehensible jumble of complexity and undefined acronyms. He acknowledges it will make him look like a poor communicator, then points at a convoluted flowchart on the screen and explains why he is showing it anyway.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly admits he is inflicting a confusing diagram on his audience because he enjoys making complex pictures more than he cares about the people watching.
summary: A presenter cheerfully confesses that he will subject his audience to a baffling diagram simply because he prefers drawing it to respecting them.

file: 1995/1995-09-19_new company slogan_act like you own the comapny_fired marketing dept_security escort.gif
tags: act like you own the comapny
title: Acting Like You Own It

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm happy to report that I have embraced the new company slogan "Act like you own the company."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This morning I fired the marketing department and had security escort them out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not exactly what we had in mind...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fortunately I anticipated your reaction.

situation: At a meeting, Wally announces he has taken the new company slogan to heart. To prove it, he fired the entire marketing department and had security walk them out. When the Boss objects that this wasn't the intent, Wally says he saw the reaction coming.
punchline: Wally takes a motivational slogan far too literally and, anticipating blame, covers himself by claiming he foresaw the Boss's objection, implying he's already prepared to dodge consequences.
summary: A worker takes an empowerment slogan to a ridiculous extreme by dismissing a whole department, then shrugs off the fallout in advance.
keywords: act like you own the company

file: 1995/1995-03-20_human resources_down sizing_acts like a freind_misery of people_bat your head_business.gif
title: Catbert, Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a new director of human resources to handle the downsizing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I needed somebody who acts like a friend but secretly delights in the misery of all people.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need to talk, Paul. But first I'm going to bat your head around and scratch you.

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Hee hee!! That's so cute!

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and a cubicle
situation: The Boss explains to Dogbert that he has hired a new Director of Human Resources to carry out downsizing, someone who seems friendly but secretly enjoys everyone's misery. The new director turns out to be Catbert, who confronts an employee named Paul about a serious talk, then bats and scratches him while Paul laughs, charmed.
punchline: Paul is so taken in by the cat's cute, friendly act that he doesn't realize he's being abused and is about to be laid off.
summary: A manager introduces his cuddly new HR chief, an evil cat who cheerfully torments a charmed employee before delivering layoff news.

file: 1995/1995-11-15_accomplishment_this week_agent of change_foster and reward_culture_team work_slightly cynical.gif
title: Dilbert Admits Growing More Cynical

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: My accomplishment this week is that I've become an agent of change.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I foster and reward those behaviors that contribute to a culture of teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've become slightly more cynical.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Keep up the good work, buddy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pat pat

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: At a meeting, a bald coworker boasts about becoming an agent of change and fostering teamwork, using full management jargon. Dilbert then reports his own accomplishment: he has become slightly more cynical. The coworker cheerfully pats him on the back and encourages him to keep it up.
punchline: The coworker is so wrapped up in buzzwords that he praises Dilbert's growing cynicism as a positive accomplishment, oblivious to the fact that it is a criticism of the workplace.
summary: Surrounded by gushing management-speak at a status meeting, Dilbert offers a gloomy confession that gets mistaken for progress.

file: 1995/1995-04-01_write objectives_sculpt disparate pieces_elegant tapestry_business plan_clay tapestry_quote boss_clueless.gif
title: Clay Tapestry Business Plan Metaphor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each of you will write your objectives and give them to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I will sculpt these disparate pieces of clay into an elegant tapestry which will be our business plan.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Our business plan will be like a clay tapestry?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Feel free to quote me.

situation: The Boss tells his team to submit their objectives, which he will then shape into a business plan. He describes the process as sculpting clay into a tapestry, mixing two incompatible crafts. When Carol points out the absurdity, he proudly invites her to quote him.
punchline: The Boss is so pleased with his nonsensical mixed metaphor that he mistakes Carol's incredulous question for admiration and encourages her to repeat it.
summary: A manager waxes poetic about turning his staff's goals into a masterpiece, but his garbled artistic comparison makes no sense, and he is delighted anyway.

file: 1995/1995-09-27_results_audit_untrained_highly skilled_liars_passed audit_success.gif
title: Passing the Audit by Lying

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here are the results of my ISO 9000 audit of your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your employees are largely untrained and - I couldn't help notice - fairly unattractive.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: However, they are also highly skilled liars, so you passed the audit easily.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We succeed where it counts!!!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, delivers the results of an ISO 9000 quality audit to the Boss. He reports that the employees are untrained and unattractive, but that they are skilled enough at lying to pass the audit with ease. The Boss cheerfully celebrates the result.
punchline: The company passes its quality certification not through real quality or training but through its employees' talent for deception, and the Boss proudly takes this as a genuine success.
summary: A consultant's audit report praises the staff only for being excellent fibbers, and the delighted manager treats the passing grade as a triumph.

file: 1995/1995-07-15_study options_project zebra_make recommendations.gif
title: Translating the Boss's Vague Request

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to study our options for project "Zebra" and make a recommendation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss (thought)
transcript.text: Translation: "Read my mind then recommend the option I've already decided on."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll get right on it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Translation: "I am doomed. I will go look for naughty pictures on the Internet instead."

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to study the options for Project Zebra and make a recommendation. Thought bubbles reveal that the Boss really wants Dilbert to guess the decision he has already made. Dilbert cheerfully agrees but privately concludes the task is hopeless and plans to browse inappropriate content online instead.
punchline: Since the boss has already made his decision, the 'study' is a guessing game Dilbert can't win, so he gives up and slacks off online.
summary: A manager's request for an open-ended analysis is secretly a demand to guess his preselected answer, so the employee resigns himself to goofing off.

file: 1995/1995-08-30_brittle writer_thelma and louise_bad drivers_not offended_three stooges_all documentraies_men.gif
title: Dogbert Provokes Tina With Movie Questions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert tweaks Tina the brittle tech writer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What do you think of the movie "Thelma and Louise"?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I know what you're trying to say. You think all women are bad drivers. That's really the point of the movie, isn't it??

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: If you're not offended yet, tune in tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The "Three Stooges"?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Why are ALL of the documentaries about MEN??!

situation: Dogbert, perched on her desk, asks Tina what she thinks of the movie "Thelma and Louise." She angrily accuses him of implying that women are bad drivers. When Dogbert later asks about the "Three Stooges," she explodes again, now ranting that all documentaries are about men.
punchline: Tina is so quick to take offense that she reads sexist insinuations into innocent questions, and Dogbert exploits this by barely saying anything to set her off.
summary: A touchy coworker finds insult in every harmless movie question posed by a mischievous dog, who barely has to try to provoke her.

file: 1995/1995-04-07_improve career_ceo_refer first name_recent meeting_rule_iron fist_funny dog.gif
title: Name-Dropping the CEO Career Trick

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try this little trick to improve your career...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Anytime you want something your way, simply refer to your CEO by his first name and say he gave you directions during your very recent meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's totally unverifiable. People will fear you and do as you say. You'll rule with an iron fist!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're a funny little dog.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch at home
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert and offers a career tip: invoke the CEO by his first name and claim he personally gave you instructions in a recent meeting. Because nobody can check the claim, people will obey out of fear. Dilbert dismisses the idea as the quirky thinking of a funny little dog.
punchline: Dogbert is describing a bluff that would work perfectly in a real corporation, and Dilbert dismissively treats it as a joke without recognizing how true it is.
summary: Dogbert coaches Dilbert on bluffing his way to power by falsely citing the boss of bosses, and Dilbert brushes it off as cute nonsense.

file: 1995/1995-10-18_smell bad_perfume_killing people_cpr_let me die_dogbert_woman_bad perfume.gif
title: Dogbert Confronts Deadly Perfume Wearer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have failed in my attempt to subtly tell you that your perfume is killing people. I will try a direct approach.
