transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey!! You smell bad!!! B-a-a-a-d!!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Should I give you CPR?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No-o-o-o!! Let me die!!

situation: Dogbert, wearing a gas mask, stands on a desk and explains that his subtle hints about a coworker's overpowering perfume have failed. He then shouts at her that she smells bad. When he collapses from the fumes, she kindly offers him CPR and he begs to be left to die.
punchline: The perfume is so overpowering that Dogbert would rather die than be revived by her, which means her well-meaning offer of mouth-to-mouth would only expose him to more of the smell.
summary: A gas-masked dog bluntly tells a coworker her perfume is lethal, then faints and refuses her offer of rescue.

file: 1995/1995-03-10_performance this year_tasks_tiny raise_boss asigned_bonus_keeping salaries low_workplace violence.gif
title: Blaming Dilbert for Boss's Assignments

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your performance this year was good, but you worked on tasks that aren't important. Therefore you get a tiny raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked on the tasks YOU assigned. What's that say about YOUR performance?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's excellent. I get a bonus for keeping salaries low.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you seen any literature on workplace violence?

setting: The Boss's office during an annual performance review
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert his performance was good but he worked on unimportant tasks, so he gets only a tiny raise. Dilbert points out that the tasks were assigned by the Boss himself. The Boss cheerfully admits that his own performance is excellent because he earns a bonus for keeping salaries low, prompting Dilbert to ask about workplace violence literature.
punchline: The Boss is rewarded for the very thing that shortchanges Dilbert, and Dilbert responds with a veiled threat by asking whether the Boss has read about workplace violence.
summary: A manager docks an employee's raise for doing unimportant work he assigned himself, then gleefully admits he's paid to suppress wages, drawing a menacing remark.

file: 1995/1995-05-03_sex after marriage_depraved practice_liberals_headaches_fatigue_become consultants_extinction of mankind_right winger.gif
title: Dogbert's Talk Radio Marriage Rant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today we're talking about sex after marriage. Many liberals support this depraved practice but I do not.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It can lead to headaches, fatigue and unwanted family members who become consultants.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: "Wouldn't your philosophy lead to the extinction of mankind?"

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Cry me a river, liberal.

setting: A radio studio where Dogbert hosts a talk show at a desk with a microphone
situation: Dogbert, acting as a conservative radio talk show host, condemns sex after marriage as a depraved practice supported by liberals. He lists its downsides, including unwanted relatives who become consultants. A caller on the speaker points out that his philosophy would end mankind, and Dogbert dismisses the caller as a whining liberal.
punchline: Dogbert parodies partisan talk radio by making an absurd argument and then brushing off a valid logical objection by labeling the caller a liberal instead of answering it.
summary: A canine radio pundit rails against marital intimacy for its side effects, then waves away a caller's sound objection with a partisan insult.

file: 1995/1995-12-07_ignored recommendations_inadequate_make system work_saving money_get fired.gif
title: Boss Profits From Dilbert's Firing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, you ignored my recommendation and bought a low-cost system that's totally inadequate...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You compensated for this blunder by making it part of MY objectives to make the system work...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll get a bonus for saving money. I'll get fired, thus saving more money and earning you ANOTHER bonus.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm on a roll.

situation: Dilbert confronts the Boss, who ignored his recommendation and bought a cheap, inadequate system. Dilbert realizes the Boss made the system's success one of Dilbert's own objectives, so he will take the blame when it fails. He lays out how the Boss collects a bonus for saving money and another when Dilbert is fired.
punchline: The oblivious Boss, rather than being embarrassed by Dilbert's accurate accusation, cheerfully agrees he's on a roll, since he profits from both the bad purchase and Dilbert's firing.
summary: Dilbert spells out how his boss's bad purchasing decision will earn the boss two bonuses at Dilbert's expense, and the boss happily takes the compliment.

file: 1995/1995-03-12_draft documentation_get soon_lowly tech writer_big important engineer_fruit of labor_validate_value on planet_blank pages_bluffing for months.gif
title: Tech Writer's Blank Pages Revenge

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: Did you review my draft documentation yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... I'll get to it soon.

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: That's what you've been saying since July!!

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: I know I'm only a lowly technical writer and you're a big important engineer...

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: But is it too much to ask for you to glance at the fruits of my labors?!!!

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: Five lousy minutes is all it would take to validate my value on this planet! Read it, you fetid pile of compost!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, okay! I'll read it right now!

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: These pages are blank! You've been bluffing for months!

transcript.speaker: Tech Writer
transcript.text: I think I'll go have a yummy compost salad with delicious fetid cheese.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to look up those words.

situation: A technical writer repeatedly asks Dilbert, an engineer, to review her draft documentation and finally loses her temper, berating him. When he reluctantly reads it, she reveals the pages were blank all along and that he has been bluffing for months. She exits with a deliberately odd insult, leaving him to look up the words.
punchline: The writer proved Dilbert never read her documentation by handing him blank pages, and her elaborate insult goes over his head, showing he's both lazy and not as smart as he pretends.
summary: A fed-up documentation writer exposes an engineer's procrastination by giving him empty pages to review, then insults him with words he doesn't understand.

file: 1995/1995-09-29_alice sits boss_approve expense voucher_creature_eats snacks_security guard_problem.gif
title: Alice Demands Snack Thief Be Slain

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alice sits in for the Boss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I will approve your expense voucher on one condition.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You must slay the creature who stalks the office at night and eats our hidden snacks!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It has to be either you or the security guard.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Slay him first and see if the problem stops.

setting: Office, Alice sitting at the Boss's desk
situation: Alice is filling in for the Boss and wears a crown while holding Dilbert's expense voucher hostage. She orders him to slay the creature that sneaks into the office at night and eats hidden snacks. Dilbert, holding a baseball bat, reasons the culprit must be either himself or the security guard, and Alice tells him to kill the guard first and see if the snack theft stops.
punchline: Alice's absurd, power-drunk logic treats murdering the security guard as a reasonable trial-and-error troubleshooting step for missing snacks.
summary: Temporarily in charge, Alice makes a reimbursement contingent on a violent hunt for a midnight snack thief and casually suggests starting with the security guard.

file: 1995/1995-07-14_business cards_full title_director_product enhancemnets_acronym dope_product ehancement.gif
title: Boss's Title Acronym Spells DOPE

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, the next time you order my business cards, spell out my full title: "Director of Product Enhancements."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't use the acronym "DOPE."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I didn't know you were the Director of Product Enhancements.

setting: Office, at Carol's desk outside the Boss's office
situation: The Boss hands his business card to his secretary Carol and instructs her to print his full job title on future cards rather than the acronym. He specifically warns her not to use the acronym "DOPE." Carol deadpans that she only now realizes what his title is.
punchline: By forbidding the acronym, the Boss makes Carol notice that his title abbreviates to "DOPE," and she sarcastically implies the acronym fits him perfectly.
summary: A vain manager tries to hide an embarrassing job-title abbreviation, only to have his assistant slyly point out that she gets the joke.

file: 1995/1995-12-13_modem_not right_wrong interface_commission_pays dollar_per customer.gif
title: Commissioned Salesman Insults Modem Shopper

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: No, you fool. That modem will never fit your need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The specs look okay.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You're an idiot compared to me! Put that down! It's the wrong interface! The wrong interface!!!

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Rrrr

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is he on commission?

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Yeah, he pays us a dollar per customer.

situation: Dilbert browses modems on a store shelf while an aggressive salesman insults him and insists the modem he picked is the wrong interface. The salesman ends up tackling Dilbert from behind to stop him buying it. Dilbert asks the cashier whether the salesman works on commission and learns the salesman actually pays the store for each customer.
punchline: The salesman's behavior is explained by a backwards commission deal: he pays the store a dollar per customer, so he is desperate to be the one who gets to serve every shopper.
summary: A zealous store clerk physically restrains a shopper from buying a modem, and it turns out the clerk pays his employer for each customer he handles.

file: 1995/1995-08-12_dropped everything_career plan development_artificial emergency_ping pong ball_fax.gif
title: Career Plan Mocks Artificial Emergencies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you requested, I dropped everything and wrote my career development plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I plan to bounce from one artificial emergency to another, like a ping-pong ball in a clothes dryer, until one day I resign.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here I'm using humor to make a point...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fax this to HR now!!

situation: Dilbert hands his boss the career development plan he was asked to write, after dropping all his other work to do it. The plan sarcastically describes his career as bouncing between manufactured crises until he quits. The Boss misses the humor and the point and panics, ordering Dilbert to fax it to HR immediately.
punchline: The Boss responds to a plan criticizing his habit of creating artificial emergencies by creating another artificial emergency, demanding the document be faxed to HR right now.
summary: A sarcastic career plan about endless manufactured crises is answered with yet another urgent, manufactured crisis.

file: 1995/1995-07-11_saint dogbert_stale overused jokes_information super highway_roadkill_super highway.gif
title: Saint Dogbert Smites Superhighway Jokes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am Saint Dogbert. I have come to drive out the stale and overused jokes about the information super-highway.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Sometimes I feel like roadkill on the information superhighway!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't make me come over there!

situation: Dogbert, wearing a yellow miter and holding a small mallet, announces himself as Saint Dogbert at a meeting table, there to banish tired jokes about the information superhighway. A man at the table immediately makes the very roadkill joke he was warned against. Dogbert threatens to come over, and the man ends up knocked over backwards with his feet in the air and stars flying.
punchline: Despite a clear warning against clichéd information superhighway jokes, the man tells one anyway and is violently punished by Dogbert.
summary: A self-appointed saint of comedy enforces a ban on worn-out tech clichés with a mallet when a coworker ignores the warning.
keywords: don't make me come over there

file: 1995/1995-02-04_assignments by priority_won't waste time_unimportant stuff_a priority_personal life_must do_b priorities.gif
title: Everything Is A Priority Except Life

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ranked all of your assignments by priority so you won't waste time on unimportant stuff.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything is an "A" priority except for "personal life."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm still working on the list of "must do" "B" priorities.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a sheet of paper on which he has ranked all of Dilbert's assignments by priority. Dilbert reads that every work task is rated top priority, with only his personal life ranked lower. Dilbert remarks that this helps a lot, and the Boss cheerfully says he is still compiling a list of the must-do B priorities.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic thanks highlights that a priority list where everything is top priority is useless, and the Boss's cheerful reply shows he hasn't noticed and is even planning to add a second tier of 'must do' items.
summary: A manager proudly hands over a ranking of tasks that labels every work item as the highest priority and treats the employee's private life as the only thing that can wait.

file: 1995/1995-08-15_dehumanization_invisible to humans_fix_wear a bag_perfect solution_hear you.gif
title: Invisible Dilbert Needs a Bag

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The dehumanization of my job has rendered me invisible to humans. Only you can see me, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can we fix this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could wear a bag on your head when you're around me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not the fix I had in mind.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's not a perfect solution. I'd still be able to hear you.

situation: Dilbert complains to Dogbert that the dehumanizing nature of his job has made him invisible to other people, and that only Dogbert can still see him. He asks how to fix this, and Dogbert suggests Dilbert wear a bag over his head around Dogbert, which is not what Dilbert meant.
punchline: Dogbert's 'fix' is to hide Dilbert from the one being who can still see him, and he coolly admits the flaw is only that he could still hear Dilbert, showing his total lack of empathy.
summary: After lamenting that his soul-crushing job has made him unseen by everyone but his dog, Dilbert gets a deadpan suggestion that makes him even less visible.

file: 1995/1995-12-22_business plans fail_realistic goal_manage spectacular failures_promoted first_most cycnical.gif
title: Failure Gets You Promoted First

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Most business plans fail. Obviously, success is not a realistic goal.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But the people who manage the most spectacular failures get promoted first because of their experience.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is the most cynical thing I've ever heard in my life!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks. I'm blushing.

setting: Living room, with Dilbert and Dogbert sitting on a couch
situation: Dogbert lectures Dilbert on how business really works, claiming most business plans fail and that success is an unrealistic goal. He adds that those who oversee the biggest failures are promoted first because of their experience. Dilbert is appalled at the cynicism, and Dogbert takes it as a compliment.
punchline: Dogbert treats Dilbert's outraged accusation of cynicism as praise, implying that the cynical view of corporate promotion is simply accurate.
summary: Dogbert explains to a horrified Dilbert that corporate advancement rewards those who preside over epic flops, then happily accepts being called cynical.

file: 1995/1995-12-09_inexplicable_low cost_system_underpowered_replace_another vendors_upgrade fees_big a fool_lease option.gif
title: Underpowered System, Outrageous Upgrade Fees

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's inexplicable, but the low-cost system I sold you seems to be woefully underpowered.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could replace it with another vendor's system, thus showing everybody you made a mistake. Or you can pay my outrageous upgrade fees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How big a fool do you think I am?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I won't know until I see if you go for the lease option.

setting: Office meeting table where Dogbert, acting as a vendor or consultant, meets with the Boss
situation: Dogbert, who sold the Boss a cheap computer system, admits it is underpowered and offers him two bad choices: replace it with a competitor's product and admit his mistake, or pay Dogbert's inflated upgrade fees. The Boss indignantly asks how foolish Dogbert thinks he is, and Dogbert says he will find out by seeing whether the Boss takes the lease option.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately sold a cheap, inadequate system to lock the Boss into expensive upgrades, and he is now measuring the Boss's gullibility by whether he falls for yet another costly deal.
summary: A scheming salesdog traps his gullible client between embarrassment and extortionate fees, then uses the client's next decision to gauge just how gullible he is.

file: 1995/1995-01-17_volume of work_quiet leadership_inspires us_promote_manager_work ethic_use documents_heat house_job offering_writing.gif
title: Promotion Offered, Papers Burned for Heat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've all noticed the volume of work you carry around. Your quiet leadership inspires us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to promote you to manager so you can imbue others with your work ethic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does he know you use the documents to heat our house?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. And I asked him to put the job offer in writing.

situation: The Boss praises Dilbert for the huge stacks of paper he carries around and offers him a promotion to manager so he can inspire others. At home, Dogbert asks whether the boss knows Dilbert actually burns those documents in the fireplace to heat the house. Dilbert says no, and that he has asked for the job offer in writing, presumably so he can burn that too.
punchline: Dilbert's apparent hard work is just a stash of paper he carries around as fuel for his fireplace, so the promotion rewards a fake work ethic, and he plans to burn the written offer as well.
summary: A manager rewards an employee's impressive paper piles with a promotion, unaware they are just firewood for his home.

file: 1995/1995-07-09_person_project_headcount_contract employee_buy a computer_over budget_renting expensive_wally_16 hour days_boss thinks genius_project cancelled.gif
title: Boss Cancels Project, Dilbert Works Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We desperately need another person on my project!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're already over headcount. Get a contract employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but they cost twice as much.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plus we need to buy a computer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Rent one. We're over our capital budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Renting is expensive. We'll go over our expense budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll fire Wally. That will free up some cash.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally's on my project!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Forget it! I'll just work sixteen hours a day!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That worked out perfectly. I think I might be a genius or something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if I should have told him the project was cancelled last week.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for another person on his project, and the boss rejects each request in turn: headcount, then a contract employee, then a computer purchase, then a rental. When the boss threatens to fire Wally to free up cash, Dilbert gives up and offers to work sixteen hours a day himself. The boss smugly congratulates himself, then privately wonders whether he should have mentioned that the project was cancelled last week.
punchline: The boss manipulates Dilbert into volunteering for unpaid overtime on a project that was already cancelled, and the boss never bothered to tell him.
summary: A manager stonewalls every resource request until his engineer agrees to overwork himself, all for a project that no longer exists.

file: 1995/1995-10-11_how to program_build gui_object oriented_pronounced gooey_gun object_blast bug_hall object.gif
title: Gooey GUI Object-Oriented Game Demo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, just show me how to program so I can help out on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're going to build a "G.U.I." using object-oriented development tools...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: G.U.I. is pronounced "gooey."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I used my gun object to blast the bug object in the hall object!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Notice how gooey it is.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert and Wally to teach him programming so he can help on their project. They explain that he will build a G.U.I. with object-oriented tools, and Wally notes the acronym is pronounced 'gooey.' The Boss seems to have taken the 'object' idea literally, announcing that his gun object blasted a bug object in the hall object, and Wally points out how gooey the result is.
punchline: The Boss misunderstands object-oriented programming as a violent video game scenario, and Wally deadpans that the messy result is literally 'gooey,' playing on the GUI pronunciation.
summary: A clueless manager gets a crash course in programming and turns it into a bug-splattering shooter, proving the acronym's pronunciation right.

file: 1995/1995-11-17_sql data base_trade magazine_data base_color_mauve.gif
title: Mauve Database Has Most RAM

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think we should build an SQL database.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does he understand what he said or is it something he saw in a trade magazine ad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What color do you want that database?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think mauve has the most RAM.

situation: The Boss announces that the team should build an SQL database, and Dilbert wonders whether his boss actually understands the term or just read it in a trade magazine ad. Dilbert tests him by asking what color he wants the database to be. The Boss seriously answers that mauve has the most RAM.
punchline: The Boss's nonsensical answer, that a color determines memory capacity, proves he has no idea what a database is and was just parroting a buzzword.
summary: A manager's technical-sounding request is exposed as empty jargon when he picks a database's color based on its supposed memory.

file: 1995/1995-03-23_sell comapny_very discriminating_hate people_laws to protect_lazy but funny.gif
title: Selling Company to Discriminating Buyers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to sell the company for a huge profit. I found some very discriminating buyers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When you say discriminating, you mean...?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They hate people from this country.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's okay. We have laws to protect us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're lazy, but at least they're funny!

transcript.speaker: Buyers
transcript.text: Hee hee.

setting: Office, in front of a desk where Dogbert stands
situation: Dogbert, acting as the company's decision-maker, announces he is selling the company for a huge profit to very 'discriminating' buyers. When the employees ask what that means, he reveals the buyers hate people from this country. Dilbert reassures everyone that laws will protect them, and the buyers are shown in tall hats and long beards, with Dogbert quipping that they're lazy but funny.
punchline: The staff take comfort in anti-discrimination laws, while Dogbert's reply implies the buyers are undeterred, and his remark about them being lazy but funny reverses the usual stereotype jokes with a sarcastic jab.
summary: A dog in charge unloads the firm onto prejudiced purchasers, and the staff's faith in legal protection is met with a flippant shrug.

file: 1995/1995-06-28_benchmarked_five world class companies_comparisons_irrelevant_industries_potato chip_develop software_oil chips.gif
title: Benchmarking Against Potato Chip Makers

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: As you requested, I benchmarked our company against five world-class companies.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The comparisons are irrelevant because we're in different industries. But that didn't stop me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can they make a potato chip in one second but it takes us months to develop software?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I think they oil the chips.

situation: Carol presents the results of a benchmarking study the Boss requested, comparing their company to five world-class firms. She admits the comparisons are meaningless because the companies are in different industries. The Boss ignores this and asks why potato chips can be made in a second while software takes months.
punchline: The Boss draws a nonsensical conclusion from an irrelevant benchmark, and Carol responds with an equally absurd, deadpan answer rather than correcting him.
summary: A manager takes a flawed industry comparison at face value and demands to know why software can't be produced as fast as snack food.

file: 1995/1995-02-27_excellence in teaming_nearly ready_complete buy in_make decsions_squirrel migration patterns.gif
title: Teaming Study Becomes Squirrel Discussion

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm happy to report that the "Excellence in Teaming" read-out is nearly ready.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's taken forty people from a dozen departments to complete the study. We finally got complete buy-in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that the study of why we can't make decisions?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Originally. But it evolved into more of a discussion of squirrel migration patterns.

situation: A cheerful coworker presents the nearly finished results of an 'Excellence in Teaming' study that needed forty people from a dozen departments. Dilbert asks whether it is the study of why the company can't make decisions. The coworker admits it was, but it drifted into a discussion of squirrel migration patterns.
punchline: A huge group effort meant to explain organizational indecisiveness itself got derailed into an irrelevant topic, showing the group is too indecisive to stay on task.
summary: A big cross-department study on why the company can't decide things ends up wandering off into talk about squirrels.

file: 1995/1995-12-14_secretary_epiphany_lowest pais_job title_seniorassoicate_clerical_mistaken.gif
title: Senior Associate Realizes She's Secretary

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Wait-a-minute... I'm starting to realize something.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: My job title is Senior Associate, yet I spend my time doing clerical work... and unless I'm mistaken, I'm the lowest paid employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this a bad time?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Aaagh!! I'm a secretary!

situation: Tina, sitting at her desk, gradually works out that despite her grand job title of Senior Associate she does clerical work and earns the least of anyone. Dilbert stands nearby holding papers and politely asks if he's caught her at a bad moment as she erupts in distress.
punchline: A fancy job title was masking the fact that she is simply a poorly paid secretary, and her sudden realization is so dramatic that Dilbert's polite question is an understatement.
summary: A woman with an impressive title connects the dots about her actual duties and pay and has a meltdown when she grasps what she really is.

file: 1995/1995-04-17_financial advisor_invest_dogcart deferred earnings_fund_conflict of interest_client_interest.gif
title: Dogbert's Conflict of Interest Fund

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going into business as a financial advisor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds hard.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's easy. I'll tell all my clients to invest in the "Dogbert Deferred Earnings Fund."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that a conflict of interest?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only if I show interest in the client.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert on the couch using a laptop
situation: Dogbert announces he is becoming a financial advisor and explains that his plan is to steer all his clients into his own investment fund. Dilbert points out that this is a conflict of interest. Dogbert replies that it only counts as one if he cares about the client.
punchline: Dogbert twists the phrase 'conflict of interest' into a literal pun, claiming it only applies if he shows interest in the client, which makes his self-serving fund acceptable because he has no concern for them.
summary: A scheming dog plans to enrich himself by pushing customers into his own fund and dismisses an ethics objection with a wordplay dodge.

file: 1995/1995-07-02_new co - op employee_no pay_free_gain experience_pig project_paper towel guy_spills cofee_throw body_fire in the hole_tea_body throw.gif
title: Unpaid Co-op Becomes Human Paper Towel

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you all to meet our new co-op employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't pay him. He works for free to gain valuable job experience.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of the PTG project!

transcript.speaker: Co-op Employee
transcript.text: Wow! What is it?!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: PTG stands for "Paper Towel Guy."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: If somebody spills coffee it's your job to throw your body on it before it reaches one of us.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Oops

transcript.speaker: Co-op Employee
transcript.text: Fire in the hole!!!

transcript.speaker: Co-op Employee
transcript.text: How'd I do?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Not so good, kid. That was tea.

situation: The Boss introduces an unpaid co-op employee and eagerly assigns him to the 'PTG project'. Carol explains that it stands for 'Paper Towel Guy', meaning he must throw his body over any spill. When Carol spills a drink, he dives onto the table, only to learn it was tea rather than coffee.
punchline: The unpaid intern is exploited as a human paper towel, and after sacrificing himself he is only criticized for misidentifying the spilled liquid.
summary: A free intern is given a humiliating job soaking up spills with his own body and is then faulted for diving at the wrong beverage.

file: 1995/1995-09-17_calls friends_erases disc drives_fix the bugs_glitter_network_premier software_six months_software_quickprotect_swears at you_engineering.gif
title: Marketing Hypes Destructive Backup Software

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: It's time for marketing to put the glitter on this software you've created.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: With my guidance this will become the premier data backup software!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bear in mind that we said it would take six months to write it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You only gave us a month.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: We'll fix the bugs in the next release.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Tell me about the features.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At this point all it does is erase your disk drive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unless you're on a network.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: What happens if you're on a network?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It erases everybody's disk drives.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And heaven help you if you have a modem...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It calls all your friends and erases their PCs.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: We'll call it "QuikProtect."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you have a sound card it swears at you.

setting: Office meeting room or desk with a computer
situation: A marketing manager announces she will add glitter to the engineers' software and make it the premier data backup product. Dilbert and Wally point out the rushed schedule, then reveal the software only erases disk drives, spreads over networks and modems, and swears through sound cards. The manager cheerfully decides to market it as "QuikProtect."
punchline: Marketing is ready to sell a rushed, destructive virus-like program as a backup product, proving that the name and hype matter more than whether the software works.
summary: Engineers confess their hastily written backup program is actually a data-destroying menace, and marketing happily gives it a reassuring brand name anyway.

file: 1995/1995-09-20_technical support_gullible_optimistic_buy something_human being.gif
title: Phone Menu Mocks Desperate Callers

transcript.speaker: Phone voice
transcript.text: Press "one" for sales. Press "two" in a hopeless effort to get technical support.

transcript.speaker: Phone voice
transcript.text: Press "one" for answers to questions you don't have. Press "two" if you're gullible and optimistic.

transcript.speaker: Phone voice
transcript.text: Press "two" if you're willing to buy something just so you can talk to a human being ...

setting: Dilbert's desk at the office, with a computer and a phone
situation: Dilbert holds a phone and repeatedly presses "2" while an automated voice menu lists options for sales and technical support. Each menu choice is more insulting to the caller than the last. By the third panel Dilbert has a mallet in hand, apparently so frustrated that he is ready to hit himself on the head.
punchline: The automated phone system openly admits that the only way to reach a real person is to pretend to be a sales customer, mocking how hard it is to get actual tech support.
summary: A cynical automated phone menu taunts a persistent caller while he tries in vain to reach a live support person.

file: 1995/1995-12-15_certain religions_rid of egos_perform pointless tasks.gif
title: Bowing to the Boss's Ego

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I read somewhere that certain religions require their initiates to perform pointless never-ending tasks to rid them of their egos.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) What now?

situation: Wally explains to Dilbert that some religions make initiates do pointless, never-ending tasks to strip away their egos. The two then walk to the Boss's office and bow low over his desk. The Boss, leaning back in his chair, wonders what they want now.
punchline: Wally and Dilbert treat their pointless work as a spiritual ego-purging ritual, and their deferential bowing leaves the Boss baffled about what they are up to.
summary: After musing about ego-destroying religious rituals, two employees approach their manager's desk and bow, leaving him suspicious.

file: 1995/1995-07-26_proposed work_plan_stress test_product_network conditions_accomplish_downloading_large image files_servers_on net_naughty pictures.gif
title: Stress-Testing Network With Naughty Pictures

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My proposed work plan for the year is to stress-test our product under severe network conditions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I will accomplish this by downloading large image files from the busiest servers on the net.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was THIS close to making it my job to download naughty pictures.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's just as well; I would have had to kill you.

setting: Conference room during a work-planning meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally hands in his proposed annual work plan, which involves stress-testing the product by downloading huge image files from the busiest servers on the net. After the paperwork is passed along, he admits to Dilbert that he nearly made downloading naughty pictures his official job. Dilbert says it's lucky he didn't, since he would have had to kill him.
punchline: Wally's legitimate-sounding 'stress test' is a thin cover for getting paid to download porn, and he nearly pulled it off, which would have infuriated his hard-working colleague.
summary: A slacker coworker pitches an official-sounding plan that sounds suspiciously like a license to surf for racy pictures, and a colleague is relieved he didn't go through with it.

file: 1995/1995-10-01_desired salary_million dollars_how much expected_misleading_salary_fantasy layered_little shoulder massge_15 %_money.gif
title: Dilbert's Honest Salary Expectations Interview

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wish me luck, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you get more luck, wouldn't there be less luck available for me?

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: For "desired salary" you wrote "one million dollars."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, thanks for asking.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Perhaps the question is misleading. The application should have asked what salary you expect.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh... well, I expect you'll hire somebody more qualified and my salary will remain unchanged.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: No, too honest. I'm looking for something close to reality, with maybe twenty-percent fantasy layered on top.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... I'd like a fifteen-percent raise and a little shoulder massage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does it seem that I'm the only honest guy on Earth?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your type tends not to reproduce.

setting: A job interview in an office, then back at Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert goes to a job interview where the interviewer questions the one-million-dollar desired salary he wrote on the application. When he honestly says he expects someone more qualified to get the job, she rejects that as too honest and asks for something close to reality with some fantasy layered on top. He then asks for a raise and a shoulder massage, and later complains to Dogbert about being the only honest person.
punchline: Dogbert quips that honest people like Dilbert tend not to reproduce, implying that honesty is a losing strategy, in work and in life.
summary: A candidate learns that candor about pay is punished in hiring, then gets a cynical lesson from his dog about why honest people don't get ahead.

file: 1995/1995-06-15_lacking clerical support_highly trained_paid professionals_copier_analytical sklills_mindless_toner_five minutes.gif
title: Professionals Waiting at the Copier

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lacking clerical support, the highly trained, highly paid professionals line up at the copier.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Their amazing analytical skills are squandered in this mindless task.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No... it looks like the "toner" light doesn't turn off if you wait.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's give it another five minutes.

situation: Dilbert and Wally stand waiting at the copier with papers in hand because there is no clerical staff to do the copying. Dilbert narrates in thought bubbles how their expensive talents are wasted on a mindless chore. Wally then reports that the toner light stays on no matter how long they wait, and Dilbert proposes waiting five more minutes anyway.
punchline: Despite their supposedly amazing analytical skills, the engineers stubbornly wait for a toner warning to fix itself, showing they are no better at solving a trivial problem.
summary: Two skilled employees without support staff idle at a copier, and their lofty self-assessment collapses when they cannot figure out a simple warning light.

file: 1995/1995-05-19_assets ratio_boost_security department_brisk redcution_joking_den.gif
title: Eliminate Security, Furnish My Den

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to boost our return-on-assets ratio.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's eliminate the security department. That would cut expenses while allowing for a brisk reduction in assets.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When are you planning to tell him you were joking?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: After I furnish my den.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, then the hallway
situation: The Boss tells his staff in a meeting that they need to improve the company's return-on-assets ratio. Wally proposes eliminating the security department so the company can quickly reduce its assets. Afterward Dilbert asks when Wally will admit he was joking, and Wally says he will wait until he has furnished his den.
punchline: Wally's 'joke' is actually a scheme to carry off the soon-to-be-unguarded company assets for his own home, so he will only confess once he has furnished his den with them.
summary: A throwaway suggestion to scrap the guards turns out to be a plan to loot the office for home decor.

file: 1995/1995-11-24_bath towels_cleanest object_get clean_shower_take showers_towels get clean.gif
title: Wally's Towel Washing Theory

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't understand why some people wash their bath towels.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When I get out of the shower I'm the cleanest object in my house. In theory, those towels should be getting cleaner every time they touch me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe I could hug you every day so I don't need to take showers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are towels supposed to bend?

situation: Dilbert, Alice and Wally eat lunch together while Wally explains that he sees no reason to wash bath towels, since he is the cleanest thing in his house when he uses them. Alice sarcastically suggests she could hug him daily to avoid showering. Wally responds by asking if towels are supposed to bend, treating her as a towel.
punchline: Alice sarcastically applies Wally's logic to herself, and Wally's clueless reply shows he doesn't grasp the insult and seems to see her as a towel.
summary: A colleague's dubious reasoning for never laundering his towels gets turned back on him by a coworker who offers to use him as a cleaning aid.

file: 1995/1995-03-21_catbert_hr director_new org chart_so close_too bad_play before firing_downsized.gif
title: Catbert Toys With Doomed Employees

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the HR Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Here's the new org chart. Maybe you're on it and maybe not.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ooh! Nice try! So close. Too bad.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's fun to play with them before downsizing them.

setting: Office cubicle area, with Catbert perched on the cubicle walls
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, walks along the tops of the cubicle walls dangling a new org chart over his coworkers. He teases them by holding it just out of reach as they jump and grab for it, then pins it to a cubicle wall. He explains that he enjoys toying with employees before laying them off.
punchline: Catbert cruelly teases employees who are desperate to see whether they survived the reorganization, because he enjoys tormenting people before downsizing them.
summary: The sadistic HR cat dangles a reorganization chart out of reach of anxious workers, savoring their desperation before cutting their jobs.

file: 1995/1995-04-28_bad news 1985_replacing doctor_registered nurse_fired nurse_aspirin_vending machine_vending machine revenue.gif
title: Bad News: Healthcare Cuts Escalate

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bad news in 1985

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're replacing the company doctor with a registered nurse.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bad news in 1990

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We fired the nurse and put the aspirin and tourniquets in the vending machine.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bad news in 1995

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've been asked to increase vending machine revenue by fifteen percent.

situation: Across three panels labeled 1985, 1990 and 1995, management reads out successive pieces of bad news to the employees. First the company doctor is replaced by a nurse, then the nurse is fired and first-aid supplies are moved into a vending machine, and finally the vending machine must raise its revenue by fifteen percent.
punchline: Each cost-cutting step makes employee healthcare worse until medical supplies become a vending-machine profit centre, implying the company will profit from its workers' injuries.
summary: A manager announces a decade of shrinking workplace healthcare that ends with first aid being sold from a snack machine and expected to earn more.

file: 1995/1995-10-19_heaven_dogbert_relaxed standards_automatic_halo_frisbees_angel_pearly gates.gif
title: Dogbert Steals Angel's Halo Frisbee

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: Welcome to Heaven, Mister Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow, it looks like you guys relaxed your standards!

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: Dogs are automatic. No matter what you do, there's always a place in Heaven for every little dog.

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: I'd like that back now, if you don't mind!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What kind of distance can you get with these little "Frisbees"?

setting: Heaven, on the clouds at the pearly gates
situation: Dogbert arrives in Heaven, where an angel at a podium welcomes him. Dogbert jabs that Heaven has lowered its standards, and the angel explains that all dogs get in automatically. While the angel talks, Dogbert swipes the angel's halo and treats it like a toy.
punchline: Dogbert proves the angel's point about dogs by immediately stealing the halo and mistaking it for a Frisbee, annoying the angel.
summary: A sarcastic dog arriving in the afterlife is told he's guaranteed entry, then promptly pinches an angel's halo to play with.

file: 1995/1995-01-14_dogbert venture capitalist_invest 5 million_agree_standard conditions_chairman of board_mow lawn_wash car_touch bargainer_multimedia developers_gardening needs.gif
title: Dogbert's Absurd Venture Capital Terms

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Venture Capitalist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll invest up to five million dollars if you'll agree to some standard conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will be chairman of the board and own 99% of the company. You will work for free and wash my car twice a week.

transcript.speaker: Entrepreneur
transcript.text: Can I mow your lawn instead of washing your car?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're a tough bargainer, but I prefer multimedia developers for my gardening needs.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a venture capitalist, offers an entrepreneur up to five million dollars in exchange for 'standard conditions.' Those conditions turn out to be total ownership, free labor, and car washing. The entrepreneur tries to negotiate by offering to mow the lawn instead.
punchline: The entrepreneur's feeble haggling over a lopsided deal is brushed off by Dogbert, who adds that he wants multimedia developers doing his gardening, showing how absurdly exploitative the terms are.
summary: A dog financier demands near-total ownership and servant duties from a startup founder in return for funding, then shrugs off the founder's meek counteroffer.

file: 1995/1995-03-30_built a spreadsheet_relative qualities_twenty percent_stop dating_wrong formula_higher math skills_error intentional_batch of flowers.gif
title: Spreadsheet Proves Dilbert Outclasses Girlfriend

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: I built a spreadsheet to compare our relative qualities. I'm afraid I'm twenty percent too good for you. We must stop dating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No! Look, Liz, you have the wrong formula in this column! That must mean I have higher math skills than you! We're almost even!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You left that error in there intentionally.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: My last batch of flowers is wilting.

setting: Liz's office cubicle with a computer
situation: Liz shows Dilbert a spreadsheet she built that concludes he is twenty percent too good for her, so they must stop dating. Dilbert frantically points out a formula error in her spreadsheet to argue they are nearly equal. Dogbert observes that she left the error in on purpose, and Liz casually mentions that her flowers are wilting.
punchline: Liz deliberately planted a spreadsheet error to bait Dilbert into proving he is smarter than her, and the real point of the exercise was to hint that he hadn't sent her flowers lately.
summary: A woman uses a rigged spreadsheet to lure her boyfriend into a ridiculous defense of their relationship, all to nudge him into buying her more flowers.

file: 1995/1995-02-23_perfromance appraisel_four years_starting documentation_fire me later_24 hours aday_motivational.gif
title: Dreaded Appraisal Motivates Overwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm almost done with your performance appraisal.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gasp!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I haven't had an appraisal in four years. You must be starting a documentation trail so you can fire me later.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll work 24 hours a day!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was way more motivational than I'd hoped.

situation: The Boss tells Alice he is nearly finished writing her performance appraisal. Alice, who hasn't had one in four years, panics and assumes he is building a paper trail to fire her. She frantically promises to work 24 hours a day, and the Boss privately notes how motivating that was.
punchline: The Boss accidentally frightens Alice into extreme overwork just by mentioning an appraisal, showing that fear of being fired motivates better than any actual management effort.
summary: A casual remark about a long-overdue review sends an employee into a panic of promised overtime, which her pleased manager takes as an unexpected win.

file: 1995/1995-12-18_convince buy product_everybody is in sales_imagine_new slogan_wally_friends_convince friends.gif
title: Everybody Is In Sales: No Friends

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new slogan is "Everybody is in sales."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Imagine if all our employees convinced their friends to buy our product, eventually...

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: ...we'd have no friends?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What's this "friend" thing I keep hearing about?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces a new company slogan that everybody is in sales and suggests employees should convince their friends to buy the product. A woman at the table points out the consequence that they would end up with no friends. Wally, sitting nearby, comments that he has never heard of friends.
punchline: Pressuring friends to buy company products would destroy those friendships, and Wally's lonely, antisocial remark suggests he has no friends to lose anyway.
summary: A manager's plan to turn every worker into a salesperson aimed at their friends backfires on paper, while one colleague admits he has no friends at all.

file: 1995/1995-06-09_dysfunctional team_learned in workshop_listen_heart felt_respect_ham radio license_going first.gif
title: Workshop Lessons: Alice Loves Going First

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dysfunctional team...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like each of you to tell the team what you learned in my workshop.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I learned to listen with my heart. I gained respect for others. I understand Sanskrit. I got my ham radio license. I can divide by zero...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I love going first.

setting: Conference room during a team workshop
situation: Dogbert, acting as a workshop facilitator, asks each team member to share what they learned. Alice goes first and rattles off an absurdly inflated list of accomplishments, from heartfelt listening to Sanskrit and dividing by zero. In the last panel her thought bubble reveals she only enjoys going first so she can boast before anyone else.
punchline: Alice's supposed personal growth is really just competitive one-upmanship, so she loves going first to set an impossibly high bar for everyone else.
summary: A consultant's workshop debrief turns into a showy brag-fest when one employee piles on outlandish achievements to outdo her colleagues.

file: 1995/1995-02-14_contribution to revenue_project would fail_attributed_same project_equally valuable.gif
title: Wally Claims All Project Revenue

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should all follow Wally's example of how he quantifies his contribution to revenue.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Basically, I assumed my project would fail without me. Therefore all the revenue it generates can be attributed to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aren't we all on the same project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, but evidently we're not all equally valuable.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss holds up Wally as a model for measuring one's contribution to revenue. Wally explains that he simply assumed his project would fail without him and so credits himself with all of its revenue. Dilbert points out that everyone is on the same project, and Wally replies that some people are just more valuable than others.
punchline: Wally's self-serving logic lets him claim 100% of the credit for shared work, and he smugly dismisses his colleagues as less valuable, while the clueless Boss praises the method.
summary: A manager praises a coworker's absurd method of taking credit for an entire team's earnings by assuming nothing would succeed without him.

file: 1995/1995-08-08_new dress code_insane_fridays are casual_can't wear jeans_feel good_already own_sadistic plot_make people quit.gif
title: Casual Friday Ban on Jeans

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't understand your new dress code policy, Mr. Catbert.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you're insane.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's simple. Fridays are "casual." But you can't wear jeans because jeans look good and feel good and you already own several pairs.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's another sadistic Human Resources plot to make people quit!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Say hello to unsightly panty lines.

setting: Catbert's office in the Human Resources department
situation: A female employee comes to Catbert, the evil HR director, confused about his new dress code policy. Catbert explains that casual Fridays prohibit jeans precisely because they look good, feel good, and employees already own them. She accuses him of a plot to make people quit, and he cheerfully taunts her about the uncomfortable clothing she'll now have to wear.
punchline: The HR policy is deliberately designed to be as unpleasant and costly for employees as possible, and Catbert openly admits his sadistic intent by gleefully mentioning unsightly panty lines.
summary: An HR boss with feline cruelty bans jeans on casual Fridays precisely because people like them, then smugly rubs in the discomfort that results.

file: 1995/1995-02-16_late_makeup on_in car_save in car_sponge bath_carpool_whining_driver for car pool.gif
title: Carpool Driver Hears Whining

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I was so late I had to put on my makeup in the car.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, I had to shave in the car.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's nothing. I was so late that I had to give myself a sponge bath in the car.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Aren't you the driver for your carpool?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You've never heard such whining.

setting: Office break area, coworkers holding coffee cups
situation: A female coworker, Dilbert and Wally trade stories about how late they were this morning and the grooming they had to do in the car. Wally tops the others by claiming he gave himself a sponge bath in the car. A coworker then points out that Wally is the driver of his carpool, which means his passengers had to endure it.
punchline: Wally is the carpool driver, so his supposedly late-morning sponge bath happened with passengers in the car, and he complains that they whined about it.
summary: Colleagues one-up each other with tales of grooming on the commute until it emerges that the winner was driving the carpool at the time.

file: 1995/1995-03-24_elbonians_afford_just mud_couch shopping network_manage resources_sold country_little jars_molten lava_earths core.gif
title: Elbonians Sell Country as Mud

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could the Elbonians afford to buy this company? Their whole country is just mud.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They packaged the mud and sold it as a cosmetic on the "Couch Shopping Network." They made trillions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least they know how to manage resources.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They sold their entire country in little jars. Most Elbonians perished in molten lava at the Earth's core.

setting: Office, with Dilbert seated in his chair
situation: Dilbert wonders how the Elbonians, whose country is nothing but mud, could afford to buy his company. Dogbert explains they packaged the mud as a cosmetic and sold it on a TV shopping channel for trillions. When Dilbert praises their resource management, Dogbert reveals they sold the entire country and most Elbonians died in the Earth's core.
punchline: Dilbert's praise for the Elbonians' business savvy is undercut by the grim reveal that they literally sold their whole country out from under themselves, killing most of their population.
summary: A company's mysterious new owners turn out to have funded their purchase by selling off their own homeland as beauty product, with deadly consequences.

file: 1995/1995-06-04_attractive product_another vendor_stupid deciosn_careers ruined_contract_loyal employees_million units_nice raises.gif
title: Vendor Threatens, Then Gets Rewarded

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your company makes an attractive little product, Jim.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But we've decided to go with a vendor whose product actually works.

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: Fools!!! I'll crush you!!!

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: I'll tell your boss you made a stupid decision!! Your careers will be ruined and I'll get the contract anyway!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't scare us! Do you think our boss will believe a vendor over his own loyal employees?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Must... keep... a... straight... face...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must... keep... a... straight... face...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll take a million units.

transcript.speaker: Jim
transcript.text: Take two million and I'll see that you get nice raises.

setting: Conference room during a vendor meeting
situation: Dilbert and a coworker tell a vendor salesman that they chose a competitor because his product doesn't work. The vendor flies into a rage and threatens to ruin their careers by going to their boss. When they burst out laughing at the idea, he abruptly switches tactics and offers them raises in exchange for buying a larger order.
punchline: The vendor's threats are an empty bluff, and when they fail he reveals the real game is bribery, offering personal perks to buyers for a bigger sale.
summary: A furious salesman's threats get laughed off, so he pivots to sweetening the deal with a kickback.

file: 1995/1995-02-20_project cancelled_rumor has it_give raise_come work_transfer_pathological liar_super prowers.gif
title: Pathological Liar Claims Super Powers

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Reliable sources say your project will be cancelled, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You should abandon it now and come work on MY project. When my big promotion goes through next month, I'll transfer you to my group and give you a raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's very tempting except for the fact you're a pathological liar.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Be careful what you say - I have super powers.

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's workspace
situation: A smiling coworker in a white lab coat tells Dilbert that his project is about to be cancelled and tries to recruit him, promising a transfer and a raise once a big promotion comes through. Dilbert declines, pointing out that the coworker is a pathological liar. The coworker responds with a threatening warning that he has super powers.
punchline: Caught out as a compulsive liar, the coworker doesn't deny it but simply tells another absurd lie, claiming super powers to intimidate Dilbert.
summary: A schemer trying to poach Dilbert with grand promises gets called out as a habitual fibber and responds by fibbing even bigger.

file: 1995/1995-12-10_help desk_reengineered_out of existence_never call again_pie chart_crush computer_ass flour_bake one hour_free novel_manual_repeat process.gif
title: No Help Whatsoever Desk

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hello, is this the "Help Desk"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, that group got reengineered out of existence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm the new "No Help Whatsoever Desk." My job is to make sure you never call again.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Can you tell me how to make a pie chart?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Crush your computer into small chunks, add flour and bake one hour.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: While you're waiting, read the free novel we sent you. It's a Spanish story about a guy named "Manual."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Repeat the process until you get the desired result.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: This lost a LOT in the translation.

setting: Help desk phone call; caller at home or office, Dogbert at his desk
situation: A bald caller in a red sweater phones the help desk, only to be told by Dogbert that the department was reengineered away and replaced by a "No Help Whatsoever Desk." When asked how to make a pie chart, Dogbert gives literal baking instructions and tells him to read a 'Spanish novel' called Manual. The caller ends up sitting by his oven with the computer manual, realizing the advice makes no sense.
punchline: The new help desk exists only to discourage calls, so it gives absurd, useless advice that misreads 'pie chart' as a recipe and 'manual' as a Spanish name.
summary: A tech support line staffed by Dogbert is deliberately designed to be useless, answering a software question with nonsensical cooking directions.

file: 1995/1995-05-11_divide check_engineers_unpopular subsidy_water_13%_tip amount_questionable.gif
title: Engineers Overanalyze Splitting the Check

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could simply divide the check by three...

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: Uh-oh. Engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that would result in an unpopular subsidy of Wally's salmon. Does anybody have a calculator-watch?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hours later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the tie-breaker round of water to decide if you get 13% or 13.5%.

transcript.speaker: Waitress
transcript.text: Rrrr

situation: Dilbert and two coworkers are at a restaurant trying to settle the bill. Dilbert refuses to simply split it three ways because Wally ordered the expensive salmon, and asks for a calculator-watch. Hours later they are still arguing over the tip percentage while the exasperated waitress stands by growling.
punchline: Engineers turn a simple bill split into an hours-long calculation over a half-percent tip difference, leaving the waitress waiting and frustrated, likely with a smaller tip than she would have gotten.
summary: Three engineers dining out cannot settle a restaurant bill without exhaustive calculations, keeping the weary waitress waiting for hours.

file: 1995/1995-12-03_alice_janitor_over time pay_75k per year_basment_reading magazines_fishing_engineer_no over time_sports_engineering.gif
title: Janitor Out-Earns Exempt Alice

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Working late again, huh, Alice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Seventy hours this week...

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Me too. Thank goodness for overtime pay!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Overtime pay?

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Allow me to explain.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Unlike you so-called "exempt" employees, my income increases if I work additional hours.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: I'm pulling in seventy-five thousand a year. And half the time I just hide in the basement reading "Fishing" magazine.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: The only down side is that I don't get to enjoy the intellectual stimulation of my co-workers the way you do.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: I don't know what I like better — deep sea fishing or cubicle fishing.

setting: Office cubicle area at night, then the basement
situation: A janitor finds Alice working late and cheerfully mentions how thankful he is for overtime pay. Alice, who is an exempt salaried employee, realizes she gets nothing for her seventy-hour week, while he explains with a graph that his pay rises with hours and he earns $75,000 a year while slacking in the basement. He ends up sitting in the basement with a fishing magazine, musing about fishing.
punchline: The janitor earns more than the overworked salaried engineer, gets paid extra for hours he spends idle, and is smugly entertained by watching the exempt employees toil for free.
summary: A cheerful custodian shows an exhausted colleague that his hourly wage beats her unpaid long hours, all while he lounges in the basement.

file: 1995/1995-11-01_catbert_sadistic plot_different objectives_staus report_staple himself.gif
title: Dotted Line Boss Means Staple Suicide

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Guess what, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What sadistic plot has H.R. come up with now, Catbert?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're giving you a real boss plus a "dotted line" to another boss who has different objectives.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The status reports alone will take forty hours a week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm gonna staple myself to death.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, appears over the cubicle wall to announce a new reporting arrangement to Wally. Wally will now have a real boss plus a dotted-line boss with conflicting objectives. When Catbert adds that the status reports alone will eat forty hours a week, Wally grabs a stapler and threatens to staple himself to death.
punchline: The matrix reporting structure is so burdensome and absurd that Wally would rather inflict a painfully ridiculous form of self-harm with office supplies than endure it.
summary: An HR cat delivers news of a double-boss reporting setup, and the resulting paperwork load drives an employee to threaten a stationery-based demise.

file: 1995/1995-07-27_bob_self esteem_improve_job_opening_procurement dept_hit people_with tail_prevent desired computers_business.gif
title: Bob Dinosaur Joins Procurement Department

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bob, your self-esteem might improve if you got a job.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: As what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's an opening in our procurement department. You'd be perfect.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: What does procurement do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Their job is to prevent us from getting the computers we want.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Can I hit people with my tail?

setting: Dilbert's home, with Bob the dinosaur sitting on a couch
situation: Dilbert suggests that Bob the green dinosaur get a job to boost his self-esteem and offers him an opening in the procurement department. When Bob asks what procurement does, Dilbert explains that the department exists to stop employees from getting the computers they want. Bob responds by asking whether he can hit people with his tail.
punchline: Procurement is portrayed as an obstructive department whose purpose is blocking purchases, so a violent, tail-swinging dinosaur is seen as an ideal fit.
summary: A friend recommends a purchasing job to a dinosaur, and the dinosaur's only question is whether the role allows physical assault.

file: 1995/1995-12-21_payroll computer_gie raise_dogbert_not ethical_five percent raise_quality of work.gif
title: Hacking Payroll for a Raise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't ethical to hack into the payroll computer and give me a raise, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not ethical?? Is it ethical for them to make you work seventy hours a week and only pay you for forty??!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a five percent raise?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, there is the issue of the quality of your work...

situation: Dogbert is typing at a computer, hacking into the payroll system to give Dilbert a raise. Dilbert objects that it is unethical, but Dogbert points out the company underpays him for seventy-hour weeks. Dilbert then flips to bargaining for a five percent raise, and Dogbert counters by questioning the quality of his work.
punchline: Dilbert's ethical objection evaporates the moment Dogbert makes a case for the raise, and Dogbert then undercuts the justification by suggesting Dilbert's work doesn't actually merit more pay.
summary: A reluctant Dilbert is talked out of his scruples about a payroll hack, only to have his dog haggle him down by doubting his worth.

file: 1995/1995-07-18_suggestions_good idea_doubtful of wally_seen in book_no confidence_employee morale_abilities.gif
title: Wally's Idea Must Be From a Book

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's an interesting suggestion, Wally. But if it's a good idea, why aren't other companies doing it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can you imagine in your wildest dreams that maybe, just maybe I had a good idea that nobody else thought of?!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must have seen it in a book.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thanks for the confidence in my abilities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You read a book?

situation: Wally proposes an idea in a meeting and the Boss questions why no other company has done it. Wally indignantly asks whether it's possible he simply had a good original idea. The Boss assumes he copied it from a book, and Dilbert is surprised that Wally reads at all.
punchline: The Boss won't believe Wally could be original, and Dilbert's quip implies Wally is even less likely to have read a book, so Wally's idea is insulted from both sides.
summary: A manager dismisses an employee's suggestion as borrowed from a book, and a coworker adds that the employee probably never reads.

file: 1995/1995-04-25_spare cubicles_convicts_bigot_little mistake_health plan better.gif
title: Convicts in the Spare Cubicles

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think it's fair to put convicts in our spare cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't be such a bigot. These people have made one little mistake. Otherwise, they're just like employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think there are a few differences!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, their health plan is better.

situation: Dilbert complains that it is unfair to house convicts in the company's spare cubicles. Dogbert, wearing a hard hat and reading a document, scolds him for being a bigot and says convicts are just like employees apart from one small mistake. When Dilbert insists there are differences, Dogbert agrees and notes the convicts have a better health plan.
punchline: Dogbert's sarcastic agreement reveals that prisoners get better health benefits than the company's own employees, a dig at poor corporate healthcare coverage.
summary: Dogbert argues that ex-cons moving into empty cubicles are basically the same as staff, then concedes one perk that sets them apart.

file: 1995/1995-06-03_kill the messenger_finance_20% cut_budget cuts_success vector_money.gif
title: Finance Messenger Gets Thrown Out

transcript.speaker: Finance Guy
transcript.text: Here's your latest budget cuts. But please don't kill the messenger from Finance, ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Finance Guy
transcript.text: I recommended a 20% cut. A quick glance around the room tells me you're not on the success vector anyhoo, so nothing lost.

transcript.speaker: Finance Guy
transcript.text: Tough room.

setting: Conference room during a budget presentation, then outside an office building
situation: A cheerful finance employee presents budget cuts with an overhead projector and jokes about not being killed as the messenger. He then casually insults the audience, saying they are not on the success path anyway so a 20% cut loses nothing. In the last panel he is hanging upside down outside the window, tied up by his own projector cord, after the audience has thrown him out.
punchline: The finance guy joked about not being killed as the messenger, then insulted his audience so badly that they literally threw him out the window.
summary: A smug accountant delivering bad budget news and an insult ends up dangling upside down outside the building.

file: 1995/1995-04-22_urgent message_disregard_healthy compnay_herd stampedes_resume_voicemail.gif
title: Merger Rumor Voicemail Causes Stampede

transcript.speaker: Voicemail
transcript.text: "To hear your urgent voice mail message press one..."

transcript.speaker: Voicemail
transcript.text: "This urgent message is to all employees. Please disregard the rumors of a merger with a healthy company."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now spooked, the herd stampedes.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Résumé!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Where's my interview suit??!!

situation: Dilbert listens to an urgent company-wide voicemail telling employees to disregard rumors of a merger with a healthy company. Dilbert observes his panicked coworkers stampeding through the office, shouting about résumés and interview suits.
punchline: By denying a merger with a 'healthy' company, the message implies the company is in such poor shape that it is being merged with a failing one, so everyone rushes to find new jobs.
summary: A corporate voicemail meant to calm everyone instead reveals the firm's dire state and sends the staff running to polish their job-hunting gear.

file: 1995/1995-06-10_increase budget_training_leave the company_more money_competitor_down side.gif
title: The Downside of Training Employees

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You've got to increase the budget for training!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I train you, then wouldn't you just leave the company to make more money working for our competitor?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I guess there is a down-side.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the downside would be...?

situation: An employee urges the Boss to increase the training budget. The Boss objects that trained employees would simply leave for higher pay at a competitor. The employee concedes there is a downside, and the Boss asks what it would be, as if the employee leaving were not a problem.
punchline: The Boss has unwittingly argued that he would lose trained staff to better-paying competitors, yet asks what the downside is, showing he does not grasp that his own underpayment is the real problem, and that untrained staff are the alternative.
summary: A manager refuses to fund employee training for fear that educated workers will defect to rivals, then oddly asks what the drawback of keeping them untrained would be.

file: 1995/1995-05-21_company vision_business plan_business plan blank_confidentail_not empiwered_doomed_haven't seen plan.gif
