title: Empowered Employees, Blank Confidential Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the company vision and business plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Vision: Empowered employees working toward a common plan." Sounds good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But the business plan is blank.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's confidential.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How am I supposed to know what to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll yell at you if you do the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought I was empowered.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be so literal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just keep doing what I was doing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No!!! You fool!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're doomed, aren't we?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know. I haven't seen the plan.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert the company vision statement and business plan, but the business plan page is blank because it is supposedly confidential. He tells Dilbert he will yell at him if he does the wrong thing, and when Dilbert says he will keep doing what he was doing, the Boss screams at him anyway. Dilbert concludes they are doomed, and the Boss admits he has not seen the plan either.
punchline: The Boss demands employees follow a secret plan, but he himself has never seen it, so the company is being run with no actual direction.
summary: A manager gives his employee an empty strategy document, scolds him for guessing wrong, and then confesses that he too is in the dark.

file: 1995/1995-11-23_ousource_functions_knowing_not good ta.gif
title: Outsourcing What We're Bad At

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company has decided to outsource all of the functions that we're not any good at.

transcript.speaker: Wally, Dilbert, Alice
transcript.text: Yippee! Yay!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When's your last day?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh... they're not good at knowing what they're not good at...

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that the company will outsource every function it is not good at. Wally, Dilbert and Alice cheer, and Wally cheerfully asks a coworker when their last day is. Alice then realizes that management is not good at identifying what it is bad at, so everyone may be at risk.
punchline: Management is so incompetent that it cannot accurately judge what it is incompetent at, so the outsourcing could hit anyone, including the cheering employees.
summary: Staff celebrate a plan to outsource whatever the company does poorly until one of them realizes leadership can't tell what that is.

file: 1995/1995-11-06_personal digital assistant_write messages_state of the rat_technology_interoret handwriting.gif
title: Ratbert the Handwriting-Recognition PDA

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've come to be your personal digital assistant.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Use the little pen to write messages on my stomach. I'll use state-of-the-rat technology to interpret your handwriting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Weave... me... a... cone... yoo... cupid... bat...

situation: Ratbert shows up at Dilbert's desk offering to serve as his personal digital assistant. He tells Dilbert to write on his stomach with a small stylus while Ratbert interprets the handwriting. Dilbert then holds Ratbert and scribbles on him, reading out the garbled results.
punchline: The gibberish Dilbert reads out mimics the notoriously poor handwriting recognition of early PDAs like the Apple Newton, with the rat as the gadget.
summary: A rat volunteers to be a living handheld organizer whose belly serves as the writing screen, and it fumbles the handwriting translation just like the real gadgets of the era.

file: 1995/1995-12-19_act as sales people_dilberts mother_primary rate circuit_frame delay drop_packet data_tough sale.gif
title: Dilbert's Tech-Savvy Mom Rejects Sale

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company asked all employees to act as salespeople to friends and family. I think you could use this, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Why would I need a primary rate circuit? I've already got a frame relay drop to my web server in the sewing room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is going to be a tough sale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Hello-o-o! Earth to Dilbert! This is packet data...

setting: Mom's living room, sitting on a green couch
situation: Dilbert tries to sell his company's telecom product, a primary rate circuit, to his mother after the company orders all employees to sell to friends and family. His mom turns out to be more technically sophisticated than expected, already having a frame relay connection to a web server in her sewing room. Dilbert realizes he is in for a tough sale while she snaps him out of his daze to lecture him about packet data.
punchline: Dilbert's elderly mother knows more about networking than he does and has better infrastructure at home, making her an impossible customer for his forced sales pitch.
summary: A mandatory family-and-friends sales drive backfires when Dilbert's mom turns out to already own better networking gear than the product he's pushing.

file: 1995/1995-09-13_writing email_protest new policy_empty trash_highly paid engineers_unproductive tsak_inventing the future_quality faire.gif
title: Protesting Trash Duty With Long Email

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm writing an e-mail to protest the new policy of making the employees empty their own trash at night.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's stupid to have highly paid engineers doing unproductive tasks when we could be inventing the future!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you coming to the "Quality Faire"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, this will take another hour.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer typing an e-mail to protest a new policy that makes employees empty their own trash at night. He argues that highly paid engineers should be inventing the future rather than doing unproductive tasks. A coworker asks if he is coming to the Quality Faire, and Dilbert says he can't because the e-mail will take another hour.
punchline: Dilbert complains that engineers waste time on unproductive tasks, yet he spends an hour writing a protest e-mail and skips the company's quality event, wasting far more engineering time than emptying trash would.
summary: An engineer fires off a long complaint about wasting engineers' time on chores while spending his own hours on the complaint instead of attending a company event.

file: 1995/1995-07-04_guy in marketing_alter dna_structure_animal_weasel_notice change_marketing guys_helix_one helix.gif
title: Marketing Guy's Single-Helix DNA

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told a guy in marketing that I programmed his computer to alter his DNA structure.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hee hee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He thinks he'll turn into some kind of animal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell him you set it to "weasel." It'll take longer to notice any change.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Tell me the truth, Alice. Can Dilbert reprogram my DNA?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yeah. You marketing guys only have one helix.

setting: Office break room and Alice's cubicle
situation: Dilbert and Wally eat lunch while Dilbert brags about tricking a marketing guy into believing his computer can rewrite his DNA. Wally suggests telling the victim he's turning into a weasel, since nobody would notice the change. The worried marketing guy then asks Alice if Dilbert can really reprogram his DNA, and she replies with an insult.
punchline: Alice implies marketing people are so unintelligent and primitive that they have only a single strand of DNA, so reprogramming them is entirely plausible, and the weasel jab suggests they already resemble one.
summary: Two engineers prank a gullible marketing employee with a bogus genetic-engineering scare, and a coworker caps it by mocking marketing's biology.

file: 1995/1995-10-22_obstacle to success_poor graphics_inability to communicate_beyond communication_think clearly_high five_broke code_participate_meetings.gif
title: Boss's Meaningless Graphic Deciphered Wrongly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This graphic shows our biggest obstacle to success.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: RDS ZPL ABP NDP QRT LNP

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you saying our biggest obstacle to success is poor graphics?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think he's saying our biggest problem is his overall inability to communicate.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think his point goes beyond communication. He's showing us that he doesn't even think clearly!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's it!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: High five!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You broke the code!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You know how I said you should participate more in meetings?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't mean it.

situation: The Boss presents an overhead graphic filled with meaningless letter codes and claims it shows the company's biggest obstacle to success. Alice, Dilbert and Wally puzzle over it, then decide the real obstacle is the Boss's inability to communicate and think clearly, and celebrate their insight. The Boss, stung by the critique, retracts his earlier encouragement to participate in meetings.
punchline: When employees finally take his advice and participate, they correctly diagnose the Boss himself as the problem, so he takes back his request for participation.
summary: A manager's incomprehensible chart leads his team to conclude that he is the real obstacle, and he regrets inviting their input.

file: 1995/1995-07-10_engineering_uses program_marketing_prodcut_urrelevant_engineers_same as marketeers_sitting in cave_rocks are edicble_recipes_business.gif
title: Engineer's Program Fails Marketing Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everybody in Engineering uses this program I wrote. I think Marketing should turn it into a product.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy this.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's irrelevant because the target market would be engineers.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Engineers think the same as marketeers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If that were true we'd be sitting in a cave trying to decide if rocks are edible.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: You know, you could keep recipes on this.

situation: Dilbert pitches a program he wrote to a marketing employee, suggesting it be turned into a product because all of Engineering uses it. The marketer says he wouldn't buy it, and Dilbert argues that the target market would be engineers, who he assumes think differently. The marketer then grudgingly finds a use for it while Dilbert insults marketers.
punchline: After Dilbert insults marketers by implying they are so clueless they'd debate whether rocks are edible, the marketer cheerfully reveals he only sees the program as a place to store recipes, proving the program has no real market appeal.
summary: A programmer's attempt to sell his in-house tool to marketing collapses when the marketer dismisses it and finds only a trivial use for it.

file: 1995/1995-05-16_marketings approval_flex power_useless data_major stallion_wife address.gif
title: Marketing VP Flexes Power Over Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Marketing VP
transcript.text: I could give you marketing's approval right now...

transcript.speaker: Marketing VP
transcript.text: Or I could flex my vice presidential power and send you to gather more useless data... My ego would expand and I'd be a major stallion with my wife tonight.

transcript.speaker: Marketing VP
transcript.text: Do you think you can top that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll try, sir. What's your wife's address?

situation: Dilbert waits in a marketing VP's office for approval on his project. The VP admits he could simply approve it, but would rather send Dilbert off to collect pointless data because abusing his power boosts his ego and, he claims, his performance with his wife. Dilbert responds by asking for the wife's address.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically offers to top the VP's petty power trip by implying he could satisfy the VP's wife better than the VP can.
summary: A power-tripping executive brags that stalling an approval makes him feel virile, and Dilbert answers with a cheeky insult aimed at the man's marriage.

file: 1995/1995-10-24_flight to ny_many stopovers_third world countries_rebel insurrections_wear red cross symbol_on back_bullseye_wants boss killed.gif
title: Carol Books Boss a Deadly Itinerary

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, about this flight to New York that you booked for me...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it really necessary to make all these stopovers in third-world countries that are experiencing rebel insurrections?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You'd better wear the international symbol of the "Red Cross" on your back.

situation: The Boss complains to his secretary Carol about the itinerary she booked for his flight to New York, which includes stopovers in war-torn third-world countries. Carol calmly advises him to wear a Red Cross symbol on his back, then holds up a sheet showing a bullseye target.
punchline: Carol deliberately routed him through dangerous war zones and hands him a bullseye instead of a Red Cross, showing she wants him shot.
summary: A secretary who has arranged her employer's trip through rebel-torn countries cheerfully offers him a target to pin on his back for protection.

file: 1995/1995-06-11_three day workshop_sahring_form teams_paper airplanes_blindfolded_flight_unconditional love_co workers_accountants_marketers_secreatries_competitive lion_workload_eraser pilot_group hug.gif
title: Team-Building Workshop Debrief Goes Silly

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Let's go around the circle and share what we learned in the three-day workshop.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At first I thought it was a waste of our training budget...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then you asked us to form teams and make paper airplanes while blindfolded...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't know if it was because of the darkness or the way we shared our thoughts about flight...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But suddenly I found unconditional love for my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Be they accountants, be they marketeers or be they secretaries.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As a result, I've become a competitive lion, eager to pounce on my workload and increase stockholder values!!

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Thank you, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Facilitator
transcript.text: Dilbert, what did you learn?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I learned that you shouldn't put a little eraser-pilot in your paper airplane.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Somebody needs a group hug!

setting: Office training room during a workshop debrief
situation: A facilitator leads a circle discussion about a three-day team-building workshop. Wally gushes about blindfolded paper airplane exercises awakening unconditional love for his co-workers and turning him into a competitive lion. When it's Dilbert's turn, he gives a deadpan, absurdly literal lesson instead.
punchline: After Wally's over-the-top corporate-speak enthusiasm, Dilbert's only takeaway is a trivial, silly observation about paper airplanes, showing the workshop taught nothing useful.
summary: A workshop leader asks for takeaways, and one employee gushes about blindfolded airplane-folding while another mentions only a pointless detail about an eraser.

file: 1995/1995-06-24_computer holy wars_scruffy beard_suspenders_smug expression_unix computer user_nickel_better computer_holy wars.gif
title: Unix User Offers Nickel Insult

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Computer holy wars

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: Hold it right there, buddy.

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: That scruffy beard... those suspenders... that smug expression...

transcript.speaker: Bald Man
transcript.text: You're one of those condescending Unix computer users!

transcript.speaker: Unix User
transcript.text: Here's a nickel, kid. Get yourself a better computer.

situation: A bald man in glasses and a green tie stops a bearded man in suspenders. He identifies him as a condescending Unix user from his scruffy beard, suspenders and smug expression. The bearded man replies by offering him a nickel to buy a better computer.
punchline: The Unix veteran confirms the stereotype by responding with a patronizing quip implying the other man's computer is inferior and that he is too poor to afford a good one.
summary: A confrontation between rival computer camps ends with the bearded Unix guru out-condescending his accuser.

file: 1995/1995-09-07_contract employee_more income_wind in hair.gif
title: Contract Work And Wind In Hair

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I should quit and become a contract employee. Then I'd have more income and I'd feel the wind in my hair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's possible you'd have no income at all...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And if you want wind in your hair you'll have to take off your shirt and run around with your arms up.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thank you for your support.

situation: Wally, the bald coworker, walks beside Dilbert and fantasizes about quitting to become a contract employee, imagining higher pay and wind in his hair. Dilbert sceptically points out he might earn nothing, then sarcastically adds that he would have to run around shirtless with his arms up to feel wind in his hair. Wally dryly thanks him for the support.
punchline: Dilbert mocks Wally's rosy fantasy by pointing out that, being bald, wind in his hair is impossible, while also warning him that contract work could mean no income at all.
summary: A balding coworker daydreams about freelancing for more money and a breezy hairstyle, and his colleague deflates both hopes in one sarcastic breath.

file: 1995/1995-08-16_invisible to coworkers_compensate_symbiotic realtionship_visible creature_ratbert_visual_auditory link_columbian coffee.gif
title: Ratbert Becomes Dilbert's Visible Proxy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're invisible to your co-workers. But you can compensate by forming a symbiotic relationship with a visible creature.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert will cling to your back. He'll be your visual and auditory link with your co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So... working hard? Or hardly working?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I knew this Colombian coffee was trouble.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert that his co-workers cannot see him, and suggests he compensate by letting Ratbert cling to his back as a visual and auditory link. Ratbert then appears among the co-workers, and a woman and a bald co-worker react to the sight of a rat in the office.
punchline: A co-worker blames his strong Colombian coffee for the hallucination of seeing a talking rat, while Dilbert remains invisible to everyone.
summary: Dogbert advises an unseen Dilbert to rely on Ratbert as his eyes and ears, and the baffled co-workers blame their coffee for the strange sight.

file: 1995/1995-01-02_more work_same tiny raises_clever shift_management philosophy_simple application_annoy_effect pay.gif
title: Double the Work, Same Raise

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I accomplished twice as much as Wally this year, but we got exactly the same tiny raises.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wondering if this is a clever shift in management philosophy or a simple application of your ignorance?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're starting to annoy me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that would affect my pay how?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that he accomplished twice as much as Wally yet received the same tiny raise. He sarcastically asks whether the pay system reflects a deliberate management philosophy or just the boss's ignorance. The boss says Dilbert is annoying him, and Dilbert points out that this would change nothing about his pay.
punchline: Because raises are identical regardless of performance, even irritating the boss cannot hurt Dilbert's pay, which exposes the pay system as meaningless.
summary: An overachieving engineer confronts his boss about a flat raise structure and realizes that nothing he does can change what he earns.

file: 1995/1995-07-17_bring to read_book of tips_new computer golf game_reading book_computer simulation_almost sport_non organic life form_driving little cart.gif
title: Reading About Computer Golf Tips

transcript.speaker: Friend
transcript.text: What did you bring to read?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a book of tips for my new computer golf game.

transcript.speaker: Friend
transcript.text: So... you're reading a book... about a computer simulation... of an activity that's almost a sport...

transcript.speaker: Friend
transcript.text: That's about as close as you can get to being a non-organic life form.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This chapter is about driving the little cart.

setting: Outdoors, sitting against a tree trunk on a grassy lawn
situation: Dilbert and a friend sit under a tree reading. Dilbert explains he is reading a book of tips for his new computer golf game, and the friend mocks how many layers removed this is from real activity. Dilbert answers by saying his current chapter covers driving the little cart.
punchline: Dilbert shows no embarrassment at his absurdly artificial hobby and responds to the insult by cheerfully mentioning he's reading about driving the golf cart, the least sporty part of an already not-quite-sport.
summary: A man's pal ridicules him for studying a manual about a video game version of golf, and he calmly counters by citing the chapter on the cart.

file: 1995/1995-05-24_create illusion_work long hours_voice mails_dilbert_in underwear_obscene message_group code.gif
title: Fake Overtime Voicemail Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can create the illusion that you work long hours by leaving voice mails for your boss at 4 A.M.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, this is Dilbert. It's 4 A.M. and I'm in my underwear and I thought of you... Oops... Erase... Oops...

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Beep beep

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you just send an obscene message to your boss?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... I think I hit the group code.

situation: Dogbert advises Dilbert to fake long working hours by leaving voice mails for his boss at 4 A.M. Dilbert, in his underwear, records a message that accidentally turns into an obscene-sounding one and fumbles trying to erase it. Dogbert asks if he just sent an obscene message to his boss, and Dilbert says he thinks he hit the group code.
punchline: Dilbert's botched attempt to look hard-working ends up broadcasting an embarrassing, suggestive message to the whole company instead of just his boss.
summary: A scheme to impress the boss with middle-of-the-night voicemails backfires when a clumsy message is blasted to an entire distribution list.

file: 1995/1995-03-05_security guards in space_need badge_search lunch box_watch lunch_cart to car_space travel safe_for animals_ratbert_security guard_dogbert.gif
title: Dogbert's Lunch Box Bomb Prank

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're going downtown to play "Security Guards in Space."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to know.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's try that building.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: I'll need to see your I.D. badge, sir.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Look fast!! There it is!! Not a pack of matches!!

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zip!

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: I'll have to search your lunch box.

transcript.speaker: Security Guard
transcript.text: It's just a bunch of wires and gizmos.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're making me so hungry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Could you watch my lunch while I take the cart back to my car?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I feel bad, but it's the only way to test if space travel is safe for us animals.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I feel safer already.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then the lobby of a downtown office building
situation: Dogbert and Ratbert haul a rocket-shaped "lunch" box on a red wagon to an office building lobby. They distract the security guard with a quick ID flash, then talk him into inspecting the box and leaving him in charge of it while they leave. The final panel shows the guard blasted off into the air and the animals watching from below.
punchline: Dogbert tricks a security guard into sitting on an actual rocket disguised as a lunch box, using him as an unwitting test subject for space travel, and Ratbert's relief is that it wasn't him.
summary: Two scheming pets use a gullible building guard as a crash-test dummy by leaving him to babysit a disguised rocket.

file: 1995/1995-05-01_pursue goal_world domination_talk radio host_unique conservative view_deserve mockery_flawed view_intelligent questions.gif
title: Dogbert's Talk Radio Domination Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think the best way to pursue my goal of world domination is to become a talk radio host.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll promote my unique conservative viewpoint that people are idiots who deserve to be mocked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Won't people show your viewpoint to be flawed by virtue of their intelligent questions?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Like that one?

situation: Dogbert announces that becoming a talk radio host is the best path to world domination, and that his show will promote the view that people are idiots who deserve mockery. Dilbert, seated at his computer, objects that intelligent callers would disprove that view. Dogbert replies by pointing at Dilbert's question as an example.
punchline: Dogbert treats Dilbert's intelligent objection as a mocking target, showing how talk radio hosts dismiss any challenge to their worldview by ridiculing the questioner.
summary: A scheming dog plans to conquer the world through radio punditry and swats away his friend's sensible objection with ridicule.

file: 1995/1995-01-30_laptop in case_anything lighter_delete files_technically.gif
title: Delete Files to Lose Weight

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This laptop computer weighs too much. Do we have anything lighter?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why don't you just delete files to lower the weight on that one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's a thought.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Technically, I only asked why not.

situation: The Boss complains that his laptop is too heavy and asks for a lighter one. Wally sarcastically suggests deleting files to reduce the weight, and the Boss takes the idea seriously and starts fiddling with the laptop. Wally then distances himself from the idea, noting he only asked a question.
punchline: Wally makes a nonsensical suggestion that the gullible Boss believes, and Wally immediately dodges all responsibility with a technicality.
summary: A boss who thinks digital files add physical weight to a computer gets a bogus tip from a coworker who quickly disowns it.

file: 1995/1995-01-16_paper burning stove_lower heating bills_useless documents_love your work_warm feeling.gif
title: Burning Useless Work Documents for Heat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm installing a paper-burning stove to lower our heating bills.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll fuel it with all the useless documents I get at work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been noticing how much stuff you take home. You must love your work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It gives me a warm feeling.

setting: Dilbert's home (stove installation) and the office
situation: Dilbert installs a paper-burning stove at home and explains he will feed it with the pointless documents he receives at work. The Boss sees Dilbert carrying a big stack of papers home and assumes he is dedicated to his job. Dilbert replies that the papers give him a warm feeling, meaning literally from burning them.
punchline: The Boss mistakes Dilbert's stack of useless paperwork for devotion to his job, while Dilbert's 'warm feeling' comes from burning it as heating fuel.
summary: An employee turns the worthless paperwork he gets at the office into home heating fuel, while his oblivious manager reads it as work devotion.

file: 1995/1995-11-04_wall art_low bid_assistant scourcing_earth_low cost art.gif
title: Low Bid Wall Art Contract

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you get the contract to supply our company with wall art?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Low bid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As we speak, my assistant is scouring the earth in search of low-cost art.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll take it!!

setting: Dogbert's office, then outside the School-o-Art building
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert how he won the contract to supply the company's wall art, and Dogbert says he submitted the lowest bid. Dogbert explains his assistant is searching for the cheapest art possible. Ratbert is then shown outside an art school, where he has kicked open the door and an art student is flying out, with Ratbert grabbing the artwork.
punchline: Dogbert's low-cost sourcing strategy amounts to having Ratbert violently steal art from an art school, showing that winning on the lowest bid means cutting corners, even illegal ones.
summary: A consultant wins a decorating contract by underbidding everyone, then fulfills it by sending his assistant to rob an art school.

file: 1995/1995-03-15_stock_shares_timely leaks_media_value plunged_sell now_fair share price_want copy_entertainment.gif
title: Dogbert Tanks Stock, Then Buys Cheap

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your stock was $30 per share when I offered to buy the company, but thanks to some timely leaks to the media your value has plunged.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: However, if you sell right now I'll pay the full $30 for your stock.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I recommend we do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Done. $30 per share is more than fair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, "per share" would have been fair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Anybody want a copy?

setting: Conference room during a company buyout meeting
situation: Dogbert, sitting at the head of a conference table, tells the board that the company's stock has plunged because of leaks he made to the media after his original $30-a-share buyout offer. He then offers to pay the full $30 per share if they sell right now, and the Boss and Dilbert agree. Dogbert admits that the $30 figure is actually for the whole stock, not per share, and offers copies of the deal.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately sabotaged the company's value, then exploited the board's ambiguous wording so that the $30 was a total price for the stock rather than a per-share price, and the Boss and Dilbert sign without reading carefully.
summary: A scheming dog engineers a stock crash through media leaks, then buys the company for a tiny fraction of its worth by hiding behind loose phrasing in the contract.

file: 1995/1995-01-07_ratbert_entire  computer_silicon chip_ate computer_cyborg.gif
title: Ratbert Eats the Computer Chip

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look, Ratbert. An entire computer has been baked into one silicon chip.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Thanks! I don't mind if I do!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Snatch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Gulp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You ate my computer.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm a cyborg.

situation: Dilbert shows Ratbert a silicon chip, explaining that an entire computer is baked into it. Ratbert takes it as an offer of food, snatches it and swallows it. Dilbert points out that Ratbert has eaten his computer, and Ratbert cheerfully declares himself a cyborg.
punchline: Ratbert treats a computer chip as a snack and then justifies eating it by claiming that having a computer inside him makes him a cyborg.
summary: A tiny pet mistakes a showcased microchip for a treat, gobbles it down, and then cheekily rebrands himself as part machine.

file: 1995/1995-04-10_ergonomic key board_big q_porgram_quality_tletter q_whiny customers.gif
title: Quality Keyboard Missing Its Q

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This ergonomic keyboard is our first product developed under the "Big Q" program.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The "Q" stands for quality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Speaking of Q...it's missing the letter Q.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You sound just like our whiny customers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess the "Q" stands for "uality."

situation: A product manager shows off a new ergonomic keyboard that came out of the company's "Big Q" quality program. Dilbert examines it and points out that the keyboard has no Q key. The manager dismisses him as a whiny customer.
punchline: A product launched under a quality initiative ships with a glaring defect, and the company treats the person who spots it as a complainer, so Dilbert concludes the Q really stands for "uality."
summary: A flagship quality program delivers a keyboard that lacks the very letter its name celebrates, and the person noticing is brushed off.

file: 1995/1995-06-17_prodcutivity_moving_cubcile_phone_comaputer_disconnected_boxed_lost_abandoned pretense_loser.gif
title: Productivity Punished With Cubicle Move

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I see signs of productivity here. I'm moving you to another cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your phone and computer will be disconnected for weeks. Your files will be boxed and lost.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good Lord, you've abandoned all pretense of being on our side!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Loser.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's cubicle, notices he is being productive, and announces he will be moved to another cubicle. The move means his phone and computer will be disconnected for weeks and his files boxed and lost. Dilbert is appalled at the Boss's open hostility, and the Boss calls him a loser.
punchline: The Boss punishes productivity by deliberately sabotaging an employee's ability to work, and no longer even pretends to be on the employees' side.
summary: Spotting an employee actually getting work done, the manager responds by relocating him in a way that guarantees he can't work for weeks.

file: 1995/1995-12-11_email_fax it_goodby paperless_hello cluless.gif
title: Paperless Office Becomes Triple Delivery

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Send this by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fax it, too, in case he doesn't check his e-mail. And mail the original so he has a clean copy.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Goodbye "paperless," hello "clueless."

situation: The Boss hands a piece of paper to his secretary and tells her to send it by e-mail. He then keeps adding instructions, asking her to also fax it and mail the original in case the recipient misses the e-mail. After he leaves, she mutters that the paperless office has turned into a clueless one.
punchline: Despite adopting e-mail, the boss distrusts it so much that he sends the same document by every channel, defeating the paperless promise and showing his cluelessness.
summary: A manager who doesn't trust technology orders a single document sent three different ways, leaving his secretary to mourn the paperless office.

file: 1995/1995-05-28_putting in charge_biff_big improvements for free_recommend ways_increase profit_spend mpney_make money_more money_so called_report tomorrow_lava lamps_few bucks.gif
title: Big Improvements For Free Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of Project "BIFF."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "BIFF" stands for "Big Improvements For Free."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your job is to recommend ways to increase profits without spending money or changing anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to spend money to make money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we HAD money to spend we wouldn't need to MAKE money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Duh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The point is that you can make MORE money than you spend.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not following your so-called "point."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Logically, anything I don't understand is unimportant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have your report tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you recommend... replacing all managers with lava lamps.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's a few bucks for the lava lamps.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to lead a project that must raise profits without spending money or changing anything. Dilbert points out that you need to spend money to make money, and the Boss can't follow the logic, dismissing anything he doesn't understand as unimportant. The next day Dilbert's report recommends replacing all managers with lava lamps, and he cheekily hands over some cash for them.
punchline: Having been told that anything the Boss doesn't understand is unimportant, Dilbert gets revenge by recommending that managers be replaced with lava lamps, and slyly pockets the point that the Boss was the one wasting money.
summary: A boss demands free profit boosts, scorns his employee's reasoning, and gets a report suggesting that decorative lamps could do management's job.
keywords: anything I don't understand is unimportant

file: 1995/1995-02-22_black outs_lights_motion detectors_hired a temp_walk around_go off_another journalism major_waste_fan us.gif
title: Temp Waves Arms for Lights

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've been having a problem with black-outs. The office lights are controlled by motion detectors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a temp to walk around and flap his arms so the lights won't go off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Another journalism major enters the workforce.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seems like a waste. Maybe he could fan us.

situation: The Boss explains to Dilbert and Wally that the office lights, which run on motion detectors, keep going out. His fix is to hire a temp worker to walk around and flap his arms so the sensors keep detecting motion. The temp, a journalism major, stands waving his arms while Dilbert and Wally comment.
punchline: The Boss's absurd solution to a sensor problem is to pay a human to flail around all day, and Wally sarcastically suggests the temp could make himself more useful by fanning them.
summary: To stop motion-sensor lights from shutting off, the boss pays a temp to wave his arms around all day while the staff look on.

file: 1995/1995-12-12_poor communications_act interested_acronyms_whiny monotone_lose idealism.gif
title: Sarcastic Boss Opens Status Report Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's status report time where each of you gets to prove what poor communicators you are while I act interested!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember to use lots of acronyms that only you understand. And speak in a whiny monotone that makes us all want to slap you!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm starting to lose my idealism.

setting: Conference room during a status report meeting
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by cheerfully announcing that employees will now demonstrate how poorly they communicate while he pretends to be interested. He then coaches them to use incomprehensible acronyms and a whiny monotone that will irritate everyone. Wally, seated at the table next to Dilbert, remarks that he is losing his idealism.
punchline: The Boss is unusually honest about how pointless and irritating status report meetings are, and Wally's remark shows that even the staff are being worn down by the unvarnished truth.
summary: A manager candidly describes the useless theatre of status meetings, leaving a coworker disillusioned about corporate life.

file: 1995/1995-11-14_bug fixed_code_ratbert_rat dance_bugs to fix_web browser_authored browser.gif
title: Ratbert Dances Up Bugs for Bounty

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The company pays me ten dollars for every bug I fix in my code, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want you to do your little rat dance on my keyboard so I'll have lots of bugs to fix.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How am I doing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not so good. You just authored a web browser.

situation: Dilbert explains that the company pays him a bounty for every bug he fixes, so he asks Ratbert to dance on his keyboard to generate bugs in his code. Ratbert dances on the keyboard and asks how he is doing. Dilbert is unimpressed because the random keystrokes accidentally produced a working web browser.
punchline: Ratbert's random keyboard mashing produced working software, a sarcastic jab at how buggy and haphazardly written real software (like early web browsers) is, and at schemes that reward bug fixing.
summary: An engineer tries to game a per-bug bonus by having a rat stomp on his keyboard, but the rat's random keystrokes somehow yield a functioning program instead of defects.

file: 1995/1995-01-24_team leader_perks_staus_special agent_like wally but thicker_cubicle walls.gif
title: Thicker Cubicle Walls as Status Perk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As team leader, I think I should get some perks so people know my status.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll have your cubicle walls sprayed with a special thickening agent. It might look the same, but trust me, people will know how thick you are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm just like you, Wally, but thicker.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've noticed.

setting: Office: the Boss's desk and the cubicle area
situation: Newly made team leader Dilbert asks the Boss for perks that show off his status. The Boss offers to have his cubicle walls sprayed with an invisible thickening agent. Dilbert then brags to Wally over the cubicle wall that he is just like Wally but thicker, and Wally dryly agrees.
punchline: The Boss's 'thick' perk is really an insult to Dilbert's intelligence, and Dilbert fails to notice, so Wally sarcastically confirms that he has indeed noticed how thick Dilbert is.
summary: A promoted Dilbert fishes for a status symbol and ends up with a worthless perk that doubles as a jab at his intelligence.

file: 1995/1995-01-27_reduce budget.gif
title: Boss Offers Dilbert's Project as Cut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've been asked to reduce our budget. I'm going to offer to cut your project because it's the most critical.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The finance guys won't dare cut that project. My ploy will spare us from any cuts at all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I panic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me again what your project is about. They might ask.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he plans to offer Dilbert's project up for budget cuts, betting that finance will refuse to cut something so critical. Dilbert panics at the risk to his project, and the Boss then asks him to explain what the project actually is, since finance might ask.
punchline: The Boss is gambling Dilbert's project on a clever bluff while not even knowing what the project does, so the ploy is both risky and ill-informed.
summary: A manager plans to dodge budget cuts by offering up his employee's most vital project, then admits he has no idea what that project is.

file: 1995/1995-06-16_heavy weight_boxing cahampion_new goal_ratbert_too small_slow_clueless_catching on.gif
title: Dream Big, Too Clueless Anyway

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: My new goal, Bob, is to be the next heavyweight boxing champion of the world!!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Don't let anybody ever tell you that you're too small or too slow or too uncoordinated.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Or too clueless.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Exactly! Now you're catching on.

setting: A plain room with a blue floor or table surface
situation: A large green dinosaur announces his new goal of becoming heavyweight boxing champion. He lectures a small orange rat that no one should be allowed to say he is too small, slow, or uncoordinated. When the rat adds 'too clueless', the dinosaur happily agrees, missing that the rat is insulting him.
punchline: The dinosaur's motivational pep talk is undercut by the rat's sarcastic insult, which the dinosaur cheerfully accepts as agreement, proving his cluelessness.
summary: A confident green dinosaur plans a boxing career and praises a tiny rat for finishing his list of obstacles, not noticing that the rat is mocking him.

file: 1995/1995-01-01_voicemail_wally_simple incompetence_preview_sinister_defensive strategy_incomplete answers_over worked_irrational_asking questions_recount war stories_thwart me_team up.gif
title: Wally's Strategy of Withholding Information

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you never really answered the question I left on your voice-mail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this a case of simple incompetence or a preview of something far more sinister?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's the sinister one.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've adopted a defensive strategy. I'm withholding information to make myself appear more valuable.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now I only return phone calls late at night and leave incomplete answers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In person, I act overworked and irrational so people stop asking questions.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If cornered, I sigh deeply and recount old war stories that don't relate to the question.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Got it!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No co-worker can thwart me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if they team up?

situation: Dilbert asks Wally why he never answered a voicemail question, wondering whether it was incompetence or something sinister. Wally cheerfully admits he deliberately withholds information, returns calls only at night with incomplete answers, and acts overworked and irrational in person. Dilbert points out that coworkers could simply team up against him.
punchline: Wally's elaborate scheme to make himself indispensable by hoarding information falls apart as soon as coworkers cooperate with each other.
summary: A deliberately unhelpful employee proudly explains his tactics for looking valuable by stonewalling colleagues, until someone notes a flaw in the plan.

file: 1995/1995-12-06_attractive sales person_vendor_dogbert technology_hardware solution_half cost_save money_upgrade later_expensive_price sheet.gif
title: Dogbert Undercuts Vendor, Hides Prices

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your employees have recommended a vendor who has an attractive salesperson.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But the "Dogbert Technology Company" can provide you with a hardware solution for half the cost!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll save money!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if I need to upgrade later? Is it expensive?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I must have left that price sheet in my other fur.

setting: Boss's office, across a conference desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that his employees recommended a vendor only because of an attractive salesperson. He then pitches his own company's hardware at half the cost, and the Boss eagerly agrees. When the Boss asks about the cost of future upgrades, Dogbert claims he left the price sheet elsewhere.
punchline: Dogbert lures the Boss in with a low initial price and dodges the question of upgrade costs, a classic vendor lock-in bait-and-switch, with a pun on leaving the price sheet in his "other fur" instead of his other suit.
summary: A scheming dog consultant badmouths a rival vendor, offers cut-price hardware, and conveniently loses the pricing details for later upgrades.

file: 1995/1995-02-02_company dress code_dress like a woman_high heels_panty hose_little ornaments_male viwers.gif
title: Alice Protests Dress Code, Wally Disavows Pleasure

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm protesting the company's dress code. I refuse to dress like a woman.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: High heels and pantyhose are designed to make women look like helpless little ornaments for the pleasure of male viewers!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've never had pleasure viewing you. I swear.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you for your support.

situation: Alice stands in front of Dilbert and Wally wearing a shirt and tie and jeans, announcing that she is protesting the company dress code. She explains that high heels and pantyhose turn women into helpless ornaments for male viewers. Wally earnestly assures her he has never enjoyed looking at her, which she dryly accepts as support.
punchline: Wally's attempt to show solidarity is really a backhanded insult, and Alice's deadpan thanks acknowledges that it's both support and an insult.
summary: A coworker's well-meant declaration of solidarity with a dress code protester turns out to be a left-handed compliment she accepts with weary sarcasm.

file: 1995/1995-06-13_having retreat_mountain resort_loud noises_avalnaches.gif
title: Shouting Hello Into Avalanche Country

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hello, is this the mountain resort where all our executives are having a retreat?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it true that loud noises can cause avalanches?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you see my boss, tell him I said...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: HI!!

situation: An employee phones the mountain resort where the company's executives are holding a retreat. He first confirms they are there, then asks whether loud noises can trigger avalanches. He offers to pass along a greeting to his boss and then screams it into the phone.
punchline: The employee deliberately shouts into the phone in the hope of triggering an avalanche that will bury the executives at their retreat.
summary: A worker calls the resort hosting his bosses' getaway and bellows a greeting down the line, hoping the noise will bring a snowy disaster upon them.

file: 1995/1995-02-03_actually a woman_claim_crying game_dress code_dress like a man_the boss.gif
title: Protesting Dress Code By Dressing Like Man

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm dressing like a man to protest the company's dress code.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, what you're saying is that you're actually a woman. Is that your claim?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's not exactly the point.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saw "The Crying Game." Don't do anything that would make me heave.

situation: Alice, her wild hair in full effect, tells the Boss she is wearing a shirt and tie like a man to protest the company dress code. The Boss responds by asking if she is claiming to be a woman, missing her point entirely. He then warns her not to do anything that would make him sick, referencing the film The Crying Game.
punchline: The Boss completely misses her protest and instead fixates on a movie plot twist, fearing a gender reveal that would make him nauseated.
summary: A woman's protest against workplace attire rules is derailed when her clueless manager mistakes it for a confession and cites a movie twist he found revolting.

file: 1995/1995-02-13_quantify contributions_designing future products_billion daollars_track numbers_boss_dilbert.gif
title: Dilbert Claims a Billion Dollars

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm asking everybody to quantify their contributions to revenue. Your pay will depend on it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I realize this is hard to quantify because you're designing future products but...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here you go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A billion dollars? It's as if you cynically believe we can't track these numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That crossed my mind.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his pay will depend on how much revenue he can say he contributed, admitting it is hard to measure for someone designing future products. Dilbert immediately writes down a figure and hands it over. The Boss is shocked that it is a billion dollars and accuses him of cynicism, which Dilbert cheerfully admits.
punchline: Dilbert inflates his revenue contribution to an absurd billion dollars because he correctly suspects management cannot actually verify the numbers.
summary: Told to put a number on his financial impact, an engineer simply writes down an outrageous sum and admits he doubts anyone can check it.

file: 1995/1995-04-30_introduce you_engineers_karen_new vp_value employee_open communications_emailing freind_window seat_ask raining_made raincoat_garbage bag.gif
title: Raincoat Made From Trash Bag

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me introduce you to one of our engineers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Karen is our new Vice President. And you are...?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dilbert: Valued employee.

transcript.speaker: Karen
transcript.text: I believe in open communications, Dilbert. Feel free to talk about anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh

transcript.speaker: Karen
transcript.text: So, what were you working on?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh-no

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... I was just sending an e-mail to somebody who sits by a window to ask if it's raining.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it's raining I'll fashion a raincoat from a large trash bag.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Watch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Three holes and you're ready to go!

transcript.speaker: Karen
transcript.text: Are you planning to go out at lunch?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only if it rains.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Karen, the new vice president, who invites him to speak openly about anything. The Boss panics as Dilbert admits he was emailing a coworker by a window to ask if it is raining, then demonstrates how he would turn a trash bag into a raincoat. When Karen asks if he plans to go out at lunch, he says only if it rains.
punchline: Given an invitation to speak openly, Dilbert reveals he wastes time on trivial things and is happy to wear a garbage bag, and the Boss's worry about the exposure is borne out by the absurd, deadpan exchange.
summary: Meeting the new executive, a nervous boss watches as his engineer cheerfully admits to idle email habits and models a homemade garbage bag poncho.

file: 1995/1995-08-27_changes to design_work around clock_work smarter_not harder_violate laws of physics_create radiation_ill user_mention in documents_beta tester.gif
title: Design Changes Violate Physics, Boss Shrugs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I made a few changes to the design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll have to work around the clock for months to make these changes!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Work smarter, not harder.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're trying to violate the laws of physics!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Rules were made to be broken.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This design would create enough radiation to instantly kill the user!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Be sure to mention that in the documentation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's work smarter not harder.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think we found the only "beta" tester we'll need.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert and Wally a set of design changes that would require months of overtime. When they object that it breaks the laws of physics and would emit lethal radiation, he dismisses the concerns and tells them to just note it in the documentation. Dilbert and Wally then plan to test the product on the Boss.
punchline: Since the Boss insists on a design that would instantly kill its user, the engineers decide he should be the only beta tester, turning his own 'work smarter' advice against him.
summary: Faced with a manager's impossible and deadly redesign, two engineers quietly decide to let him personally try it out.
keywords: rules were made to be broken

file: 1995/1995-07-30_open door policy_new vp_drop in_last vp was aloof_sourballs_furniture_cubicles are hot_huge insincere spider.gif
title: Open Door Policy Meets Sourballs

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our new VP says he has an "open door policy." Let's check it out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Knock knock.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hi ho. Nothing important. We just wanted to drop in.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This open door policy is great. Our last VP was aloof.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are those sourballs?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Look at all the furniture in here!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call couch!

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: Is there something I can do for you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well...sometimes our cubicles are too hot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you have somebody look into it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Boy, those sourballs sure lull you into a false sense of security.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The man is like a huge insincere spider.

setting: Office hallway and the new VP's office
situation: Wally and Dilbert take the new VP up on his open door policy and barge into his office with no real purpose. They lounge on his furniture and eat his sourballs, and when he asks what they want, they casually mention that the cubicles are too hot. Afterwards they realize the candy and friendliness have made them lower their guard.
punchline: The VP's open door policy is a trap: the candy and welcoming gestures disarm employees, and Wally's comparison to a huge insincere spider hints that the openness is a manipulative show.
summary: Two employees happily drop in on a new executive's office, only to realize afterward that his hospitality was a lure.

file: 1995/1995-07-25_change_prehistoric times_ancestors_caves_grunting_not very productive_all day long.gif
title: Cavemen Weren't Productive, Unlike Us

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's amazing how much we've changed since prehistoric times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our ancestors just sat around in caves, grunting and drawing on the wall.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not very productive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was just this, all day long.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mmm. Yup.

situation: Dilbert tells Wally how much humanity has changed since prehistoric times, describing cavemen who sat around grunting and drawing on walls. Wally calls that unproductive. In the last panel Dilbert is seen in his cubicle drawing on a whiteboard while Wally stands by, grunting agreement.
punchline: Modern office workers are doing exactly what cavemen did, sitting around grunting and drawing on a wall, so the supposed progress is an illusion.
summary: Two coworkers mock the idleness of cavemen while unwittingly behaving just like them in their cubicles.

file: 1995/1995-05-04_dogbert show_gettung givernment back_buy liquor_buy cigarettes_buy firearms_drive thru_gets rid of people.gif
title: Dogbert's Drive-Thru Deregulation Radio Show

transcript.speaker: Radio (Dogbert)
transcript.text: Welcome to the Dogbert Show. Today I talk about getting government off our backs.

transcript.speaker: Radio (Dogbert)
transcript.text: I dream of a world where someday you can buy liquor, cigarettes and firearms at a drive-thru window and use them all before you get home.

transcript.speaker: Radio (Dogbert)
transcript.text: Basically, anything that gets rid of people is okay with me. But before you go, buy my new book...

setting: Inside and outside Dilbert's car while he drives, listening to the radio
situation: Dilbert drives along listening to a radio talk show hosted by Dogbert, who champions less government interference. Dogbert proposes a drive-thru where people can buy liquor, cigarettes and firearms and use them all before getting home. He admits he just wants anything that eliminates people, then plugs his new book.
punchline: Dogbert's libertarian rhetoric is revealed to be a misanthropic wish to kill off the population, ending with a shameless plug for his book.
summary: A radio host's push for deregulation turns out to be a scheme to thin out humanity, capped with a sales pitch for his latest book.

file: 1995/1995-04-02_advertisingmaterials_technical accuracy_supposed to be funny_technical help_look up something_dictionary_engineers_not comedians_tech help_picked colors.gif
title: Engineers Critique Ad for Humor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you guys to check Anne's advertising materials for technical accuracy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is this supposed to be funny?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't get it.

transcript.speaker: Anne
transcript.text: I'm only looking for technical help here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey! Maybe you could say something about those warning tags on mattresses! Now THAT would be funny!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or how about the fact that you can't look up something in the dictionary if you can't spell it? THAT'S funny!

transcript.speaker: Anne
transcript.text: You're engineers, not comedians!! I want TECHNICAL help!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This guy has an XP-6. It should be an XP-7.

transcript.speaker: Anne
transcript.text: That's better.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And he should be saying "I've fallen and I can't get up."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who picked these colors?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert and Wally to review a marketing employee's advertising materials for technical accuracy. The engineers keep critiquing the humor and joking about mattress tags and dictionary spelling, and Anne gets angry and demands only technical help. They then make technical-sounding comments but quickly slide back into joking and criticizing the design.
punchline: The engineers are asked only for technical accuracy but can't stop critiquing the ad's humor and aesthetics, with Wally even slipping in a joke about a famous medical alert slogan.
summary: Two engineers asked to proofread a coworker's ad copy for facts instead keep poking fun at its jokes and looks, until she scolds them.

file: 1995/1995-09-15_time sheet_increments_15 minutes_meetings_shower time thinking_designing circuits_complaining.gif
title: Timesheet Coding: Meetings Count, Thinking Doesn't

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my time sheet, filled out in increments of fifteen minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As usual, I coded the useless hours spent in meetings as "work," whereas the time I spent in the shower designing circuits in my mind is "non-work."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Interestingly, even the time I spend complaining about my lack of productivity is considered "work."

transcript.speaker: Timesheet clerk (thought)
transcript.text: I hate my life.

setting: Office cubicle area where timesheets are turned in
situation: Dilbert hands his completed time sheet to a bored office clerk and explains how he categorized his hours. He points out that pointless meetings and complaining about unproductivity count as work, while real engineering thinking done in the shower does not. The clerk silently thinks about how much she hates her life.
punchline: Time tracking rules reward useless activity like meetings and complaining while ignoring the genuinely productive thinking that happens outside the official system.
summary: Dilbert turns in his timesheet and notes the absurd way it credits wasted hours while ignoring his best engineering ideas.

file: 1995/1995-05-02_dogberts talk radio_smartest creature_dolts_taking calls_understand complex_crossfire.gif
title: Dogbert's Talk Radio Caller Insults

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Talk Radio

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm the smartest creature in the universe and you are all dolts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today I'm taking calls from people who think they understand complex issues because they watch "Crossfire" on CNN.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: "... So why not put all poor people in orphanages?"

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Put your head up to the speaker, Bob.

situation: Dogbert hosts a talk radio show, opening by insulting his listeners and announcing he will take calls from people who think TV political debate shows make them experts. A caller then proposes a simplistic and absurd solution: put all poor people in orphanages. Dogbert invites the caller to put his head up to the speaker, implying he intends to hit or shout at him through it.
punchline: The caller's ridiculous oversimplified policy idea proves the host's point about TV-informed pundits, and Dogbert responds with an implied threat of violence through the speaker.
summary: A radio host who scorns his audience takes a call from a viewer of a TV debate show whose half-baked solution to poverty earns him a menacing invitation.

file: 1995/1995-08-13_marketing dept._best engineers_leverage technology_ant farms_speadsheets_ant milk_ant fram engineer_ordered dilbert_milk from ant_no risk_bite sized ant jerky.gif
title: Marketing's Ant Farm Retention Plan

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Here's how your marketing department can help retain your best engineers.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing gets an idea

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: We'll leverage our technology by building ant farms.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Spreadsheets make the idea look profitable.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: The ant milk alone will be a positive NPV!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's an NPV?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Don't forget the "worst case scenario."

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Worst case, somebody builds a gigantic magnifying glass next door...

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Solution: Bite-sized ant jerky!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no risk!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: An engineer will be assigned to the project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ant farms! Do it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The engineer will challenge the assumptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't get a gallon of milk from an ant!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you know about marketing?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Result: The engineer will never leave the company.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: So... your current job is "ant farm engineer"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm doomed.

situation: A marketing representative explains how marketing can retain top engineers, walking through a ridiculous plan to build ant farms, justified by spreadsheets and a dismissed worst-case scenario. The Boss, who doesn't know what NPV means, approves it and assigns Dilbert. When Dilbert objects that ants can't produce milk, he's brushed off, and he ends up permanently stuck as an ant farm engineer.
punchline: The 'retention strategy' works only because the engineer is trapped on an absurd doomed project that makes him unemployable elsewhere.
summary: Marketing pitches a silly ant-based product, the clueless boss approves it, and the engineer saddled with it is stuck for good.

file: 1995/1995-04-21_lots howard_cubicle neigborr_immortal soul_laser printer_dogbert doesn't care.gif
title: Loud Howard Threatens Cubicle Neighbor Deal

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Allow me to introduce Loud Howard.

transcript.speaker: Loud Howard
transcript.text: HI!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I will make Loud Howard your cubicle neighbor in the new office unless you give me your immortal soul!!

transcript.speaker: Loud Howard
transcript.text: NICE DAY!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Fortunately I convinced him to take my laser printer instead...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What did I say that sounded like "Tell me about your day"?

setting: Office hallway, then a therapy session with Dilbert on a couch
situation: Wally introduces Dilbert to the deafeningly loud Loud Howard and threatens to make him Dilbert's cubicle neighbor in the new office unless Dilbert hands over his immortal soul. Dilbert, lying on a therapist's couch with Dogbert taking notes, recounts that he escaped by giving up his laser printer instead, and Dogbert snaps at him for rambling.
punchline: Dilbert treats a demonic soul-for-cubicle bargain as a minor office negotiation and unloads it on his therapist, who has no interest in hearing about his day.
summary: A coworker blackmails Dilbert with a noisy neighbor, and Dilbert's retelling of the saga bores his therapist.

file: 1995/1995-06-01_cell phone_laptop_allow work_lug around_worry_broken_stolen_technology.gif
title: Portable Tech Isn't That Liberating

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My cellular phone and laptop computer allow me to work any time and anyplace...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: While driving?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In restaurants?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too rude.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Outdoors?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Basically, you lug them around and worry that they'll get stolen or broken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop it. You're scaring them.

situation: Dilbert boasts that his cell phone and laptop let him work anywhere at any time. Dogbert questions him about driving, restaurants and outdoors, and Dilbert admits each is impractical or inappropriate. Dogbert concludes the gadgets are just things to carry and worry about, and Dilbert jokes that he's scaring the devices.
punchline: Dilbert's claim of 'work anywhere' collapses under scrutiny, and he responds by treating his gadgets as if they have feelings that Dogbert's blunt assessment might hurt.
summary: A man praising his mobile gadgets as freedom machines gets a reality check about how little they actually help and how much they burden him.

file: 1995/1995-03-27_elbonians_run comapony_only female engineer_watch discrimination_coffee wenches.gif
title: Alice Welcomes Elbonian Discrimination Against Men

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In a way, I'm glad the Elbonians run this company now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: After years of being the only female engineer I'll enjoy watching the Elbonians discriminate against you guys.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I didn't realize you had coffee wenches in this country too.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hope you don't want children, Yorgi.

situation: Alice arrives at a meeting with Dilbert and Wally and says she is looking forward to seeing the new Elbonian owners discriminate against the male engineers after years of being the only woman in engineering. In the meeting, an Elbonian man mistakes her for a coffee wench as she serves him coffee, and she sarcastically tells him she hopes he doesn't want children.
punchline: Alice's smug expectation that she will benefit from the Elbonians' discrimination collapses when they treat her as a coffee server, and she responds with a threat of violence.
summary: A female engineer gloats about her new corporate overlords until they mistake her for the help and she retaliates.

file: 1995/1995-11-03_low cost paintings_walls_in a frame_how much paintings_corporate art source_dogbert art dealer.gif
title: Art Sold By The Pound

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The "Dogbert Corporate Art Source" will provide low-cost paintings for your walls.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our motto is "If it's in a frame it will look like art to you."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much do the paintings cost?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Six dollars a pound.

setting: Office meeting table in a conference room
situation: Dogbert pitches his new business, a corporate art supplier, to The Boss, who sits across the table browsing a catalog. Dogbert explains that anything in a frame will pass as art. When The Boss asks about price, Dogbert reveals the paintings are sold by weight.
punchline: Pricing paintings by the pound shows the art is treated as a bulk commodity with no real value, and The Boss is gullible enough to consider buying it.
summary: A canine salesman pitches cheap framed artwork to his boss and casually reveals it is priced by weight like produce.

file: 1995/1995-12-26_living document_plan to update.gif
title: Living Document Scares The Boss

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: This is a living document.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aaaah!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Next time, just say you plan to update it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mine's dead.

situation: At a meeting, a bald coworker announces that the document he is handing out is a 'living document.' The Boss recoils in terror, taking the phrase literally. Alice advises the coworker to say he plans to update it instead, while Dilbert glumly notes that his own document is dead.
punchline: The Boss takes the jargon 'living document' literally and panics, and Dilbert's deadpan remark that his is 'dead' mocks both the buzzword and the unmaintained state of most documentation.
summary: A coworker's corporate buzzword about a 'living document' sends the boss into a literal panic, prompting a dry suggestion for plainer language.

file: 1995/1995-12-31_boss idea_email system_stupid idea_universe_debate is futile_nuclear power_good or evil.gif
title: Facts About the Boss's Stupid Idea

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're doomed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got an idea!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't we run our inventory database over our e-mail system?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fact: That is the stupidest idea in the universe.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fact: His comprehension is so limited that debate is futile.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fact: We could spend hours unsuccessfully explaining why it's a stupid idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fact: He would never know if we used his idea or not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. We'll get right on it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My work is done.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stupidity is like nuclear power; it can be used for good or evil.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you don't want to get any on you.

situation: The Boss bursts into a meeting with an idea to run the inventory database over the e-mail system. Dilbert and Wally silently reason through a list of 'facts' concluding that arguing is pointless, so Dilbert simply agrees to go along, and the Boss congratulates himself.
punchline: Employees decide that explaining why an idea is stupid is a waste of effort, since the clueless boss will never know whether they actually implement it, and compare stupidity to nuclear power that you don't want to get on you.
summary: Faced with a ridiculous technical suggestion, two employees quietly agree it's easier to pretend to comply than to educate their uncomprehending manager.

file: 1995/1995-08-07_catbert the hr director_invent illogical policies_annoy emplyees_diabolical dress code_question sanity_casual clothes_wally insane.gif
title: Catbert's Diabolical Casual Dress Code

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the HR Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I think I'll invent some illogical policies to annoy employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My diabolical new dress code will make them question their own sanity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
