transcript.text: ...So, casual clothes don't lower our stock value... but only if worn on Fridays... unless somebody sees us... got it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I'm insane.

setting: Catbert's HR office, then a workplace office
situation: Catbert, the HR director, sits at his desk plotting to invent illogical policies that will annoy employees. He devises a convoluted casual-dress code. Dilbert then recites its contradictory rules to Wally, who clutches his head and declares he is going insane.
punchline: The dress code is so riddled with contradictions that it works exactly as Catbert intended, driving employees to doubt their own sanity.
summary: An evil HR cat dreams up a self-contradicting casual clothing rule and watches it leave a coworker convinced he is losing his mind.

file: 1995/1995-07-12_more than me_like computer_girl friend_jealous of computer_that computer_ask about lap top.gif
title: Dilbert Likes Computers Over Girlfriend

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: I think you like that computer more than you like me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not true, Liz. I do NOT like that computer more than I like you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) Please, please don't ask about the laptop.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: "That" computer?

setting: Dilbert's desk at home or in the office, in front of his computer
situation: Dilbert's girlfriend Liz accuses him of preferring his computer to her. He carefully denies liking 'that' computer more than her, while privately hoping she won't bring up his laptop. Liz catches the wording and calls it out.
punchline: Dilbert's carefully worded denial only covers one computer, revealing he actually does like his other computer (the laptop) more than his girlfriend, and Liz notices the loophole.
summary: A nerd's careful hedging about which computer he prefers over his girlfriend gives away that he's hiding a bigger tech obsession.

file: 1995/1995-07-08_teamwork_egyptians_pyramids_slaves_built by slaves_shooting_guided by ufos.gif
title: Pyramid Teamwork Built by Slaves

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want us to have the same kind of teamwork as the Egyptians who built the pyramids!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Some scholars believe the pyramids were built by slaves.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But there's some doubt; that's all I'm shooting for.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think they were guided by UFOs too.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team he wants them to have the same teamwork as the Egyptians who built the pyramids. Alice points out that scholars believe the pyramids were built by slaves. The Boss says there is some doubt about that, and Dilbert sarcastically adds that the pyramid builders were probably guided by UFOs too.
punchline: The Boss is so desperate to preserve his motivational analogy that he clings to the slim doubt that the pyramid builders were slaves, which Dilbert mocks by pointing out the same flimsy reasoning would let you believe UFOs were involved.
summary: A manager holds up ancient pyramid builders as a teamwork model, then grasps at fringe doubt when his team notes they were slaves.

file: 1995/1995-11-28_be my couch_dysfunctional internet connections_huge ball yarn_human resources_treatment prgrams_used as furniture_yarn therpay_ropes_business.gif
title: Yarn Therapy From Catbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does Human Resources offer any treatment programs for people with dysfunctional Internet connections?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I recommend the "Yarn Therapy." You'll be wrapped in a huge ball of yarn and used as furniture in my office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this like the famous "ropes" course where I learn to solve problems as part of a team?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Exactly, except here you learn to be my couch.

situation: Dilbert asks the Human Resources director, Catbert, whether the company offers treatment programs for people with dysfunctional Internet connections. Catbert recommends 'Yarn Therapy,' showing a picture of a turtle wrapped in a ball of yarn, in which Dilbert would be wrapped up and used as furniture. Dilbert compares it to a team-building ropes course, and Catbert cheerfully agrees, except that he'd be learning to be a couch.
punchline: Catbert twists a well-meaning HR wellness or team-building program into a scheme to turn an employee into his personal furniture, showing HR's disregard for employees.
summary: Seeking help for a flaky network link, an engineer is offered a bizarre HR cure that would turn him into a cat's living-room furniture.

file: 1995/1995-03-04_predicted success_salaries_die in stapler mishap_disagree_precition_opinion_analysis_science.gif
title: Salary Based on Predicted Stapler Death

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, salaries will be based on your predicted success, not your past performance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We ran a computer model against your education and DNA information. We predict you'll die in a stapler mishap within a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I disagree with this prediction?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write up your opinion and staple it to the analysis.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that pay will now be set by a computer model's prediction of future success rather than past performance. The model, fed Dilbert's education and DNA, predicts he will die in a stapler accident within a week. When Dilbert asks how to dispute it, the Boss tells him to write up his opinion and staple it to the analysis.
punchline: The Boss's dismissive appeal process involves stapling, the very instrument of Dilbert's predicted death, so the objection will go nowhere and may even risk the prediction coming true.
summary: A manager announces a pay system driven by an absurd computer forecast and brushes off the employee's objection with a stapling instruction.

file: 1995/1995-06-25_over worked_engineer_more work_too many projects_success impossible_same result_honk honk_inventory_office building_engineering.gif
title: Alice Embraces Impossible Workload

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take care of this, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "Take care of this"? This would double my workload.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've already got so many projects that I can't do anything useful with any of them.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But if success is impossible then...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm...free.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Free! Free! Ha ha ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The result will be the same no matter what I do! Yes yes yes

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Honk honk!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Moving along...we need to inventory our office equipment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a job for Alice.

situation: During a meeting the Boss dumps another task on Alice, who already has too many projects to accomplish anything. She realizes that since success is impossible, she is liberated from caring, and she gleefully celebrates and honks the Boss's nose. The Boss ignores it and assigns the next task, and Dilbert volunteers Alice for it.
punchline: Alice's moment of liberation from an impossible workload doesn't save her, because the oblivious Boss and Dilbert simply keep piling more work onto her.
summary: An overloaded engineer finds joy in the fact that nothing she does can matter, yet is promptly handed yet another assignment.

file: 1995/1995-11-25_run to post offcie_buy more than one stamp_float.gif
title: The Boss Explains Float

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've gotta run to the post office.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You go to the post office every day. Are you aware that you can buy more than one stamp at a time?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Apparently you don't understand the concept of "float."

situation: The Boss announces he has to leave for the post office, and Alice points out that he goes there every day and could simply buy several stamps at once. The Boss condescendingly replies that she doesn't understand the concept of "float."
punchline: The Boss uses a misapplied financial term, "float," to justify his daily errand, which is really just a way to get out of the office, and makes Alice look ignorant for questioning it.
summary: A manager defends his daily trips out of the office by dismissing a coworker's practical suggestion with a piece of business jargon.

file: 1995/1995-06-19_hired_finance_dept_cut spending_studying_inefficeincy_boldface_electricity_money.gif
title: Cost-Cutting Ratbert Targets Boldface Electricity

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've been hired by the finance department to help cut spending.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll be studying your every move and looking for waste and inefficiency.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Those words in boldface look like they're sucking up the ol' electricity.

situation: Ratbert introduces himself to Dilbert as a cost-cutting consultant hired by the finance department, saying he will study Dilbert's every move for waste. While watching Dilbert work at his computer, Ratbert points to bolded text on the screen and claims it uses extra electricity.
punchline: The supposed efficiency expert's big discovery of waste is a ridiculous, nonsensical claim that boldface text consumes more electricity, mocking shallow and uninformed cost-cutting.
summary: A small pet-like rodent hired to trim expenses watches an engineer work and decides that bold lettering on a monitor must be draining power.

file: 1995/1995-02-17_the problem_under staffed_six weeks_behind_the analysis_add people_the result_daily stats reports_situation.gif
title: Daily Reports for Late Project

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The problem...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're so understaffed that the project is six weeks behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The analysis...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't add people... I can't change the due date... I can't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The result...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He wants daily status reports until the situation improves.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the project is six weeks behind because the team is understaffed. The Boss ponders his options in a thought bubble, ruling out adding people, moving the deadline, and ignoring the problem. Dilbert then explains to Wally and Alice that the Boss's solution is to demand daily status reports.
punchline: Faced with a problem caused by too little staff, the Boss picks the one action that adds work and fixes nothing, making the team's situation worse.
summary: A manager who rules out every real remedy for a late, understaffed project settles on burdening the team with paperwork.

file: 1995/1995-06-07_dysfunctional team_admore_vocalize admiration_leathery skin_right from left_get paid_admire co workers.gif
title: Backhanded Compliments in Team-Building Exercise

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dysfunctional team...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like everybody to turn to the right and say what you admire about that person.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I admire your leathery skin, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I admire your ability to figure out which side is your right in only two tries.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I admire your ability to get paid for this.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Despite the fact your face scares children, I admire your co-workers.

setting: Conference room around a round meeting table
situation: The Boss leads a team-building exercise in which everyone must turn to the person on their right and say something they admire about them. Instead of sincere praise, each coworker delivers a thinly veiled insult, and the insults chain around the table.
punchline: Forced admiration exercises on a dysfunctional team just produce passive-aggressive insults disguised as compliments.
summary: When a manager orders his bickering staff to compliment one another, they respond with a round of barbed, backhanded praise.

file: 1995/1995-08-21_rejected by accounting_emptiness_shallow_validate_pathetic exitsence_fear this up_philosophy.gif
title: Why Accounting Rejected My Expenses

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your expense report was rejected by Accounting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Because the emptiness of their shallow lives makes them want to hurt others in order to validate their pathetic existence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you help me clear this up?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: To be honest, I'm kinda buying in to their philosophy.

setting: Office hallway outside a cubicle or doorway
situation: A coworker hands Dilbert a paper and tells him Accounting rejected his expense report. When Dilbert asks why, the coworker gives a bitter explanation that the accountants are hollow people who hurt others to feel significant. Dilbert asks for help sorting out the rejection, and the coworker admits he is starting to agree with the accountants' outlook.
punchline: The messenger who is supposed to help resolve the problem has been so persuaded by the cynical view of Accounting that he sides with the people causing it.
summary: A rejected expense claim leads to a scathing diagnosis of the accountants' motives, ending with the messenger quietly admitting he finds their worldview appealing.

file: 1995/1995-10-08_primitive_donut scavenging man_yellow sticky notes_humiliation_live off land_bountiful harvest_dance to gods_meeting notices.gif
title: Donut Scavenger Calls the Meetings

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's four hours that I'd like to have back.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who called that meeting anyway?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I must have left my calendar in there.

transcript.speaker: Scavenger
transcript.text: Oooh

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've discovered a primitive donut-scavenging man clad only in yellow sticky notes!!

transcript.speaker: Scavenger
transcript.text: I was once like you, before the Great RIF.

transcript.speaker: Scavenger
transcript.text: But rather than leave in humiliation I decided to stay and live off the land like our proud ancestors.

transcript.speaker: Scavenger
transcript.text: To ensure a bountiful harvest I do my donut dance to the gods.

transcript.speaker: Scavenger
transcript.text: When that doesn't work I distribute meeting notices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're the one!!

setting: Office conference room after a meeting
situation: After a four-hour meeting, Wally and Alice wonder who called it while Dilbert realizes he left his calendar in the conference room. Inside he finds a former employee dressed in yellow sticky notes, living on the meeting room's donuts since being laid off. The man explains he stayed after a mass layoff and survives by scavenging donuts, calling meetings whenever his donut dance fails to bring food.
punchline: The mysterious meetings that waste everyone's time are being called by a laid-off employee who secretly lives in the office and just wants the free donuts.
summary: A downsized worker who never left the building survives like a caveman on leftover pastries, scheduling pointless meetings to restock his food supply.

file: 1995/1995-05-13_interview successful people_start with you_alarm clock_jello bed_boy im tired_ratbert_dogbert.gif
title: Dogbert's Nonsense Success Tips

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm going to interview successful people and write a book of their tips. I'll start with you, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Set your alarm clock to go off every hour. Keep a big vat of "Jell-O" by the bed. When the alarm goes off, stick your head in the "Jell-O" and yell "Boy, I'm tired!"

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Thanks!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Beware the advice of successful people; they do not seek company.

setting: Dogbert's lounging spot on a cushion, in a plain room
situation: Ratbert, holding a notepad, announces he will interview successful people for a tips book and starts with Dogbert. Dogbert gives absurd instructions involving an hourly alarm and a vat of Jell-O, and Ratbert gratefully writes them down. Dogbert then thinks a warning about taking advice from successful people.
punchline: Dogbert gives Ratbert ridiculous, useless advice, and his private thought reveals that successful people don't want company, so they happily send imitators off on pointless tasks.
summary: A trusting rodent collects wisdom for a book and gets silly instructions from a dog who quietly mocks anyone who takes advice from the successful.

file: 1995/1995-12-27_tidy cucbicle_cleanliness_work space_cleaner_fantasize_maid_five more minutes.gif
title: Dilbert Fantasizes About Being a Maid

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay! This is one tidy little cubicle now!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The cleanliness of one's work space is a sign of how much one enjoys one's job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Give me the cleaner; it's my turn to fantasize that I'm a maid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Five more minutes... please.

situation: Dilbert finishes scrubbing his cubicle spotless, then wipes his nameplate while declaring that a clean workspace shows how much someone enjoys their job. Alice arrives with her hand out and demands the spray bottle because it's her turn to fantasize she's a maid. Dilbert begs for five more minutes of cleaning.
punchline: Dilbert's obsessive cleaning is revealed to be an escapist fantasy, as both he and Alice would rather pretend to be maids than do their actual jobs, implying they hate their work.
summary: Two coworkers take turns scrubbing the cubicle as an escape from their real jobs, which quietly contradicts the idea that tidiness signals job satisfaction.

file: 1995/1995-10-04_dogbert_corporate jet pilot_captain dogbert_first flight_training budget_look out window_jump_in case of crash.gif
title: Dogbert's First Flight Training Warning

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, corporate jet pilot

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Attention, passenger.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm Captain Dogbert. This is my first flight. I'll bet you wish you hadn't cut the corporate training budget.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For safety, keep an eye out the window... If it looks like we're gonna hit the ground, try jumping up right before impact.

setting: Corporate jet in flight, with the cockpit seen from outside and a passenger cabin
situation: Dogbert is the pilot of a corporate jet and addresses the lone passenger over the intercom. He announces it is his first flight and blames the passenger for cutting the corporate training budget. He then offers a useless safety tip: jump up just before the plane hits the ground.
punchline: Dogbert's untrained piloting and absurd crash-survival advice show the deadly consequences of slashing training budgets, delivered with deadpan sarcasm.
summary: An inexperienced dog flying a company plane lets his nervous passenger know that skimping on training has put them both in danger.

file: 1995/1995-05-12_motivational speaker_discount speakers bureau_work harder_get fired_working harder_slow class.gif
title: Discount Motivational Speaker Threatens Firing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today we have a motivational speaker from the "Discount Speakers Bureau."

transcript.speaker: Motivational Speaker
transcript.text: You should, like, work harder... otherwise you might get fired. Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would we get bonuses for working harder?

transcript.speaker: Motivational Speaker
transcript.text: This must be the slow class.

setting: Conference room during a company training session
situation: The Boss introduces a motivational speaker hired from a cut-rate speakers bureau. The speaker's whole message is vague and threatening: work harder or get fired. When Dilbert asks whether harder work would earn bonuses, the speaker dismissively says this must be the slow class.
punchline: The cheap speaker offers a lazy, threat-based pep talk and then insults the one employee who asks a perfectly reasonable question about incentives.
summary: A bargain-bin motivational speaker tells employees to work harder or face dismissal, then mocks the person who asks about rewards.

file: 1995/1995-09-08_thinking_quitting_contract emplyee_advice_sleep in doorways_hunk of coradboard_co workers_food stamps_not edible.gif
title: Alice's Advice: Contract Work Means Homelessness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Alice, I'm thinking about quitting and becoming a contract employee. Do you have any advice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sleep in doorways so it doesn't rain on you. The best shopping carts are at "Lucky." You can make an excellent sign with a black marking pen and a hunk of cardboard.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hate all of my co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Despite the name, food stamps are not edible.

situation: Wally tells Alice he is considering quitting to become a contract employee and asks for advice. Alice responds with tips for living on the street, such as sleeping in doorways, finding good shopping carts, and making a cardboard sign. Wally then says he hates his co-workers, and Alice continues with advice about food stamps.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that leaving a steady job for contract work will leave Wally destitute and homeless, and Wally is so sick of his co-workers that he keeps listening anyway.
summary: A coworker mulling a leap into freelance work gets a deadpan crash course in living as a vagrant.

file: 1995/1995-03-13_decide to buy_recommend position.gif
title: Acquirer Promises Only A 'Position'

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I promise that if I decide to buy your company I'll gladly recommend a position for each of you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Really? You'd make sure we all got jobs?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, but I'll recommend a "position."

situation: Dogbert, acting as a prospective buyer, tells the company's staff gathered around a conference table that he will recommend a position for each of them if he buys the company. Wally hopefully asks whether that means they'll all get jobs. Dogbert clarifies that he only means he'll recommend a 'position' in the abstract, not employment.
punchline: Dogbert exploits the double meaning of 'position' to make an empty-sounding promise of jobs while guaranteeing nothing, mocking vague reassurances given to employees during acquisitions.
summary: A would-be buyer's comforting pledge to the staff turns out to be a verbal loophole that guarantees no one any employment.

file: 1995/1995-12-20_'bring your dog to work day_dogbert_no such thing_through firewall.gif
title: Dogbert Hacks Personnel Records

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, what's Dogbert doing here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is "Bring Your Dog to Work Day."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's no such thing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm through the security firewall and into the personnel records.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to talk.

situation: Alice spots Dogbert sitting at Dilbert's computer and asks what he is doing there. Dilbert claims it is "Bring Your Dog to Work Day," and Alice says no such thing exists. Dogbert, still typing, announces he has broken through the security firewall and into the personnel records, and a stern Dilbert says they need to talk.
punchline: Dilbert's invented holiday excuse for Dogbert's presence is made far worse when Dogbert reveals he is actually hacking into confidential employee files.
summary: A made-up excuse for bringing a dog to the office collapses when the dog is caught breaking into the company's confidential employee database.
keywords: bring your dog to work day

file: 1995/1995-10-29_dilbert needs staples_asks secreatry_need order number_supply catalog_wally borrowed_wally needs help_alice needs meeting_new vendor_almost stapled.gif
title: Teamwork Prevents Stapling Anything

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Helen, do you have any staples in the supply cabinet?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: No, I only stock the basics: cheap pens with green ink, big jars of glue and ribbons for obsolete printers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you order some staples?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: You need to give me the order number.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. Can I see your supply catalog?

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: Wally borrowed it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better get that; it might be personal.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sob

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Rrring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, do you have the...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I need your help with this. Pull up a chair.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I need both of you to come talk to a vendor that we'll never use.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks to teamwork, I almost stapled something today.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm so proud to know you.

setting: Office cubicles and the administrative assistant's desk
situation: Dilbert tries to get some staples. Helen the supply clerk stocks only useless items, demands an order number, and says Wally borrowed the supply catalog. Dilbert's attempt to retrieve the catalog from Wally turns into getting dragged into helping Wally, then Alice recruits both for a pointless vendor meeting.
punchline: Every step of a trivial task gets derailed by bureaucracy and colleagues' demands, so Dilbert ends the day having accomplished nothing, with Dogbert sarcastically praising the 'teamwork'.
summary: A simple quest for office staples collapses into a chain of unhelpful supply rules, borrowed catalogs and pointless meetings.

file: 1995/1995-09-05_new inspirational psoter_inspired_see front_win win.gif
title: Inspirational Poster Seen From Behind

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new inspirational poster is so effective that I decided to carry it with me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you think, Alice? Are you inspired?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd really have to see the front...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... I don't think there's a win-win scenario here...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Tell me about it...

situation: The Boss proudly carries a new inspirational poster around and asks Alice if she finds it inspiring. Since he is holding it with the blank back facing her, Alice says she'd need to see the front. The Boss then holds it up in front of himself, finding himself in a no-win situation, and Alice sarcastically agrees.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he shows Alice only the blank back of the poster, and Alice's deadpan 'Tell me about it' hints at her constant experience of no-win situations working for him.
summary: A boss shows off his motivational poster to a coworker without realizing he is displaying only its blank reverse side.

file: 1995/1995-02-06_ethical question_telecommuting_owe employer_saving planet_not driving_meeting_business.gif
title: Telecommuting Ethics and Saving the Planet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an ethical question about telecommuting, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I owe my employer eight productive hours, or do I only need to match the two productive hours I would have in the office?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, when you factor in how you're saving the planet by not driving, you only owe one hour.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And this meeting counts.

setting: Dilbert's home office, where he works in a bathrobe
situation: Dilbert, working from home in his bathrobe with a cup of coffee, asks Dogbert whether he owes his employer a full eight hours or just the two productive hours he'd normally manage in the office. Dogbert reasons that the environmental benefit of not commuting reduces his obligation to one hour, then adds that their conversation already counts toward it.
punchline: Dogbert uses absurd self-serving logic to shrink Dilbert's work obligation to one hour and then immediately declares the chat itself fulfils it, so Dilbert can stop working.
summary: A robe-clad telecommuter seeks moral cover for slacking, and his canine adviser cheerfully reasons his workday down to a single hour that is already used up.

file: 1995/1995-02-24_performance review_years of rejection_general disdain_simian_perfromance.gif
title: Rated Simian, Thanks Anyway

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm terrified about my performance review tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Men have it easier. You've been conditioned by years of rejection and general disdain.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're lucky that way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Overall, I rated your performance as "simian."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks!

setting: Office hallway and the boss's office
situation: Alice tells her coworkers she is terrified of her upcoming performance review. Wally and Dilbert explain that men are better prepared for harsh judgment because they are used to rejection and disdain. In the review, the boss rates Dilbert's performance as "simian," and Dilbert cheerfully thanks him.
punchline: Years of being conditioned to expect rejection and disdain leave Dilbert so accustomed to abuse that he thanks his boss for an insulting review that compares him to an ape.
summary: Having been toughened by a lifetime of rejection, a man responds with gratitude when his boss rates his work as ape-like.

file: 1995/1995-03-07_finish program_fast_train him_prodcutive_big glowing thing.gif
title: Adding a Clueless Helper Speeds Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to finish your program twice as fast, so I'm adding a person to help you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You might need to train him a little before he's productive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Warning! Warning! Dr. Smith

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Tell me again what the big glowing thing is.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that to finish his program twice as fast he is adding another person to help. He casually adds that Dilbert may need to train the newcomer first. In the last panel the new hire sits at the computer and asks what the big glowing thing is, meaning the monitor, showing he knows nothing about computers.
punchline: The helper meant to double the speed cannot even identify a computer monitor, so adding him will only slow the project down.
summary: A manager assigns a brand-new assistant to speed up a software project, but the recruit turns out to be completely unfamiliar with computers.

file: 1995/1995-03-28_fetch coffee_surprise you_kicked into hat_alice_elbonian_sexist_coffee wench.gif
title: Elbonian Learns Coffee Custom Painfully

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In this country we have a custom when men ask women to fetch coffee.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stand up... That's it... Now this will really surprise you.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Oh God

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: I've never seen anybody get kicked into his hat before.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's gotta hurt.

situation: During a meeting, a bearded visitor in a tall hat holds out a coffee cup and expects Alice to fetch him coffee. Alice calmly explains the local custom, tells him to stand up, and kicks him so hard that he ends up jammed into his own hat. The Boss and Dilbert look on in horror and wince.
punchline: Alice's 'custom' for sexist coffee requests is a violent kick, delivered with deadpan politeness, leaving the man stuck in his hat.
summary: A visiting man who expects a woman to bring him coffee gets a very physical lesson in local manners from Alice.

file: 1995/1995-07-20_teds baby shower_stapler_paper bag dress_cubicle this morning_stapler on desk_disappeared from desk.gif
title: Stolen Stapler Becomes Baby Shower Gift

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ted's baby shower

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Oh look, it's a stapler...

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I can use this to take up the hem on the lovely hand-crafted paper bag dress that Dilbert made.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: It looks just like the one that disappeared from my cubicle this morning.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Except yours had staples.

situation: Coworkers gather around a pile of gifts at Ted's baby shower. Ted unwraps a stapler and, while joking about using it on a paper bag dress, observes it resembles one stolen from his cubicle that morning. Wally, holding a gift, quips that Ted's stapler had staples, implying this one is empty and he gave Ted's own stapler as the gift.
punchline: Wally casually admits he stole Ted's stapler and regifted it at the shower, with the only difference being he removed the staples.
summary: A baby shower gift turns out to be a coworker's own missing office supply, thinly disguised by a technicality.

file: 1995/1995-10-16_wearing enough fragrance_better increase doasge_hear compliments.gif
title: Overdosing on Office Perfume

transcript.speaker: Woman in purple dress
transcript.text: I wonder if I'm wearing enough fragrance.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (offscreen)
transcript.text: Aieeeee!!

transcript.speaker: Woman in purple dress
transcript.text: I'd better increase the dosage until I hear some compliments.

situation: A coworker in a purple dress, surrounded by clouds of perfume, wonders whether she has applied enough fragrance. Nearby colleagues are overcome by the fumes, with one falling headfirst out of view and others collapsing in the hallway, yet she remains oblivious.
punchline: She interprets the screams and collapsing coworkers as a lack of compliments and decides to apply even more perfume, completely missing that the fragrance is toxic to everyone around her.
summary: A woman drenched in perfume misreads her colleagues' agonized reactions and resolves to spray on even more.

file: 1995/1995-09-25_iso 900 audit_documented job_auditor asks_engineer_engineering.gif
title: Job Descriptions Versus Actual Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're having an ISO 9000 audit this week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take a look at your documented job descriptions and make sure that it's what you're doing if the auditor asks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to this I'm some sort of engineer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As if we'd have time for that...

situation: The Boss announces an upcoming ISO 9000 audit and tells Dilbert and Wally to check their documented job descriptions and make sure they match what they actually do if the auditor asks. Dilbert reads his description and notes it calls him an engineer. Wally replies that they never have time for real engineering work.
punchline: The official job description says engineer, but the employees spend their time on everything except engineering, so the documented description bears no relation to reality.
summary: Ahead of a quality audit, two workers discover their paperwork describes jobs they never actually get to do.

file: 1995/1995-05-14_accomplishments_who gets raises_lie about achievments_favoritism_minimizing accomplishments_billion dollars_impossible_verify_invisible rust_gets raise_three people.gif
title: Raises Reward Lying and Favoritism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write up your accomplishments so I can decide who gets raises this year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you saying our raises will depend on our ability to lie about our achievements?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, there's also favoritism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't forget the importance of minimizing the accomplishments of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "This year I saved a billion dollars in ways which are impossible to verify."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "While the others plotted against you, I was applying an invisible rust inhibitor to your car."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can drop those off for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed she's the only one who ever gets a raise?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's as if she has the accomplishments of three people.

situation: The Boss tells his staff to write up their accomplishments for raises, and admits that favoritism and belittling coworkers also count. Dilbert and Wally write absurd, unverifiable claims, then hand them to Alice, who offers to deliver them to the Boss. They later notice that Alice is the only one who ever gets a raise.
punchline: By delivering the others' write-ups herself, Alice quietly takes credit for their work, so she appears to have the accomplishments of three people, and the coworkers never realize they are the cause.
summary: After being told to exaggerate their achievements and diminish rivals, two employees hand their write-ups to a colleague who then collects every raise, unaware they've fed her success.

file: 1995/1995-08-01_hire temp_apply for job_ratbert_all of the respect_unconditional love_office and secretary.gif
title: Ratbert Dreams of Temp Glory

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're planning to hire a temp at work. You should apply for the job, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Wow! Me? A temp?!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: As a temp I would finally get all of the respect and unconditional love that I deserve!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Danger: Sharp learning curve ahead.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I assume I'll get an office and a secretary.

situation: Dilbert suggests that Ratbert apply for a temp position at the company. Ratbert excitedly imagines that being a temp will earn him respect and unconditional love. Dilbert privately thinks about the steep learning curve Ratbert will face, while Ratbert naively assumes he'll get an office and a secretary.
punchline: Ratbert has wildly unrealistic expectations of what a temp job offers, while Dilbert knows a temp will actually be thrown into a difficult, thankless role.
summary: A hopeful little pet eagerly eyes a short-term job, picturing perks no temporary worker ever receives, while his coworker silently braces for the reality.

file: 1995/1995-04-14_dogbert the pr consultant_no letter q_opportunity assignement_public_shipped keyboards.gif
title: Volunteering for Blame After Keyboard Fiasco

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the PR Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You shipped keyboards with no letter "Q." The public wants somebody to take responsibility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh ooh pick me pick me!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Responsibility means blame.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great... it's like the time I got burned on that "opportunity" assignment.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a PR consultant, tells the company that the public wants someone to take responsibility for shipping keyboards missing the letter Q. The Boss eagerly volunteers, thinking responsibility is a prize. Dilbert points out that responsibility really means blame, and the Boss compares it to a previous "opportunity" that burned him.
punchline: The Boss enthusiastically volunteers for what he thinks is an honor, not realizing that responsibility means taking the blame, and he has fallen for the same trap before when management disguised bad assignments as "opportunities."
summary: Eager to be chosen, the Boss leaps at the chance to be held accountable for a product blunder until he learns what that actually entails.

file: 1995/1995-11-02_dotted line_arch rival_secret double agent_captured and executed_immediate.gif
title: Dotted Line Double-Agent Doom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard you got assigned on a "dotted line" to our boss' arch-rival.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Groan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look on the bright side. Think of yourself as leading the exciting life of a secret double-agent!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't most double-agents get captured and executed immediately?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They wish it was immediate.

situation: Dilbert tells a groaning coworker that he has been assigned on a dotted-line reporting relationship to their boss's arch-rival. Dilbert tries to cheer him up by calling it the exciting life of a secret double-agent. The coworker notes that double-agents usually get captured and executed immediately, and Dilbert grimly says they wish it were immediate.
punchline: Dilbert implies that being caught between two warring bosses will bring a slow, drawn-out misery that is worse than a quick execution.
summary: A worker stuck reporting to his boss's rival is told he's like a spy, but the fate awaiting him is a prolonged torment rather than a swift end.

file: 1995/1995-10-31_focus core bsuiness_core business change_misdirected failure_car gets flat_rotate tires_drive home.gif
title: Wally Mocks Reorg With Flat Tire

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't understand how the new reorganization will help us "focus on our core business."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did our core business change? Or are you saying that every reorg prior to this was a misdirected failure?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, when a car gets a flat tire, what do you do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, if I'm you, I rotate the tires and drive home.

situation: Wally questions The Boss about how yet another reorganization will help the company focus on its core business, pointing out that either the core business changed or all earlier reorganizations were failures. The Boss responds with a car-and-flat-tire analogy, and Wally answers that if he were the boss he would rotate the tires and drive home, implying the boss's fix misses the real problem.
punchline: Wally sarcastically suggests that the boss's answer to a real problem is a pointless, irrelevant action, just like rotating tires when one is flat, which mirrors how reorganizations fail to fix anything.
summary: A skeptical employee challenges the logic of a new reorganization, then answers his boss's car analogy with a deadpan jab at management's habit of fixing the wrong thing.

file: 1995/1995-08-04_ratbert_temp worker_really testing self worth_compensate list of talents_walks past_ignore i eat rubber_i carry disease_i enjoy opera.gif
title: Ratbert Shouts His Talents Desperately

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Temp Worker

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: This is really testing my sense of self-worth.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I will compensate by shouting a list of my talents to anybody who walks past.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ignore him. He's trying to trick us into making eye contact.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I eat rubber! I carry disease! I enjoy opera!

situation: Ratbert, working as a temp, sits in a cardboard box on the floor and thinks that his situation is hurting his self-esteem. He decides to shout out a list of his talents to passersby. Dilbert and a coworker walk past, and Dilbert advises ignoring him while Ratbert shouts his bizarre qualifications.
punchline: Ratbert's list of 'talents' is absurdly unappealing (eating rubber, carrying disease), and Dilbert treats his plea for attention as a ploy to be avoided.
summary: A desperate temp in a cardboard box advertises his dubious skills to passing employees, who are advised to pretend he isn't there.

file: 1995/1995-01-31_ignorance_no limits_idiotic_opinions_personal hygiene_cyberspace_flame boy_step inside.gif
title: Brave Flamer Meets Cubicle Neighbor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your ignorance seems to have no limit. Your opinions are idiotic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your personal hygiene leaves much to be desired. Your family is ugly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Send e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're mighty brave in cyberspace, flame-boy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Step inside.

situation: Dilbert types an insulting, abusive e-mail to a colleague, attacking his intelligence, hygiene and family, and sends it. The offended coworker pops his head over the cubicle wall to confront him. Dilbert calmly invites him to step inside his cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert is only brave behind a keyboard, so the 'step inside' invitation is an empty bluff to avoid a real confrontation, or at least a sly dare he doesn't expect to be accepted.
summary: After firing off a nasty e-mail, a cubicle dweller is confronted by its recipient and responds with a calm invitation to settle it in person.

file: 1995/1995-10-12_original timeline_12 months_pitched in_exact end date_cold dark_cheunk_coal_size_forehead_need flashlights_sweaters_nippy.gif
title: Project Ends When Sun Dies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our original project time line was twelve months... But since you pitched in to help...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have an exact end date, but it's roughly the same time that the sun becomes a cold dark chunk of coal the size of your forehead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll need flashlights.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And sweaters. It could get nippy.

setting: Office, Dilbert's cubicle or a meeting area
situation: Dilbert reads from a long paper printout, explaining that the project's original twelve-month timeline has grown now that the Boss has pitched in to help. He estimates the new end date as roughly when the sun burns out. The Boss responds by suggesting flashlights, and Dilbert adds that sweaters will be needed.
punchline: The Boss's 'help' has delayed the project so badly that it will finish only when the sun dies, and the Boss obliviously plans for the cold and dark rather than recognizing the insult.
summary: A meddling manager's involvement stretches a one-year project to the end of the solar system, and he cheerfully plans for the darkness.

file: 1995/1995-08-31_dogbert treks tna_tech writer_technical writing_word processing_highly skilled_communications professional_inert thoughts_staff meeting_org chart_secretary meeting.gif
title: Dogbert Provokes the Brittle Tech Writer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert tweaks Tina the brittle tech writer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is technical writing the same as word processing?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: No!!!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I am a highly skilled communications professional! I can take jumbles of inert thoughts and bring them to life!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My secretary is running the staff meeting. I need you to retype this org chart.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The doctor is in!

situation: Dogbert goads Tina, a tech writer, by asking whether technical writing is the same as word processing, and she angrily insists she is a highly skilled communications professional. The Boss then walks up and asks her to retype an org chart because his secretary is running the staff meeting, proving Dogbert's point.
punchline: Tina's passionate defense of her professional status is instantly undercut when the boss treats her as a typist, confirming that management sees technical writing as word processing.
summary: After a tech writer angrily insists her job is more than typing, her boss immediately hands her a chart to retype.

file: 1995/1995-11-21_ratbert_consulting partner_jobs outsiurced_stooped over_very bad ergo nomics.gif
title: Ratbert Consultant Recommends Bad Ergonomics

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My consulting partner, Ratbert, will demonstrate how to inform employees that their jobs will be outsourced.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're history. Scram.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Boot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do I get them all stooped over?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I recommend a program of very bad ergonomics.

setting: Office desk and the Boss's office
situation: Dogbert introduces his consulting partner Ratbert, who demonstrates how to tell employees their jobs are being outsourced by kicking Dogbert off the desk. The Boss, apparently looking to get his workers all stooped over, asks how to do it, and Ratbert suggests bad ergonomics. A dazed Dogbert's tail is seen sticking out of the wastebasket.
punchline: The consultant's advice for breaking bad news is brutally dismissive, and his follow-up solution deliberately harms employees by giving them poor posture and workplace injuries.
summary: A pair of consultants show a boss how to deliver layoff news with a swift kick, then propose damaging employee health through terrible workstation design.

file: 1995/1995-05-27_fields of heather_flying dreams_important change_soon increase_somebody else_new ceo.gif
title: Dilbert's Dream Predicts Freedom, Finger Stuck

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my dream I float over fields of heather.

transcript.speaker: Heather
transcript.text: Hi! I'm Heather.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The flying dream always predicts an important change. I feel that my freedom will soon increase.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Does somebody else have a question for our new CEO?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My finger is stuck.

setting: Dream landscape, then a conference room during a meeting with the new CEO
situation: Dilbert floats through the air in a dream, passing over fields of heather where a little girl named Heather greets him, and he interprets the flying dream as a sign that his freedom will soon increase. In the final panel he is actually in a meeting with the new CEO, daydreaming, and when asked for questions he says his finger is stuck, as a woman beside him holds her finger in her mouth.
punchline: Dilbert's dream of expanding freedom is contrasted with the reality of a boring meeting where he is literally stuck, and the dream's literal flying and puns on heather and finger show how little his optimism connects to his circumstances.
summary: A hopeful flying dream promising greater freedom ends with Dilbert trapped in a meeting with a finger caught somewhere awkward.

file: 1995/1995-01-03_united charity_least valuable member_honesty_best plocy.gif
title: Wally Chosen for Being Pitiful

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations, Wally. I've selected you to head up our campaign for "United Charity."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I chose you not only because you're the least valuable member of the group, but also because you're so darn pitiful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Honesty is the best policy unless it's being done to you.

situation: The Boss congratulates Wally and puts him in charge of the company's United Charity campaign. He then cheerfully explains that Wally was picked because he is the least valuable employee and is so pitiful, which visibly rattles Wally. In the last panel the Boss thinks that honesty is only a good policy when you are not on the receiving end.
punchline: The Boss delivers brutally honest insults to Wally, then smugly admits in his own thoughts that he would not tolerate that kind of honesty if it were aimed at him.
summary: A manager hands an employee a charity assignment while insulting him as worthless and pathetic, then privately reveals he dislikes honesty when it's directed his way.

file: 1995/1995-07-22_missing years_at mall_dad at mall_looking for him_247_waiting for sale_whiner.gif
title: Dad Lost at Mall Since 1992

transcript.speaker: Woman in green
transcript.text: I can't believe your father has been lost at the mall since 1992!

transcript.speaker: Woman in green
transcript.text: If my father or my husband were lost at the mall I'd be searching for him twenty-four hours a day!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're waiting for a sale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's mother
transcript.text: You're a bit of a whiner, aren't you, dear?

setting: A table where three people are having tea
situation: Dilbert sits having tea with his mother and a woman in green. The woman is appalled that Dilbert's father has supposedly been lost at the mall since 1992, saying she would search constantly if it were her family. Dilbert deadpans that the family is simply waiting for a sale, and his mother calls the woman a whiner.
punchline: The father isn't lost at all: the family is casually leaving him at the mall until a sale comes along, and the one who gets scolded is the person horrified by it.
summary: A tea guest is shocked by a relative's years-long disappearance at a shopping centre, only to learn the family has shrugged it off as part of waiting for discounts.

file: 1995/1995-11-13_write bug free software_ten dollar bonus_find and fox_right behavior_new minivan_afternoon.gif
title: Bug Bounty Becomes Minivan Fund

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal is to write bug-free software. I'll pay a ten-dollar bonus for every bug you find and fix.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yahoo!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We're rich!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!!! Yes!!! Yes!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope this drives the right behavior.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm gonna write me a new minivan this afternoon!

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces a ten-dollar bonus for every bug the engineers find and fix, in order to produce bug-free software. The engineers immediately cheer, realizing they can get rich. Wally says he will write himself a new minivan that afternoon, implying he'll deliberately create bugs to collect the bonus.
punchline: Paying a bounty per bug fixed rewards people for creating bugs, so the incentive scheme backfires and encourages the engineers to write buggy code on purpose.
summary: A manager's reward for every fixed defect has the programmers gleefully planning to manufacture their own payday.

file: 1995/1995-02-09_fourth day_telecommuting_clothes useless_struck by question_monkeys_beards_discuss issue_attendance low_around table_introduce.gif
title: Naked Telecommuting Meeting About Monkey Beards

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: On my fourth day of telecommuting I realize that clothes are totally unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Suddenly I am struck by a question: Why don't monkeys grow beards?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: I call a meeting to discuss the issue but attendance is low.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Issue one: Monkey beards.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's go around the table and introduce ourselves.

situation: Dilbert, working from home without any clothes on, becomes fixated on why monkeys don't grow beards. He calls a meeting to discuss it, but the only attendee is Dogbert, who suggests the standard round of introductions across a table for two.
punchline: Working alone at home has stripped away both his clothes and his sense of proportion, yet he still reproduces the formal rituals of a corporate meeting, even with only one other attendee.
summary: A telecommuter who has stopped wearing clothes holds a formal meeting about an absurd question and gets exactly one attendee.

file: 1995/1995-04-15_stick to script_act sincere_forgive you_worng_sell key boards_morons_dumber than squirrels_good writing.gif
title: Scripted Apology Written by Dogbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stick to the script. Act sincere and beg your customers to forgive you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was wrong for us to sell keyboards with no "Q." We're sorry. We're morons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're dumber than squirrels. We hear voices and do what they command. I have broccoli in my socks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good writing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks.

setting: A video studio with a camera, and Dilbert's living room watching TV
situation: The Boss is filming a customer apology video about selling keyboards that have no letter Q, reading from a script handed to him by Dogbert. The script has him call the company morons, dumber than squirrels, and claim he has broccoli in his socks. Dilbert and Dogbert watch the broadcast at home and compliment the writing.
punchline: Dogbert wrote a deliberately humiliating script and the oblivious Boss sincerely read every word, even the absurd line about broccoli in his socks.
summary: A manager dutifully reads an insulting, nonsensical apology written by a scheming dog while the two watch it on TV and congratulate themselves.

file: 1995/1995-07-23_few suggestions_alice's document_bonk_guards to document_obtuse acronyms_jargon_multi topic sentences_stubby_plastic stautes.gif
title: Boss Ruins Alice's Document, Claims Authorship

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I had a few suggestions on your document, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BONK

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've made some upgrades to your document, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's just what it needed: a bunch of obtuse acronyms and jargon.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Oooh, looky! You've also made elegant multi-topic sentences out of my stubby clear ones!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you. And put me down as the author since I'm the boss.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe I should distribute little plastic statues of you with every copy. How about that?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here's your copy, here's your statue, don't ask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our quality is low, but at least we don't get credit.

situation: Wally offers a few suggestions on Alice's document, and she knocks him away with a bonk to the head. The Boss then 'upgrades' her document with jargon and convoluted sentences and demands authorship credit. Alice responds by handing out copies of the document along with little plastic statues of the Boss, while Dilbert remarks on the outcome.
punchline: Alice sarcastically thanks the Boss for making her clear writing worse, then mocks his demand for credit by pairing every copy with a voodoo-style statue of him, while Dilbert wryly notes that the poor quality at least means no one gets credit.
summary: A manager mangles an employee's clear writing with buzzwords, takes authorship credit anyway, and gets mocked with a little effigy of himself.

file: 1995/1995-03-29_elbonian owner_competetor_motto_beat em join em_humiliate_not catchy.gif
title: Company Sold, Competitor's Motto Revealed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our Elbonian owners sold the company to our biggest competitor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our motto is "If you can't beat 'em, join 'em."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder what their motto is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Their motto is "After you beat 'em, humiliate 'em."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's not very catchy.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the Elbonian owners have sold the company to its biggest competitor. He cheerfully cites the company motto about joining those you can't beat, and Dilbert asks what the new owners' motto is. The Boss reveals it is about humiliating the people you beat, and a coworker remarks that it isn't catchy.
punchline: The new owners' motto reveals they intend to humiliate the employees they just acquired, and the coworker's only complaint is that the slogan isn't catchy enough.
summary: After a buyout by a rival, the staff learn that their new corporate masters believe in rubbing defeat in the faces of those they conquer.

file: 1995/1995-04-09_ranked engineers_best to wworst_bottom 10%_includes you_logically flawed_fire_fire body parts_wally freaked outm_torsos_glands_blood and bile_fired hair.gif
title: Firing the Bottom Ten Percent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We ranked all the engineers from best to worst.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We plan to get rid of the bottom 10%. That includes you, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your plan is logically flawed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If you fire the bottom 10%, you'll still have a bottom 10%.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll fire and fire but there will always be a bottom 10%, until finally...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: When less than ten people are left you'll have to fire body parts instead of whole people!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We'll have torsos and glands wandering around unable to use keyboards... Blood and bile everywhere!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How'd it go?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He fired my hair.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway
situation: The Boss tells Wally that engineers have been ranked and the bottom 10% will be fired, including Wally. Wally argues the plan is logically flawed because there will always be a new bottom 10%, escalating to a gory vision of firing body parts. Afterward Dilbert asks how it went and Wally reveals the Boss fired only his hair.
punchline: The Boss took Wally's absurd reductio ad absurdum literally and started the process by firing a body part, Wally's hair, rather than recognizing the flaw in the policy.
summary: A worker mocks a layoff scheme by pushing its logic to a bloody extreme, only for his boss to cheerfully start carving off pieces of him.

file: 1995/1995-09-06_inspirational poster_animal research_beautiful scene_nightly eagle swoop.gif
title: Boss Tests Poster on Ratbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My inspirational posters aren't working. I need to do some animal research, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Ready!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In this beautiful scene we see a mighty eagle swooping down to capture its prey. What is your reaction?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think it's working.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Run for it, Mom!!!

setting: Office, with Ratbert standing on a desk
situation: The Boss decides his inspirational posters aren't motivating anyone, so he recruits Ratbert as a research subject. He holds up a poster of an eagle capturing its prey and asks for Ratbert's reaction. Ratbert reacts with terror, identifying with the prey.
punchline: The Boss mistakes Ratbert's panic at the predator imagery for the poster working, missing that it inspires fear rather than motivation.
summary: A clueless manager tests a predatory-bird poster on a tiny rodent and takes the animal's terrified reaction as proof of success.

file: 1995/1995-04-05_any rumors false_no plans_no relocation plans_south pole_eskimos_replaced by_liar boss.gif
title: Boss Denies South Pole Relocation Rumor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want to assure you that any rumors you've heard are false.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We are not planning to relocate the company to the South Pole where easily trainable native Eskimos will replace you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's good because there aren't any Eskimos at the South Pole.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Excuse me, I have to make a phone call.

situation: The Boss assures Dilbert and Alice that rumors about the company are false, then accidentally reveals the exact plan by denying it in detail: moving to the South Pole to replace them with easily trainable Eskimos. Dilbert points out there are no Eskimos at the South Pole, and the Boss hurries off to make a phone call, presumably to fix his plan.
punchline: The Boss's detailed denial exposes that he is actually planning the relocation, and he leaves to work out the flaw Dilbert pointed out.
summary: A manager's reassurance about a layoff rumor accidentally spells out the scheme, and an employee's geographic correction sends him scrambling to revise it.

file: 1995/1995-04-18_dogbert_financial advisor_sticks_nuuities_capital gains_reduce income taxes_give me money_die a pauper.gif
title: Dogbert Scams Client as Financial Advisor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Financial advisor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stocks... annuities... derivatives... capital gains tax...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's all too confusing for you!! Give me all your money now or you'll die a pauper!! Now! Now! Before interest rates fall!!

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: Will this reduce my income taxes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: More than you might guess.

situation: Dogbert, posing as a financial advisor, overwhelms a client with financial jargon and then pressures him to hand over all his money immediately, using scare tactics. The client, unfazed, asks only whether the deal will reduce his income taxes.
punchline: Dogbert's answer implies the client will have no income left to tax, since Dogbert is taking all his money.
summary: A con-artist canine adviser bamboozles a customer into surrendering his entire fortune, leaving him with a tax bill of nothing.

file: 1995/1995-04-08_cubicle_smaller_stauts adjusters_sendors_monitor work_adjust according_value size_tiny boxes_employees_get used to_business.gif
title: Cubicle Shrinks With Your Value

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just as I thought, my cubicle is two inches smaller today than yesterday!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We installed real-time status adjusters in the cubicle walls. Sensors monitor your work and adjust the cubicle size according to your value.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's amazing how fast you get used to it.

setting: Boss's office and the cubicle area
situation: Dilbert measures his cubicle and complains to the Boss that it is two inches smaller than yesterday. The Boss cheerfully explains that sensors in the walls monitor each employee's work and resize the cubicle according to their value. A coworker sitting in a tiny, shrunken cubicle remarks that you quickly get used to it.
punchline: Employees' worth is literally measured and displayed by shrinking cubicle walls, and the sad resignation of a coworker in a tiny cubicle shows people just adapt to being devalued.
summary: Office walls that automatically shrink to reflect how little the company values each worker leave one coworker cramped but oddly accepting.

file: 1995/1995-03-01_never time lunch_men are early_upgrading pcs_paid off_effieciency_hungry_secrets.gif
title: Lunch Break Blamed on PC Upgrades

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why is it that I never have time to eat but you men are in here every day at 11:35?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Because the hours we spent upgrading our PCs have finally paid off by greatly improving our efficiency.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought it was because we get hungry at 11:30.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We can't reveal all our secrets.

situation: Alice complains that she never gets time to eat while her male coworkers are always sitting down for lunch at 11:35. Wally claims the hours spent upgrading their PCs have made them far more efficient. Dilbert, eating a banana, honestly says they just get hungry at 11:30, and Wally dismisses it as a secret they shouldn't reveal.
punchline: Wally's claim that PC upgrades boosted efficiency is a flimsy excuse for taking early lunches, and Dilbert blurts out the real reason, which Wally tries to pass off as a trade secret.
summary: A colleague questions why the men always get to eat early, and the excuse about productivity gains from computer upgrades collapses when the simple truth slips out.

file: 1995/1995-10-13_human resources_developed policy_employees who complain_big hole_trick whiners_sand_detailed explaination_hole_business.gif
title: Catbert's Hole for Complainers

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: As Director of Human Resources I have developed a policy for handling the employees who complain.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's a big hole. I'll trick the whiners into getting in it. And then I'll cover them with sand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see how this could possibly work.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There's a detailed explanation at the bottom of the hole.

setting: Office, in front of the Boss
situation: Catbert, the Director of Human Resources, tells the Boss about his new policy for dealing with employees who complain. His plan is to dig a big hole, trick complainers into climbing in, and bury them in sand. When the Boss doubts it will work, Catbert says the detailed explanation is waiting at the bottom of the hole.
punchline: Catbert's lure for the Boss's skepticism is the same trap he uses on complainers, so anyone who asks questions about the policy ends up in the hole too.
summary: The evil HR director outlines a plan to bury grumbling workers alive and answers his boss's doubt by inviting him to go look in the pit.

file: 1995/1995-02-05_dogbert_explains leader ship_drawn to meetings_bladder to brain_impervious to logic_coffee_promited_leadership is natures way_removing morons_start as morons.gif
title: Dogbert Explains Leadership: Promoting Morons

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert explains leadership

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Leaders start their careers as morons.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They are drawn to meetings like moths to a porch light.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The successful moron will have a very high bladder-to-brain ratio.

transcript.speaker: Label
transcript.text: Brain

transcript.speaker: Label
transcript.text: Bladder

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They prevail in all decisions because they are impervious to logic or coffee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's do it my way!

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Okay!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: These qualities are perceived as leadership.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: You're promoted!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After several promotions their job tends to match their talents.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I award you this award.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Conclusion: Leadership is nature's way of removing morons from the productive flow.

setting: A lecture presentation by Dogbert, with scenes of a conference room and office
situation: Dogbert gives a mock lecture on how leaders emerge. He claims they begin as morons who love meetings, win every decision because they ignore logic, and are mistaken for leaders and promoted. Eventually they reach a job that suits them: handing out meaningless awards instead of doing real work.
punchline: Promotion of incompetent people into management is portrayed as nature's way of getting them out of the way of people who actually do the productive work.
summary: Dogbert lectures that incompetent people rise into leadership because their obliviousness looks like decisiveness, and they end up harmlessly handing out awards.

file: 1995/1995-07-24_boss late_small talk_meet with marketing_outfir_chair is springy.gif
title: Practicing Painfully Awkward Small Talk

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As usual, the boss is late. What do you want to do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's practice making small talk. It'll come in handy when we meet with marketing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So, Alice, haven't we seen that outfit a lot?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This chair is springy. Do you think they're all springy?

setting: Conference room, waiting for a meeting to start
situation: While waiting for the late boss, Dilbert suggests the group practice small talk to prepare for a meeting with marketing. Wally immediately comments on Alice's repeated outfit, and Dilbert bounces in a springy chair and asks if all the chairs are springy.
punchline: The engineers' attempts at small talk are so socially clumsy that they come out as insults and non sequiturs, showing why they need marketing-style practice.
summary: A group of engineers rehearse chitchat for marketing and fumble it with a tactless wardrobe jab and a bizarre furniture observation.

file: 1995/1995-01-21_team leader_raise_no extra money_responsibility_best epople_leave better companies_recognize them.gif
title: Promotion Without a Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm promoting you to team leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I get a raise?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no extra money, just extra responsibility. It's how we recognize our best people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought all the good people leave for better companies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's another way to recognize them.

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's boss
situation: The Boss announces that he is promoting Dilbert to team leader. Dilbert asks about a raise and is told there is no extra pay, only more responsibility. When Dilbert points out that good employees tend to quit for better companies, the Boss says that is another way they recognize their best people.
punchline: The company's only way of identifying its best employees is noticing who quits, so a promotion with no pay is just extra work for those who stay.
summary: A manager hands out a title with more duties and no money, then admits that talented staff are only noticed once they've left for somewhere better.

file: 1995/1995-06-23_mister catbert_diversity_the worse_german accent_wally_computer issues.gif
title: Computer Preference Treated as Religious Persecution

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mister Catbert, the company is trying to force me to use a different kind of computer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're the human resources director. What are you doing to stop this religious persecution??! What ever happened to "diversity"??

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The longer you verk here, diverse it gets.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Next.

situation: An employee complains to Catbert, the HR director, that the company is forcing him onto a different kind of computer, and he frames it as religious persecution that violates the company's diversity policy. Catbert replies with a pun on 'diverse' and a mangled accent, then dismisses him and calls the next person.
punchline: Catbert turns the diversity complaint into a bad pun and brushes the employee off, showing HR has no interest in his computer grievance and that the employee's attempt to exploit diversity rhetoric fails.
summary: A worker claims being switched to another brand of computer is religious persecution, and the callous HR cat answers with a groaner of a pun before moving on.

file: 1995/1995-06-30_advice_dogbert consulting comapny_business units_cross cahrging_undermining_comepotition_healthy_janitorial.gif
title: Battlin' Business Units Compete Internally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to follow the advice of the Dogbert Consulting Company and form "Battlin' Business Units."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll spend most of our time cross-charging and undermining the other BBU's.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A little competition is healthy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever you do, don't tick off the janitorial BBU.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces to the team that, following Dogbert's consulting advice, the company will split into 'Battlin' Business Units' that fight each other. He cheerfully admits they will mostly cross-charge and sabotage the other units. A coworker says a little competition is healthy, and the Boss warns them not to anger the janitorial unit.
punchline: Turning internal departments into warring factions is absurd and destructive, and the only real fear is offending the janitors, who hold the practical power to make everyone's life miserable.
summary: A manager adopts a consultant's plan to pit departments against each other, then nervously cautions against crossing the cleaning staff.

file: 1995/1995-10-27_redundant projects_big binder_seems useful_useless binders_build my addition.gif
title: Useless Binders Build Cubicle Addition

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Three other people asked for that same information. You must be on redundant projects.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Here's a big binder which at first glance seems useful, but you'll realize later it's not.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've got a few more useless binders. Do you want 'em?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I'm using them to build an addition to my cubicle.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker for information and is told that three other people asked for the same thing, which means they are all on redundant projects.
