The coworker hands over a big binder that only looks useful, then offers several more useless binders. Dilbert accepts them cheerfully, planning to use them as building material for his cubicle.
punchline: Since the binders contain nothing of value, Dilbert repurposes them as bricks, mocking both the pointless documentation and the duplicated work behind it.
summary: A pile of worthless documentation from overlapping projects finds its only real use as construction material.

file: 1995/1995-07-07_new dress policy_allows casual clothes_stick plunge_friday_only safe day_policy stupid.gif
title: Casual Friday Is Stupid, Obviously

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new dress policy at work allows casual clothes on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's good, because studies have shown that Fridays are the only safe day to dress casually; any other day would cause a stock plunge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it just me or is that policy stupid?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's not an "or" question.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch and tells Dogbert about his company's new dress policy that allows casual clothes only on Fridays. Dogbert says studies show Fridays are the only safe day for casual dress, since any other day would cause a stock plunge. Dilbert then asks if the policy is stupid, and Dogbert replies that it is not an either/or question.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically confirms the policy is stupid by pointing out that Dilbert's 'is it me or is it stupid' question has no 'or' option, meaning both are true.
summary: Dogbert mocks a company's limited casual-dress policy and then bluntly confirms to Dilbert that it is both his perception and the policy that are the problem.

file: 1995/1995-02-01_staus report_light_email_flame war_technical surperiority_simian ancestry_obligation_victims of hormones.gif
title: Flame War Excuses Light Status Report

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My status report is a bit light this week because I'm having an e-mail flame war with Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally refuses to admit my technical superiority or his simian ancestry. It is my obligation to set him straight.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Never!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking this somehow elevates my rank in the herd and improves my mating possibilities.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're victims of hormones.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Dilbert explains to the meeting that his status report is thin because he has been fighting an e-mail flame war with Wally, who won't concede Dilbert's technical superiority or his own descent from apes. Dilbert then muses that winning the argument might raise his standing in the herd and improve his chances of finding a mate, and Wally chimes in that they are both just victims of hormones.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally admit that their petty online feud is really just primitive, hormone-driven status competition, which they are using as an excuse for doing less actual work.
summary: Two coworkers justify a sparse status report by revealing their office email feud is really an instinctive contest for dominance and mates.

file: 1995/1995-01-22_protects webs prodcuts_engineer_pads schedule_six months_build prodcut_play doom_computer_add people_tiny empire_eighteen months_sales people_irrational desire_beta test_technology_engineering.gif
title: How Nature Protects Weak Products

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How nature protects weak products

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: First, the engineer pads his schedule

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Six months?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One month to build the product and five months to play "Doom" on my computer.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Then the manager pads the schedule as a clever negotiating ploy.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: One year... unless you add people to my tiny empire.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Then the vice president pads the schedule to avoid looking bad to the president.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: Eighteen months.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile, the sales people are making up numbers because nobody tells them anything.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Two months... and it solves every problem you have!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This causes the customers to develop irrational desire for the product.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Give me the "beta" test version in one month.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Thus nature disguises weak products as "beta".

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Cardboard? That's stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh... Then it's beta.

setting: Offices and meeting rooms, narrated as a nature-documentary lecture
situation: Dogbert lectures on how weak products survive, tracing the schedule as an engineer, a manager and a vice president each pad the estimate. Meanwhile sales makes up delivery promises, so customers demand the product early. The finished product is a piece of cardboard, which Dilbert excuses by calling it beta.
punchline: Calling a worthless product a "beta" makes any defect, even being a piece of cardboard, acceptable to customers.
summary: Layer upon layer of schedule padding and sales exaggeration ends with a useless product being passed off as an early test release.

file: 1995/1995-03-08_twice as afst_doubling staff_coded modules_mouse not a mic_boss understands now_pa system.gif
title: Barry Talks Into His Mouse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you working twice as fast since I doubled your staff?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've coded twelve modules... Barry is on a journey of discovery where he will find out my mouse is not a microphone.

transcript.speaker: Barry
transcript.text: Hello! Anybody!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would explain why nobody ever comments on my announcements over the P.A. system.

situation: The Boss peeks over the cubicle wall and asks whether Dilbert is working twice as fast now that his staff has doubled. Dilbert says he has coded twelve modules on his own while the new hire, Barry, is busy talking into a computer mouse as if it were a microphone. Back at his desk, the Boss draws the wrong conclusion and links this to the lack of response to his P.A. announcements.
punchline: The Boss thinks the new hire's mistake explains why nobody responds to his P.A. announcements, showing he is just as clueless as Barry and holding a mouse like a microphone himself.
summary: A manager checks whether extra headcount has sped up a programmer, learns the new hire is mistaking his mouse for a microphone, and absurdly realizes this explains the silence after his own office announcements.

file: 1995/1995-10-03_jet pilot experimce_ow hard_money_pretty boy_experience_corporate jet_budget pressure_pilot eject seat.gif
title: Dogbert Applies To Pilot Corporate Jet

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Your résumé doesn't list any experience as a jet pilot, Mister Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How hard could it be?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could spend a lot of money on some pretty boy pilot with experience, or you can save a few bucks and have me drive the corporate jet.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I am under a lot of budget pressure... and I'm not allowed on the jet myself...

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: It has a pilot eject seat, right?

setting: A manager's office during a job interview
situation: Dogbert interviews for the job of corporate jet pilot despite having no flying experience. He pitches himself as the cheaper alternative to an experienced pilot. The manager, feeling budget pressure and knowing he won't be a passenger, considers hiring him.
punchline: The manager is so intent on saving money that he is willing to hire an unqualified pilot to fly the jet, as long as the plane has an ejector seat for the pilot and he isn't aboard himself.
summary: A budget-obsessed manager is persuaded to let an inexperienced dog fly the company aircraft, as long as the pilot's seat can be launched out of it.

file: 1995/1995-06-27_benchmark_world class companies_compare_verbs_nouns_assign_engineers_field research_pointy haired idioits.gif
title: Benchmarking Against Better-Run Companies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I want you to benchmark these world-class companies. Find out how we compare.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm betting they don't make verbs out of nouns. And I'll bet they don't assign engineers to do field research.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you guys have any pointy-haired idiots running your place?

transcript.speaker: Person on phone
transcript.text: Would you like one?

setting: Office meeting room and Alice's desk
situation: The Boss orders Alice to benchmark world-class companies to see how his company compares. Alice grumbles that such companies probably don't misuse language or send engineers on field research. She then phones one of them and asks whether they have any pointy-haired idiots running things, only to be offered one.
punchline: Alice's sarcastic benchmarking question gets the answer that even the world-class companies suffer from the same incompetent managers, so her company compares just fine.
summary: Sent to compare her firm with the best in the industry, Alice learns that clueless management is a universal constant.

file: 1995/1995-02-12_strategic planning team_satisfaction_vague emotional terms_mediocre thinkers_believe options_steer the company_viewgraphs_last years viewgraph.gif
title: Strategic Planning Team Recycles Viewgraphs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you on the strategic planning team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's like work but without the satisfaction of accomplishing anything.

transcript.speaker: Strategic Planning Team Member
transcript.text: You're new, so let me explain how this works.

transcript.speaker: Strategic Planning Team Member
transcript.text: We have meetings and talk about the company's strategy in vague emotional terms.

transcript.speaker: Strategic Planning Team Member
transcript.text: In time, we convince ourselves that we're more than mediocre thinkers who sit around complaining.

transcript.speaker: Strategic Planning Team Member
transcript.text: We start believing our opinions will steer the company. We feel important. We feel ALIVE!!

transcript.speaker: Strategic Planning Team Member
transcript.text: Then we snap out of it and make viewgraphs that say we should keep doing what we're doing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like making viewgraphs.

transcript.speaker: Strategic Planning Team Member
transcript.text: Actually, we use last year's viewgraph.

characters: Strategic planning team member (woman with curly hair)
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to the strategic planning team and cheerfully admits it is work without accomplishment. A veteran team member explains the routine: vague, emotional meetings, a fleeting delusion of importance, then viewgraphs recommending no change. Dilbert says he likes making viewgraphs, only to learn they just reuse last year's.
punchline: Even the one concrete output of the strategic planning team, the viewgraph, is not newly created but recycled from last year, underscoring that the team accomplishes nothing.
summary: A new recruit learns that corporate strategy sessions are a cycle of vague talk, brief self-importance, and recycled slides endorsing the status quo.

file: 1995/1995-06-18_crossfire_cnn_only creature_televsion_each me_debate_television_same desires_experiences_disagree_stupid_over silplfying_opinion_entertainment.gif
title: Dogbert Teaches Ratbert Crossfire Debating

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I've been invited to be a guest on "Crossfire" on CNN.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm the only creature on Earth who hasn't already been on television.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Can you teach me how to debate on television, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: First, Ratbert, assume everybody has the same desires and experiences as you.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Absorb absorb.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Therefore, if they disagree with you they must be stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you're over-simplifying, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What was that opinion, Ratbert?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Stupid!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're ready for "Crossfire," Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I usually like the same movies as the fat one.

situation: Ratbert announces he has been invited onto the CNN show Crossfire and asks Dogbert to teach him how to debate on television. Dogbert's lesson is to assume everyone shares your desires and experiences, so anyone who disagrees must be stupid. When Dilbert objects that this is oversimplifying, Ratbert immediately calls his opinion stupid, and Dogbert declares him ready.
punchline: Ratbert has perfectly absorbed the lesson that disagreement means stupidity, so he dismisses Dilbert's valid criticism out of hand, which is exactly the shallow style of TV political debate.
summary: A pet coaches another to appear on a cable news shouting show by teaching him to treat every dissenting view as idiocy, and the pupil proves a natural.

file: 1995/1995-12-25_900 numbers_valuable advice_voice mail_1990s.gif
title: Ignoring the Ringing 900 Number

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I got myself one of those "900" phone numbers. I make money every time somebody calls for my valuable advice.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ring ring ring ring ring ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever answer it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Voice mail... get with the nineties.

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he has set up a pay-per-call 900 number and earns money whenever someone phones for his advice. The phone rings repeatedly while Wally sits there doing nothing. Dilbert asks if he ever answers it, and Wally says he lets voice mail take it.
punchline: Wally collects money for advice he never actually gives, since callers pay to reach a line he never answers, and he brushes off the question as if voice mail were simply modern practice.
summary: A lazy coworker profits from a paid advice hotline while letting every call go unanswered.

file: 1995/1995-03-14_no surpirses_hideous thing_scares me_auditor_sound.gif
title: Auditor Screams at Company Books

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My consultant will audit your company to make sure there are no surprises before I buy it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I use him because he's seen such hideous things that nothing scares him.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Erk.

transcript.speaker: Grim Reaper
transcript.text: Aaaaeeii!! Ooouwaa waa!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's not the sound you want from your auditor.

situation: Dogbert, planning to buy the Boss's company, introduces his consultant, a Grim Reaper figure, to audit the books. Dogbert boasts that the consultant has seen so many hideous things that nothing frightens him. The consultant then reads the company's documents and screams in terror, papers flying.
punchline: The company's finances are so horrifying that even a fearless Grim Reaper auditor screams in terror, revealing how bad the books must be.
summary: A death-figure hired to audit a company before an acquisition is reduced to hysterical shrieking by what he finds in the paperwork.

file: 1995/1995-02-15_same meail_last week_best of wally_cube sabbaticle_first notice.gif
title: Wally's In-Cube Sabbatical Reruns

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you just sent me the same e-mail you sent last week.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm rerunning the "Best of Wally" while I'm on in-cube sabbatical.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long is your sabbatical?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Six months so far, and you're the first to notice.

situation: Dilbert looks over the cubicle wall and complains that Wally just resent him last week's e-mail. Wally, slouched at his computer, explains he is rerunning his greatest hits while on an 'in-cube sabbatical'. Dilbert asks how long it has lasted, and Wally says six months, with Dilbert the first to notice.
punchline: Wally has done essentially no real work for six months while pretending to be on sabbatical, and nobody in the company has noticed his absence of productivity.
summary: A lazy coworker recycles old messages while quietly coasting at his desk for half a year without anyone catching on.

file: 1995/1995-08-18_increased my visibility_invisible_management_known by all.gif
title: Visibility Gained By Screwing Up

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I significantly increased my visibility at work today, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yesterday I was invisible to my management. But today I am known by all.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You screwed up, huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh yeah. Big time.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert lying on the floor
situation: Dilbert proudly tells Dogbert that he has greatly increased his visibility at work, going from unnoticed by management to known by everyone. Dogbert deadpans that he must have screwed up, and Dilbert confirms he did, in a big way.
punchline: The only way an ordinary employee becomes noticed by management is by making a major mistake, so greater visibility is really notoriety.
summary: An engineer brags about newly gained recognition at work, and his dog correctly guesses it came from a spectacular blunder.

file: 1995/1995-03-18_own company_dogbert_trim middle management_fire anyone_fyi on documents_fyi files in barrel.gif
title: Dogbert Fires FYI Document Senders

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that you own the company, what do you plan to do?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Trim middle management.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll fire anybody who gives me a document marked "FYI". Those people have too much time on their hands.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Are you sure this will set me apart from the other managers?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll be surprised how quickly.

situation: Dogbert has bought the company and, sitting behind a big desk, announces he will trim middle management by firing anyone who sends him a document marked FYI. A manager then pushes a wheelbarrow stacked with FYI-stamped papers toward him, asking whether this will make him stand out from other managers.
punchline: The manager, oblivious to the new policy, delivers a cartload of FYI documents, and Wally sarcastically notes he will indeed stand out quickly, since he is about to be fired.
summary: A new corporate owner announces a purge of paper-pushing managers, and one clueless manager promptly wheels in a mountain of exactly the forbidden paperwork.

file: 1995/1995-04-11_shipped million keyborads_free upgardes_royal family.gif
title: Keyboards Missing the Letter Q

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, so we shipped a million keyboards that don't have the letter "Q." What do we do?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We could offer free upgrades to users who can prove they need a "Q."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many users need a "Q"?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well... there's the Royal Family...

situation: At a meeting, the Boss admits the company shipped a million keyboards with no letter Q and asks what to do. A coworker proposes free upgrades only for users who can prove they need a Q, and when asked how many such users exist, can only think of the Royal Family.
punchline: The coworker's cost-cutting plan assumes almost nobody needs the letter Q, with the Royal Family (Queen, Quentin) as the only users he can name, which makes the absurd product defect seem like no big deal.
summary: Managers shrug off a huge manufacturing blunder by betting that practically no one will ask for the missing key.

file: 1995/1995-01-25_being team leader_stressful_no authority_behavioral study_plus sude_pellets_excelllent.gif
title: Team Leader Lab Rat Pellets

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate being team leader. It's so stressful.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have responsibility but no authority. I feel like I'm an animal in some warped behavioral study.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ding

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the plus side, the pellets are excellent.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer, thinking about how stressful it is to be team leader with responsibility but no authority. After a ding, he compares himself to a lab animal in a behavioral study, then reaches over to a dispenser labeled 'Take Pellet' on the wall and eats a pellet.
punchline: Dilbert's workplace literally resembles a lab experiment, with a pellet dispenser like those used for lab animals, and he is reduced to praising the quality of the food as the only upside of his powerless job.
summary: A stressed-out team leader likens his powerless position to being a lab rat and finds his only comfort in the tasty reward pellets.

file: 1995/1995-01-23_team leader_decide raises approve expenses_fire people_leader_manager.gif
title: Team Leader Without Any Authority

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As you know, I've been promoted to team leader.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Will you decide raises?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you approve expenses?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you fire people?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a leader, not a manager.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Well, run along and we'll be right behind you.

situation: Dilbert announces to his team that he has been promoted to team leader. Alice questions him on whether he controls raises, expenses, or firing, and he answers no to each. He insists he is a leader, not a manager, and Alice sarcastically tells him to go ahead while they follow.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that a leader with no real authority has no power to make anyone follow him, so she and the team will politely stay behind him.
summary: A newly named team leader admits he holds none of the powers that would make anyone obey him, and his skeptical team mocks the empty title.

file: 1995/1995-08-11_reorganizing_department_fast moving_powerless_micro managed_team_less experienced people_g forces_killing me_business.gif
title: Fast-Moving Teams Fool Powerless Serfs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm reorganizing the department into fast-moving teams.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good plan. We'll never realize we're powerless, micro-managed serfs after we call ourselves a "team."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need some less experienced people.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel faster already.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The G-forces are killing me.

situation: The Boss announces he is reorganizing the department into fast-moving teams. Wally sarcastically praises the plan, saying relabeling employees as a team will hide that they are powerless, micro-managed serfs. Wally and Alice then joke about feeling faster and being pressed by G-forces, while the Boss privately thinks he needs less experienced people.
punchline: Calling a reorganized, micro-managed workforce a "fast-moving team" changes nothing but the label, and the staff mock the buzzword by pretending to feel the speed.
summary: A manager rebrands his staff as speedy teams, and his sardonic employees say the new name will keep them from noticing they are still underlings.

file: 1995/1995-11-27_password_not working_help request line_password doesn't work_email message_stinking network_worthless.gif
title: Locked Out, Told to Go Online

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My password for the network isn't working

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Worker
transcript.text: Fill out a a help request online.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't get online because my password doesn't work...

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Worker
transcript.text: Send me an e-mail message about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't send e-mail because I can't get on the stinkin' network !!!

transcript.speaker: Tech Support Worker
transcript.text: Geez, you're worthless...

setting: Office cubicle area, at the tech support worker's desk
situation: Dilbert tells a network support worker that his password isn't working. The support worker keeps telling him to use online channels, first a help request form and then e-mail, which Dilbert can't access without a working password. When Dilbert finally explodes in frustration, the support worker calls him worthless.
punchline: The support worker insists on solutions that require the very network access that is broken, then blames the user for being worthless.
summary: A man locked out of the network is told to fix it using tools that need network access, and he ends up insulted for his trouble.

file: 1995/1995-04-24_big job_downsizing_hired dogbert construction_lease to state_new carpet_prison cells_empty cubicles.gif
title: Converting Empty Cubicles Into Prison Cells

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've got a lot of empty cubicles because of downsizing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Construction Company to convert part of the office into prison cells which we'll lease to the state.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like a big job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nah. A little paint, new carpet and we're there.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that downsizing has left many empty cubicles, so he has hired Dogbert's construction company to turn them into prison cells to lease to the state. Dilbert remarks that it sounds like a big job, but Dogbert, wearing a hard hat, says it only needs paint and new carpet.
punchline: Cubicles already resemble prison cells so closely that converting them requires nothing more than cosmetic changes, implying office workers are effectively imprisoned.
summary: A manager repurposes vacant workspaces as jail cells and the contractor admits the existing cubicles are practically ready to go.

file: 1995/1995-02-11_current resume_new vp_obvious prelude_massive staff cut_worried_all have resume_massive disloyalty.gif
title: Resumes Handed Over, Layoffs Denied

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like each of you to give me a current résumé.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now, don't be alarmed. It's just so the new VP can get to know you. It's not an obvious prelude to massive staff cuts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should I be worried that you all have a current résumé on you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't worry. It's not an obvious prelude to massive disloyalty!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss asks his team to hand in current résumés, insisting it is only so the new VP can get to know them and not a sign of layoffs. When the employees all produce résumés instantly, he asks if he should be worried. Wally answers by mirroring his own phrasing about disloyalty.
punchline: Employees who keep an up-to-date résumé at the ready show they already expect layoffs, and Wally turns the Boss's own reassurance back on him, implying staff are prepared to jump ship.
summary: A manager's flimsy cover story for collecting résumés is mocked when the team reveals they were already carrying them, ready to leave.

file: 1995/1995-11-22_bent over_chairs_key boards_lower back pain_management kick ass_new policy_on floor_only explination_uncomfortable.gif
title: Keyboards on the Floor Policy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This new policy of keeping our keyboards on the floor is ridiculous!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only possible explanation is to make us all stooped over so it's easier for management to kick our behinds! Ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait a minute... That is the only explanation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Cover me; I'm going to the printer.

situation: Dilbert complains that a new policy requiring keyboards to be kept on the floor is ridiculous while a coworker is bent over typing on the floor. Dilbert jokes that the only reason must be to keep employees stooped over so management can kick them. He then realizes with alarm that this really is the only explanation, and a coworker asks to be covered while he slips away to the printer.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic joke about management's motive turns out to be the only logical explanation for the absurd policy, leaving everyone fearful of being kicked.
summary: A senseless rule forces workers to type bent double, and one sarcastic guess about why management wants it suddenly seems perfectly plausible.

file: 1995/1995-05-29_hands on manager_move the mouse_micromanaging_click it.gif
title: Hands-On Boss Backseat Mouse Driving

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to be more of a hands-on manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Move the mouse...up...up...over...more... Now click it!! Click it!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No!!! You fool!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This has "long day" written all over it.

situation: The Boss announces he will be a more hands-on manager, then hovers over Dilbert's shoulder and dictates every mouse movement and click. When Dilbert's action apparently goes wrong, the Boss throws his arms up and screams at him, and Dilbert realizes the day will be long.
punchline: Being a hands-on manager just means micromanaging trivial computer tasks and berating the employee anyway, which promises a miserable day for Dilbert.
summary: A manager's resolve to get involved turns into him barking step-by-step mouse instructions and then shrieking when things go awry.

file: 1995/1995-05-26_boss's ignorance_advantage_impresses him_accomplishments_barney suit_secret identity.gif
title: Impressing the Boss with Barney

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You must learn to use your boss's ignorance to your advantage.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Find out what impresses him and list it on your accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're the actor in the "Barney" suit?!! I love that guy!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't tell anybody my secret identity.

setting: Dilbert's office and the Boss's office during a performance review
situation: Dogbert advises Dilbert to exploit his boss's ignorance by finding out what impresses him and listing it among his accomplishments. Dilbert follows the advice, and during his review the Boss is thrilled to learn that Dilbert is the actor inside the "Barney" suit.
punchline: Dilbert has taken Dogbert's advice so literally that he claims to be the Barney costume actor, and the Boss's delight lets him gain credit for something utterly irrelevant to his job.
summary: After a canine tip about flattering a clueless supervisor, an engineer lists a children's TV mascot role on his résumé and wins instant admiration.

file: 1995/1995-05-10_frivolous email_bogs down network_noticed_too much communication_about time.gif
title: Frivolous Email Reply-All Gag

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: To: All users. From: Network admin.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Please refrain from frivolous e-mail. It bogs down the network.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: To: Network admin. From: Dilbert. CC: All users.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: I agree!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed there's too much communication in the world, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, every day at about this time.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and his home or office with Dogbert
situation: The network admin emails all users asking them to stop sending frivolous email because it bogs down the network. Dilbert replies to the admin to say he agrees, copying every user on the message. He then muses to Dogbert that there is too much communication in the world, and Dogbert sarcastically replies that it happens every day at about this time.
punchline: Dilbert's reply-all agreeing with a request to cut email adds to the very network clutter being complained about, and Dogbert's dry reply mocks the idea of too much communication.
summary: A plea to stop pointless emails prompts a needless company-wide reply, and a dog quips about the daily flood of chatter.

file: 1995/1995-05-22_policy_employ best_technical professionals_industry average_bright_clueless_feel sorry.gif
title: Best Employees, Average Pay, Clueless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our policy is to employ only the best technical professionals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't it also our policy to base salaries on the industry average?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right. We like them bright but clueless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel sorry for people like that.

situation: The Boss tells his staff in a meeting that the company only hires the best technical professionals. Dilbert points out that the company also bases salaries on the industry average. The Boss replies that the company likes its employees bright but clueless, and Wally says he feels sorry for such people, apparently not realizing he is one of them.
punchline: Paying only average salaries means the company can only attract employees who are smart but unaware they could earn more elsewhere, and Wally's pity for 'people like that' shows he doesn't realize it describes him.
summary: A manager's boast about hiring top talent collapses when paying merely average wages is shown to depend on staff being too naive to know better.

file: 1995/1995-10-20_angel_promoted top angel_angel on earth_help people_mission assigned_halo given_wally_new hair_buns of steel_price list.gif
title: Angel Dogbert Sells Vanity Upgrades

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: Mister Dogbert, we've decided to send you back to Earth as an angel.

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: Your mission is to help people in need. We have given you special powers.

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: We'll be watching.

transcript.speaker: Balding Man
transcript.text: Okay, so what's the price for new hair plus buns of steel?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's all on the price sheet.

transcript.speaker: Angel
transcript.text: Ahem

setting: Heaven among the clouds, then an earthly office
situation: Two angels tell Dogbert he is being sent back to Earth as an angel to help people in need, and they grant him special powers. On Earth, Dogbert sits at a desk with a price sheet and a balding customer asks what it costs to get new hair plus buns of steel. The angels' "Ahem" suggests they are watching and disapprove.
punchline: Dogbert turns a mission to help people in need into a paid service, charging for his miraculous powers, as the watching angels clear their throats in disapproval.
summary: Handed divine powers and a charitable mission, Dogbert immediately sets up shop and sells miracles by the price list.

file: 1995/1995-09-02_records retention_valuable documents_stored_so much easier_asks for anything.gif
title: Records Retention Means Trash Can

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These valuable documents should be stored for five years.

transcript.speaker: Records clerk
transcript.text: This job got so much easier when I realized that nobody ever asks for anything back.

situation: Dilbert walks into the Records Retention room and hands a stack of documents to the clerk at the counter, saying they must be kept for five years. In the final panel, the clerk thinks to himself that his job got easier once he realized no one ever asks for documents back, while he tosses the folder into a trash bin.
punchline: The records clerk simply throws away the supposedly valuable documents, since nobody ever checks on archived files, making the retention job pointless.
summary: A records clerk reveals his secret to an easy job: he discards everything handed to him because no one ever comes looking for it.

file: 1995/1995-02-25_old rating system_friendlier method_animal_similar traits_tyrannosaurus rex_mightiest dinosaur_brain size.gif
title: Boss Rates Alice as T. Rex

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've replaced the old rating system with a friendlier method. Now I compare each of you to an animal with similar traits.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I rated you "Tyrannosaurus Rex."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: T. Rex - the mightiest dinosaur!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Think in terms of brain size.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss announces he has swapped the old performance rating system for a friendlier one that compares employees to animals. He tells Alice she was rated Tyrannosaurus Rex, and she proudly takes it as a compliment about being mighty. He then deflates her by pointing out the comparison is about the dinosaur's tiny brain.
punchline: The Boss disguises an insult as a compliment, since the T. Rex is famously powerful but had a very small brain, so the 'friendlier' rating is really calling Alice stupid.
summary: A manager's cheerful new animal-based review scheme turns out to be a thinly veiled put-down when the impressive-sounding creature he picks is known for its small brain.

file: 1995/1995-08-24_dilbert expense voucher_meals on trip_travel guidelines_pigeon_hotel_travel iron_taking long_wool setting.gif
title: Expense Report Audited by Dragon

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert's expense voucher

transcript.speaker: Dragon
transcript.text: You spent nearly $10 per day on meals during your trip.

transcript.speaker: Dragon
transcript.text: The travel guidelines require you to stun a pigeon with your briefcase on the way to the hotel then fry it up on your travel iron.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried... but it was taking so long.

transcript.speaker: Dragon
transcript.text: Try the "wool" setting.

setting: A cave or dungeon-like lair where Dilbert hangs upside down
situation: Dilbert is tied up and hanging upside down while a green dragon reviews his travel expense voucher. The dragon criticizes him for spending nearly $10 a day on meals, citing absurd guidelines that require catching and cooking a pigeon with a travel iron. When Dilbert says he tried but it took too long, the dragon helpfully suggests a hotter iron setting.
punchline: The dragon treats an absurd and grotesque travel policy as perfectly reasonable, and rather than doubting it, offers cooking tips, which mocks how stingy and rigid expense rules can be.
summary: A dragon auditing a captive Dilbert's expenses insists company policy demands he cook pigeons on a hotel iron instead of buying meals.

file: 1995/1995-08-02_temporary employee_blink and gone_balance of power_shifted.gif
title: Ratbert's Blink-and-Gone Temp Application

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I submit myself as a candidate for the position of "temporary employee."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm very temporary. First I'll be in one place and then you blink and I'm gone! Blink, gone, blink, gone, blink, gone...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop saying "blink, gone." It's making me nuts.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It appears that the balance of power has shifted my way.

situation: Ratbert sits in a chair behind a desk and applies for a temporary employee position, pitching himself as being extremely temporary. He repeats "blink, gone" over and over until the unseen boss, speaking from off-panel, demands he stop because it is driving him crazy. Ratbert realizes he now has the upper hand.
punchline: Ratbert's annoying sales pitch irritates the boss so much that the job applicant ends up with the power in the interview.
summary: A tiny job candidate turns a repetitive gimmick into leverage over the person interviewing him.

file: 1995/1995-12-02_boss give orders_get in trouble_dogbert detective_embarass_happiest moment_my career.gif
title: Dogbert Detective Agency Exposes Boss

transcript.speaker: TV announcer
transcript.text: Does your boss give you orders and later deny it? Do you get in trouble for doing what you're told?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: TV announcer
transcript.text: The "Dogbert Detective Agency" will videotape it all and embarrass your boss with proof!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What??! Why did you do this??!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is the happiest moment of my career.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lights!

setting: Dilbert's living room, then the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert watches a TV commercial for the Dogbert Detective Agency, which promises to videotape bosses who give orders and later deny them. Dilbert answers yes to the ad's questions and hires them. In the office, the Boss is confronted with the evidence while Dilbert happily enjoys the moment and Dogbert directs the lighting.
punchline: Dilbert finally gets to see his boss caught and humiliated on tape for denying his own orders, making it the highlight of his career.
summary: After seeing a TV ad for a spy service that catches lying bosses on camera, a downtrodden employee hires it and savors his manager's exposure.

file: 1995/1995-05-20_never answered email_secretary out_message on hardcopy_out of paprus_chiseled on pyramid_ufos.gif
title: Hardcopy Email Chiseled on Pyramid

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You never answered my e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My secretary is out, so there's nobody to print my e-mail for me. Bring me your message on hardcopy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was out of papyrus so I chiseled my message on a little pyramid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did he work alone or were UFOs involved?

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert complains that the Boss never answered his e-mail. The Boss explains his secretary is out and nobody can print his e-mail, so he demands a hardcopy. Dilbert returns with a tiny pyramid carved with his message, and the Boss wonders whether aliens helped build it.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the Boss's absurd demand for paper by delivering the message in ancient-Egyptian style, and the clueless Boss only wonders whether UFOs were involved in making it.
summary: A boss too helpless to print his own email gets his message back as a stone pyramid and responds with alien conspiracy theories.

file: 1995/1995-09-22_add resource_human beings_not resources_most valuable asset.gif
title: Humans Are Not Resources, Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I've decided to add a resource to your project.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We're human beings, not "resources"!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would it help if I told you that resources are our most valuable asset?

situation: The Boss tells Alice he is adding a 'resource' to her project. Alice angrily objects to people being called resources. The Boss tries to placate her by saying resources are the company's most valuable asset, which misses her point entirely.
punchline: The Boss's attempt at reassurance only reinforces the dehumanizing term, treating people as assets and showing he doesn't understand her objection.
summary: A manager's cheerful reassurance about valuable assets only proves his employee's point about being treated as an object.

file: 1995/1995-04-19_dogbert_financial advisor_living in dumpster_twenty years_dogcart deferred income_own a mansion_photo of mansion.gif
title: Dogbert's Photograph Investment Fund

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Financial Advisor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's a picture of you living in a dumpster in twenty years.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But if you invest in the "Dogbert Deferred Income Fund" take a look at what you could own someday!!

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I could own a mansion?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could own a photograph.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a financial advisor, shows a worried client a picture of her future living in a dumpster. He then pitches his Deferred Income Fund and shows a picture of a mansion. When she excitedly asks if she could own it, he reveals that all she would own is the photograph.
punchline: Dogbert's investment fund guarantees nothing of value; the only thing the client would actually get for her money is a picture of wealth.
summary: A scam financial advisor frightens a client with a bleak forecast, then sells her a fund whose only payoff is a snapshot of a house.

file: 1995/1995-07-06_told stan_marketing_dna_gullibility_reverse process_entire reality_unverified_anecdotes_rumour_alleged focus group_becoming weasel_business.gif
title: Gullible Stan and the Weasel Rumor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I jokingly told Stan in Marketing that I reprogrammed his DNA. He's so gullible that he's actually changing!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You must use his gullibility to reverse the process. Remember, his entire reality is shaped by unverified customer anecdotes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I heard a rumor of a story of an alleged focus group where a quote taken out of context indicates you're not becoming a weasel.

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: I'm not?!

transcript.speaker: Stan
transcript.text: Yipeee!

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert on the sofa and Dogbert lounging on a cushion
situation: Dilbert confesses that he jokingly told Stan from Marketing that he had reprogrammed his DNA, and Stan is so gullible he is actually changing. Dogbert advises exploiting that gullibility with a fabricated, unverified story to reverse the effect. Dilbert then tells Stan a rumor of a rumor about a focus group, and the weasel-like Stan joyfully believes he is not becoming a weasel.
punchline: Marketing decisions are based on flimsy secondhand anecdotes, so Stan will believe anything, even a ridiculously hedged rumor about a focus group, which cures him of becoming a weasel.
summary: A prank about rewriting a coworker's genes backfires into a transformation that is undone by feeding him an equally flimsy secondhand story.

file: 1995/1995-04-29_turn the house_gambling casino_illeagl_tiny republic_dogbertland_seed from repressive_morning_voting_green card.gif
title: Dogbert Secedes and Opens Casino

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm planning to turn the house into a gambling casino.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that illegal?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not in the tiny republic of Dogbertland. I seceded from the repressive homeland this morning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't remember voting on that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's your green card.

situation: Dogbert, sitting at a desk with blueprints, announces plans to convert Dilbert's house into a gambling casino. When Dilbert points out it's illegal, Dogbert claims he has declared his own sovereign nation, Dogbertland, where it is legal. Dilbert objects that he never voted on it, and Dogbert hands him a green card.
punchline: Dogbert's self-declared country makes Dilbert an immigrant in his own home, so he gets a green card instead of a vote.
summary: A scheming dog dodges the law by declaring his owner's house a separate nation and treating the owner as a foreign resident.

file: 1995/1995-11-19_ship prodcut_two months early_nothing exists_proptype_more funidng_froze money_frozen budget_boss_creepy boss_dysfunctional.gif
title: Shipping the Only Prototype Tomorrow

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to ship the V-1 product tomorrow. I promised our CEO he can announce it at the shareholder meeting.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: That's two months early!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We haven't added any features yet!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What would we ship? Our lab prototype is the only V-1 in existence!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: No...you wouldn't!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've scheduled press tours so you can do demos all next week.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: On what?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll need twenty thousand dollars to build another prototype!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That reminds me; I froze the budget for the rest of the year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If there's anything you'd like me to do, don't hesitate to ask.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd like you to do something...

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Ooh... I think I should have hesitated to ask that.

situation: The Boss announces that the unfinished V-1 product must ship tomorrow because he promised the CEO an announcement at the shareholder meeting. The engineers protest that no features are added and the lab prototype is the only unit, so he schedules press demos on it. When they ask for money to build another prototype, he reveals he froze the budget, then invites them to ask for anything.
punchline: The boss's open offer to help is hollow, and the engineer's request is met with something implied to be unpleasant, so he realizes he should have hesitated to ask.
summary: A manager commits an unfinished prototype to a premature launch, cuts off the funds to build a spare, and then sinister-sounds his offer of help.

file: 1995/1995-12-05_lousy vendor_sales rep_gorgeous_field engineer_without shirt_indian chief_maintenance package.gif
title: Vendor Chosen for Shirtless Engineer

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't believe you're recommending this lousy vendor just because the sales rep is gorgeous.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a picture of Thor, their field engineer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Does he really work without a shirt?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only if you buy the "Indian Chief" maintenance package.

situation: Alice confronts the Boss for recommending a poor vendor merely because the sales rep is attractive. The Boss shows her a photo of the vendor's field engineer, Thor, and Alice's attitude shifts as she asks whether he really works shirtless. The Boss reveals that this only comes with the premium maintenance package.
punchline: Alice's outrage at superficial vendor selection collapses the moment she is tempted by the same thing, and the vendor upsells shirtless service as a premium maintenance tier.
summary: A colleague scolds her manager for letting good looks sway a purchase, then quickly gets drawn in by the vendor's shirtless technician and his pricey support plan.

file: 1995/1995-07-21_christmas of 92_mall_filberts dad_different not worse_death_loss_missing_lives at mall_medical.gif
title: Dilbert's Dad Lost at Mall

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: It's really different around here since we lost Dilbert's dad.

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: When did he die?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's not dead. We lost him at the mall, Christmas of '92.

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: Shouldn't you be looking for him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I said it's different, not worse.

setting: Dilbert's family home, around a table having tea
situation: Dilbert's mother pours tea for a guest and remarks how different things are since they lost Dilbert's dad. The guest assumes he died, but Dilbert corrects them: the dad was simply lost at the mall years earlier. When the guest asks why they aren't searching for him, the mother says that things are different, not worse.
punchline: The family has been so content without the father that they never bothered to look for him after losing him at the mall.
summary: A tea-time chat reveals that the family misplaced their patriarch at a shopping centre years ago and would rather not retrieve him.

file: 1995/1995-01-05_united charity_kick off_headless man_inspirational speaker_dignity_quations_head count report.gif
title: Headless Man Inspires Charity Drive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Be at the "United Charity" kickoff tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a headless man to be our inspirational speaker.

transcript.speaker: Headless Speaker
transcript.text: ...And that's how "United Charity" gave me back my dignity. Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: How do you show up on a headcount report?

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to attend the company's United Charity kickoff and mentions he has hired a headless man as the inspirational speaker. At the event, the headless speaker finishes his story about regaining his dignity and asks for questions. An employee asks how he appears on a headcount report.
punchline: The charity's supposed success story is a man without a head, and the employee's question mocks how corporate headcount reports would count (or fail to count) him, a jab at the company's obsession with headcount.
summary: A manager books a literally headless motivational speaker for a charity event, and a worker responds with a headcount-related question.

file: 1995/1995-05-18_business case_various mangers_being misplaced_kill for personal gain_buried_not cremeated_lasting impression_earth_mail corpse.gif
title: Business Case Dies in Bureaucracy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I distributed 36 copies of my business case to various managers for approval.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By my count, 20 are being misplaced, 6 managers will try to kill it for personal gain and 10 will come back with irrelevant questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I die I want to be buried, not cremated, so I can at least make ONE lasting impression on the Earth.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was planning to mail your corpse to somebody I don't like.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dilbert talking to Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he sent 36 copies of his business case to managers and predicts exactly how each will fail: lost, sabotaged for personal gain, or answered with irrelevant questions. Gloomy, he says he wants to be buried so he can leave at least one lasting impression. Dogbert replies that he planned to mail Dilbert's corpse to someone he dislikes.
punchline: After a bleak rundown of how his proposal will be wasted, Dilbert's morbid wish for a lasting legacy is met with Dogbert's deadpan plan to use his corpse as a weapon against an enemy.
summary: A dejected engineer forecasts the doom of his proposal across management and muses about his own burial, only to have his dog offer a darkly comic alternative.

file: 1995/1995-11-16_write programs_punch cards_rather be fishing_snap suspenders_alice threat_snap you into next week_space time continum.gif
title: Snapped Into Next Week

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: I used to write programs using punch cards... But I'd rather be fishing...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Look, you bearded road apple, if you answer one more of my questions with an irrelevant story I'll snap you into next week!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sometime next week...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Looks like a hole in the space-time continuum.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you hear a snap?

setting: A conference room, then an office hallway the following week
situation: Alice is trying to get answers from a rambling bearded man who keeps telling irrelevant stories about punch cards and fishing. She threatens to snap him into next week with a giant rubber band. A week later, Dilbert and Wally find a swirling hole in space-time with the man's legs sticking out, and Dilbert wonders if he heard a snap.
punchline: Alice's idiom about snapping someone into next week is carried out literally, leaving the old programmer stuck in a rip in the space-time continuum.
summary: A frustrated woman slingshots a long-winded old programmer through time, and his dangling legs later puzzle two coworkers.

file: 1995/1995-09-04_profits down_male sinking_bold leadership_inspirational posters_variety_relevant nature scenes_relate to scene_seagull_clam.gif
title: Inspirational Poster: Seagull or Clam

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Profits are down, morale is sinking; it's time for bold leadership!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I got some inspirational posters featuring a variety of relevant nature scenes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you can relate to this scene.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Am I the seagull or the clam?

situation: The Boss announces that profits and morale are low and calls for bold leadership. His solution is to hand out inspirational posters of nature scenes, and he holds one up for his employees. Wally studies it and asks whether he is the seagull or the clam.
punchline: The poster apparently depicts a seagull eating a clam, so Wally's question implies that the Boss's motivational effort casts employees as either predator or helpless victim, unintentionally highlighting how bleak things are.
summary: A manager's answer to sinking morale is a nature poster, and an employee's innocent question reveals the grim message it actually sends.

file: 1995/1995-01-04_united charity_below average_pay level_income_local agroups_approved list_team player_fund agency_away from scoiety.gif
title: Charity Donations Below Company Average

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your contributions to "United Charity" are below average for your pay level.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, I donate ten percent of my income and thousands of hours to local groups not on your approved list.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ..."Not a team player."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I fund an agency that keeps people like you away from society.

situation: The Boss reviews a printout and criticizes Dilbert for giving less than average to the company-backed United Charity. Dilbert explains that he gives a tenth of his income and thousands of volunteer hours to local groups that aren't on the approved list. The Boss writes him up as not a team player, and Dilbert retorts that he funds an agency that keeps people like the Boss away from society.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's judgment around by implying the Boss is a danger to the public who belongs locked away, and that Dilbert's real charity work is funding that.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for stingy giving to the corporate charity, only to be insulted when the employee reveals his far larger private generosity and a barbed final remark.

file: 1995/1995-08-17_alarmed_rat floating_mid air_rendered invisible_worthless assignments_bad attitude_quality meeting.gif
title: Invisible Employee Carries a Rat

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Don't be alarmed. I'm not really a rat floating in midair.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm clinging to the back of an employee who has been rendered invisible by a long succession of worthless assignments.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looks like an isolated case of bad attitude.

transcript.speaker: Invisible employee
transcript.text: Which room is the "quality" meeting in?

situation: Ratbert appears to float in midair in front of The Boss and explains that he is actually clinging to the back of an employee who has become invisible from being given worthless assignments. The Boss dismisses the whole thing as an isolated bad attitude. The invisible employee, seen only as a floating shape, cheerfully asks where the quality meeting is.
punchline: Management ignores the real problem of employees being made invisible by pointless work, blaming it on individual attitude, while the employee still dutifully heads to a meeting about quality.
summary: A rat appears to hover in the air because he is riding an employee who has vanished from sight after too much meaningless busywork, yet the boss only sees a morale issue.

file: 1995/1995-09-03_laptop_freezing up_telecommuting_distracted at home_virtual cubcile_invisible walls_cone of prodcutivity_dedicated_cone_focused_corporate vision_firm commitment_work at hime_victory.gif
title: Dilbert's Virtual Cubicle Cone of Productivity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My laptop PC keeps freezing up. Come take a look at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm telecommuting, Dogbert. I can't be distracted by home projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't come another step closer. This is my virtual cubicle, within which I can not be disturbed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These invisible walls form a cone of productivity around me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Within this zone I am a dedicated employee, totally focused on the corporate vision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing can distract me from my firm commitment to the work-at-home principle.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fine. I think I'll set the couch on fire.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Another victory for the distractor!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I swear, someday principle will win!

setting: Dilbert's home, where he works at his computer in a bathrobe
situation: Dilbert is telecommuting and refuses to help Dogbert with a frozen laptop, declaring an invisible 'virtual cubicle' around himself where he cannot be disturbed. After a grandiose speech about his dedication to the work-at-home principle, Dogbert calmly says he will set the couch on fire, and Dilbert immediately abandons his principles to deal with it.
punchline: Dilbert's lofty talk of principled focus collapses the instant a real distraction (a couch fire) arises, showing that working from home principles lose to distractions every time.
summary: A telecommuter boasts of an imaginary productivity barrier against interruptions, only to drop it the moment his dog threatens something truly distracting.

file: 1995/1995-02-26_chocolate cake_engineer_railroad_big corproation_fix typrwriters_debugged tcp_driver aplication_isdn bonding_cuts down to size_dilmom_cake to packing foam_insulted cake_engineering.gif
title: Dilbert's Mom Misunderstands His Engineering Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Here's some nice chocolate cake for you and Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Tell me all about your job at the railroad.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not a railroad. I'm an engineer at a big corporation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Do you fix the typewriters when they break?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... Today I debugged a TCP/IP driver for an application that runs over ISDN with bonding.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: You mean, all you do is slap a BRI analyzer on a circuit and look for bad packets?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... yeah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it's really hard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was doing okay until she offered to pay my tuition to typewriter repair school.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You shouldn't have compared her cake to packing foam.

setting: Dilbert's mother's living room, then outdoors on a lawn
situation: Dilbert's mother serves cake and asks about his job, wrongly assuming he works at a railroad and fixes typewriters. Dilbert explains his real technical work in jargon, and she dismisses it as simply looking for bad packets. She then offers to pay for typewriter repair school, and Dogbert says he has no one to blame but himself for insulting her cake.
punchline: Dilbert's mother cuts his sophisticated engineering career down to size and offers to fund typewriter repair school, and Dogbert reveals Dilbert had earlier insulted her cake by comparing it to packing foam.
summary: A mother who understands nothing about her son's high-tech career keeps belittling it while serving him dessert.

file: 1995/1995-04-04_dogbert the consultant_relocate russia_hire engineers_weed out dumb_like heaven.gif
title: Relocating to Russia for Cheap Engineers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your best bet is to relocate the company to Russia.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can hire engineers for two cents a year!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it difficult to weed out the dumb ones?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No. And that leads me into the good news about their occupational safety laws.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's like heaven!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss to move the company to Russia where engineers can be hired for almost nothing. The Boss asks if it's hard to weed out the incompetent ones. Dogbert says no and pivots to the lax occupational safety laws, which the Boss gleefully calls heaven.
punchline: The implication is that weak safety laws let the company get rid of the dumb engineers through workplace accidents, and the Boss is delighted by this.
summary: A consultant dog sells a gleeful manager on an offshore move where labor is practically free and unsafe working conditions solve the problem of bad employees.

file: 1995/1995-10-05_dogbert_corporate jet pilot_captain speaking_land safely_ceo_not funny.gif
title: Dogbert Pilot Demands CEO Stunt

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Corporate Jet Pilot

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is your captain speaking...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you'd like to land safely, there's something I've always wanted to see a CEO do.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: This is so NOT funny.

situation: Dogbert is piloting a corporate jet and announces over the intercom that he is the captain. He then holds the plane's safe landing hostage, saying he wants to see a CEO perform some stunt. The CEO, pressed back in his seat with his tongue and tie streaming from the speed, thinks that this is not funny.
punchline: Dogbert uses his control of the plane to extort a humiliating performance from a powerful executive, who is helpless and terrified.
summary: A dog flying an executive's private plane makes the passenger's survival conditional on a request he has long wanted to see fulfilled.

file: 1995/1995-05-09_dating_lucky_replace you_same scale_relationships.gif
title: Dating Scale Rating Gets Brutal

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm so lucky to be dating you, Liz. You're at least an eight.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: You're a ten.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we using the same scale?

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Ten is the number of seconds it would take to replace you.

setting: Outdoor hillside with mountains in the background
situation: Dilbert sits on a hillside with his girlfriend Liz and compliments her by rating her at least an eight out of ten. She says he is a ten, which he takes as flattery and asks whether they are using the same scale. She reveals the ten refers to how many seconds it would take her to replace him.
punchline: What sounds like a high compliment is actually an insult, since her rating measures how quickly and easily he could be replaced as a boyfriend.
summary: A man's sweet compliment on a romantic date is answered with a rating that turns out to be a cutting remark about how disposable he is.

file: 1995/1995-03-09_thought leaders_whats worng_no thoughts_cloud_no ideas_blank head bos.gif
title: Thought Leader With No Thoughts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, the managers at my level will be called "Thought Leaders."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: Dilbert and Wally sit quietly at the conference table, staring ahead.)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's wrong with this picture?

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces that managers at his level will now be known as "Thought Leaders." Dilbert and Wally stare at him in silence. In the last panel Dilbert asks what is wrong with this picture, while the Boss's empty thought bubble shows he has no thoughts at all.
punchline: The Boss's new title is ironic because his thought bubble is completely empty, showing that these so-called thought leaders have no thoughts.
summary: A manager awards himself a grand new title just as his blank thought bubble shows how little thinking he actually does.

file: 1995/1995-10-25_terrible news_valuable porject_three morons_assigned_crush them_carl_nothing valauable_shoo shoo.gif
title: Dilbert Sabotages Rivals' Fun Projects

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Terrible news: My boss assigned me to a fun and valuable project.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. That means at least three morons will be assigned to similar projects. You must find them and crush them...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carl, old buddy, whatcha workin' on these days?

transcript.speaker: Carl
transcript.text: Nothing fun and valuable. Shoo shoo!!

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then a coworker's cubicle
situation: Dilbert lies on his couch and tells Dogbert that his boss gave him a fun and valuable project, which he calls terrible news. Dogbert explains that others will have been given similar projects and that Dilbert must find and crush them. Dilbert then visits his coworker Carl and cheerfully asks what he's working on, and Carl, suspicious, shoos him away.
punchline: Dilbert treats a good assignment as terrible news because he knows it will make him a target for coworkers who covet fun projects, so he preemptively seeks out rivals and Carl, equally paranoid, brushes him off.
summary: Landing a desirable assignment makes Dilbert a target, so he goes hunting for competitors, only to be rebuffed by a coworker who guards his own secrets.

file: 1995/1995-08-26_self conscious_tiny brain_war wax_bob the donisoaur.gif
title: Bob the Dinosaur's Tiny Brain

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Sometimes I feel self-conscious because my brain is so tiny.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Here, let me reach in my ear and pull it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think that's ear wax, Bob.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'm putting it back just in case.

setting: A living room, with the two sitting on a couch
situation: Bob the dinosaur confesses he feels self-conscious about his tiny brain. He reaches into his ear to pull the brain out and show it, and Dilbert points out that what he's holding is just ear wax. Bob admits it might be, but pushes it back in anyway.
punchline: Bob is so dim that he can't tell his brain from ear wax, and he reinserts it just in case, which proves he really does have a tiny brain.
summary: A dinosaur worried about his small brain digs something out of his ear and cheerfully puts it back even after being told it's wax.

file: 1995/1995-04-12_pundits_press_keyboard with no q_public relations_fiasco_engineering solution_graphics program_semi colon.gif
title: Keyboard Missing the Letter Q

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The pundits in the press are nailing us for shipping a keyboard with no "Q."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a public-relations fiasco. Obviously, we need an engineering solution.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm on the case.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Users could use a graphics program to draw a "Q" in the unlikely event that they need one.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Or we could replace the semi-colon; nobody uses them.

setting: Office and conference room at a tech company
situation: Dilbert reads a newspaper reporting that his company shipped a keyboard with no letter Q, and the Boss declares it a PR fiasco needing an engineering solution. Dilbert and a fellow engineer then propose absurd workarounds, such as drawing a Q in a graphics program or replacing the semicolon key.
punchline: Engineers respond to an obvious product defect with ridiculous patches and downplay the missing letter as something users will rarely need, rather than admitting the design mistake.
summary: A company ships a keyboard lacking a key letter and its engineers brainstorm silly workarounds instead of fixing the oversight.

file: 1995/1995-09-12_janitor expenses_empty trash_new employee fitness_trashercise.gif
title: Trashercise Replaces the Janitor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to cut janitor expenses. Do you think I'll have any HR issues if I make employees empty their own trash?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We'll soften the bad news by simultaneously introducing a new employee fitness program...

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Okay, everybody, it's time to trashercise!!!

setting: Catbert's office and the office cubicle area
situation: The Boss asks Catbert, the evil HR director, whether he'll face HR problems if he cuts janitor costs by making employees empty their own trash. Catbert suggests disguising the cut by launching a fitness program at the same time. In the cubicle area, the janitor leads employees in 'trashercise'.
punchline: The company spins forcing employees to do the janitor's work as a wellness perk, rebranding a cost-cutting measure as exercise.
summary: Management dresses up a layoff-style cost cut as a fun fitness initiative by making workers haul their own garbage.

file: 1995/1995-09-09_outside the box_creative design_push chair_hallway_view point_stimulate_fire hazard_thinking_inside box.gif
title: Thinking Outside the Box, Literally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to think "outside the box" to come up with a creative design...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I push my chair into the hallway to change my viewpoint and stimulate my creative juices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly my juice dries up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're a fire hazard. Do your thinking inside your box.

situation: Dilbert wants to think outside the box to produce a creative design, so he takes the idea literally and pushes his chair out of his cubicle into the hallway. The Boss walks up and tells him he is a fire hazard and must do his thinking inside his cubicle.
punchline: Dilbert takes the 'think outside the box' cliché literally, and the Boss shuts it down with the opposite rule, showing that management slogans about creativity collapse against petty rules.
summary: A designer who tries to be creative by moving his chair into the corridor is promptly ordered back into his cubicle by his supervisor.

file: 1995/1995-10-26_same task_other people_clever ploy_create healthy internal competition_average cauliflower_brain_fruit kingdom.gif
title: Wally Wins Cauliflower Intelligence Bet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally and I have a bet about why you assigned me to the same task as three other people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I believe it's a clever ploy to create healthy internal competition. Wally thinks you're just dumber than the average cauliflower.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: May I point out that cauliflower is the brain of the fruit kingdom.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!

situation: Dilbert and Wally stand before the Boss's desk and ask him why Dilbert was given the same task as three other people. Dilbert explains that he thinks it's a ploy to foster healthy competition, while Wally believes the Boss is simply dumber than an average cauliflower. The Boss responds by defending cauliflower's intelligence.
punchline: The Boss misses the insult entirely and proudly defends cauliflower as the brain of the fruit kingdom, which both proves Wally's point and is factually wrong, since cauliflower is a vegetable.
summary: Two employees quiz their boss about duplicated work assignments, and he answers a thinly veiled insult with a confidently wrong botanical boast.

file: 1995/1995-04-26_prison talk_not prisoner_own free will_freak section.gif
title: Freak Section: Choosing to Work

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, buddy, what are you in for?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unlike yourself, I am not a prisoner here. I choose to work here of my own free will!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Great... I'm in the freak section.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to work.

situation: A bald coworker peers over the cubicle wall and jokingly asks Dilbert what he's 'in for', treating the office like a prison. Dilbert insists he isn't a prisoner and works there by choice. The coworker concludes he's been seated in the section with the weirdos.
punchline: Dilbert's sincere claim that he chooses to work and likes it marks him as a freak, since everyone else sees the job as a prison sentence.
