summary: Dilbert's neighbor treats the office like a jail, and learns his cubicle mate actually enjoys being there.

file: 1995/1995-02-19_boss types_handy refrence_hostage taker_cucbicle_talks ear off_vigorous head noodling_subnet_ip addresses_motivational lair_mushroom_qualitize_paradigm_inundate_bonus_80 hour weeks_moses_perfect boss_died thursday afternooon.gif
title: Field Guide to Terrible Bosses

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Boss types

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Find your boss on this handy reference.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hostage taker: Traps you in your cubicle and talks your ears off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Blah blah

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ow!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Fraud: Uses vigorous head-nodding to simulate comprehension.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Then we'll subnet our I.P. addresses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh yeah oh yeah

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Motivational liar: Has no clue what you do but says you're the best.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nobody can do what you do!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Except a mushroom.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Over promoted: Tries to mask incompetence with poor communication.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's qualitize our paradigm so we don't over inundate with datums.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Weasel: Takes credit for your hard work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This bonus is for brilliantly forcing your staff to work 80 hour weeks.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It wasn't easy!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Moses: Perpetually waits for clear signals from above.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't do anything important yet.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Never have.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Perfect boss: Dies of natural causes on a Thursday afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Should we do something?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Three day weekend!

setting: Office cubicles and a conference room, framed as a reference chart
situation: Ratbert introduces a handy reference of boss types, and each panel defines a type with a short example. The types include a hostage taker who talks endlessly, a head-nodding fraud, a liar who flatters, an over-promoted jargon user, a credit-stealing weasel, an indecisive Moses, and finally a perfect boss who dies on a Thursday.
punchline: The perfect boss is one who dies of natural causes on a Thursday afternoon, giving everyone a three-day weekend.
summary: A tongue-in-cheek catalogue sorts bad managers into categories before concluding that the ideal one is conveniently dead and out of the way.

file: 1995/1995-10-07_planes going down_one parachute_harvard mba_dog_knapsack_old joke_ceo grabs_animals.gif
title: CEO Steals Dogbert's Parachute Knapsack

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like the plane's going down and there's only one parachute.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Give it to me!!! I'm a CEO with a Harvard MBA. You're a dog!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's my knapsack.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Old joke.

setting: Passenger airplane cabin, then freefalling in the sky
situation: On a doomed plane, Dogbert warns a CEO that there is only one parachute. The CEO angrily grabs a pack from Dogbert, claiming priority because of his title and Harvard MBA, and then jumps. In midair Dogbert, wearing the real parachute, points out the CEO has only taken his knapsack, and the CEO admits he knows this is an old joke.
punchline: The arrogant CEO grabs what he thinks is the parachute but it is just Dogbert's knapsack, and he falls to his doom, with the weary 'old joke' line acknowledging the well-worn parachute gag.
summary: A pompous executive snatches a bag he assumes is a lifesaving parachute, only to plummet while the dog he bullied floats safely.

file: 1995/1995-10-21_special powers_angel_dogbert_snap of paw_what people want_instinctive_boobs on man_aim sticks.gif
title: Dogbert's Angelic Powers Misfire

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying that you're an angel now? And you have special powers to help people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Exactly. I instinctively know what people want and I can give it to them with a snap of the paw.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Snap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you having any trouble controlling it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My aim stinks.

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit at a restaurant table while Dogbert, wearing a halo, claims to be an angel who can grant people what they want with a snap of his paw. He snaps, and the nearby waiter suddenly appears with a feminine bust while the waitress is now wearing a halo. Dilbert asks if he has trouble controlling the power, and Dogbert admits his aim is poor.
punchline: Dogbert's supposed wish-granting powers go to the wrong people, giving the waiter a bust and the waitress a halo instead of benefiting Dilbert.
summary: A self-proclaimed angel dog shows off a miracle power that hits all the wrong targets in a restaurant.

file: 1995/1995-10-30_headquarters_chucks looking unhappy_big guy_bad decisions_some bodies_changes will allow_core business.gif
title: Reorg Covers Executives' Bad Decisions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Headquarters

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Hey, Chuck's looking unhappy today. What's the problem, big guy?

transcript.speaker: Chuck
transcript.text: All of my bad decisions are catching up to me. Could we do another reorg to cover my tracks?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Yeah, I've got some bodies to bury, too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "...These changes will allow us to focus on our core business."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa! Let me get my reorg boots.

setting: Company headquarters conference room, then the office
situation: At headquarters, a group of executives notices that Chuck looks unhappy. Chuck admits his bad decisions are catching up with him and asks for another reorganization to hide the evidence, and a colleague agrees he has some mistakes to bury too. Later the Boss announces the reorg as a way to focus on the core business, and Wally jokes that he needs his reorg boots.
punchline: Executives use reorganizations as a cover-up for their failures, dressed up as strategic focus on the core business, so wading through the mess requires special boots.
summary: Managers conspire to stage a company-wide shake-up purely to hide their past blunders, while the staff brace for the fallout.

file: 1995/1995-03-11_managers_another closed door_meeting_pay cuts_layoffs_resume_leadership vsion_inspire employees_action_upgardes_business.gif
title: Closed-Door Meeting Triggers Layoff Panic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... The managers are going to another closed-door meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be about pay cuts or layoffs. I'm doomed. I'd better work on my résumé now.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Okay, so far our "leadership vision" says "We inspire employees to action." Does anybody have upgrades?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Nah.

setting: Office hallway and a conference room
situation: Dilbert watches the managers file into another closed-door meeting and assumes they are planning pay cuts or layoffs, so he frantically starts updating his résumé. Inside the meeting, the managers are actually just reviewing their company's leadership vision statement and have no suggestions to improve it.
punchline: The employees' dread of secret layoff plans is unfounded, because the managers' mysterious closed-door meeting is only a lazy wordsmithing exercise on a vision statement, ironically one about inspiring employees to action.
summary: A worried employee sees managers heading into a secret meeting and panics, only for the meeting to be a bland review of a corporate slogan.

file: 1995/1995-07-16_cahnges_corporate culture_longer hours_without pay_management says same_team_vapid slogans_notepads_useless meetings_culture change_fad menu_rule by fear_business.gif
title: Corporate Culture Change, Predicted by Staff

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to make some changes to our corporate culture.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me guess what that means.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We'll work longer hours without extra pay...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your management style will remain exactly the same because Lord knows there's no need for YOU to change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll start calling ourselves a "team" so it doesn't seem like work!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I predict there will be vapid slogans printed on notepads, and maybe some useless meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's psychic!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it just me or is the culture already changing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel it! We're changing!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What's next on the fad menu?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if it's too late to rule by fear.

situation: The Boss announces he plans to change the corporate culture. Wally, Dilbert and Alice take turns predicting exactly what that will mean: longer hours for no pay, calling themselves a team, slogan notepads and useless meetings. They then mockingly pretend to feel the culture changing while the Boss privately wonders whether old-fashioned fear tactics are still an option.
punchline: Employees can predict every cliched management fad so precisely that the change is meaningless, while the Boss's real instinct is to fall back on ruling by fear.
summary: Staff mock a culture-change announcement by listing every tired management cliche the boss is about to inflict, as he daydreams about intimidation.

file: 1995/1995-11-10_beta prodcut_fix problems_logically impossible_schedule_manager_not engineer.gif
title: Fixing Problems Before Finding Them

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will it take to fix any problems we find in our beta product?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is logically impossible to schedule for the unknown.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try to think as a manager, not as an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, we'll fix the problems before we find them.

setting: Conference room, at a meeting table
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long it will take to fix problems discovered in the beta product. Dilbert says you can't schedule for unknown problems, and the Boss tells him to think like a manager instead of an engineer. Dilbert then adopts the illogical managerial approach and says they'll fix the problems before finding them.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically mimics management logic by proposing the impossible, fixing bugs before they are discovered, showing how absurd the Boss's demand for a schedule is.
summary: A manager demands a fix-time estimate for bugs nobody has found yet, and the engineer answers with equally impossible managerial reasoning.

file: 1995/1995-06-21_3d rendering_career_computing needs_finance dept.gif
title: Obsolete 286 PC for 3D Rendering

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The finance department has analyzed your computing needs and decided to give you a 286 PC.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That should be sufficient for the 3D-rendering you need to do.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Besides, how many times are you going to do 3D-rendering in your career?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Once, if I hurry.

situation: Ratbert, acting as an office functionary, tells Dilbert that the finance department has decided to issue him an ancient 286 PC. He claims it is enough for Dilbert's 3D-rendering work and asks how often Dilbert will ever need to render in his career. Dilbert replies that it will only get done once, if he hurries.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically points out that a 286 is so slow that he'd only manage a single 3D rendering in his whole career, and only if he works fast.
summary: A cost-cutting finance department hands an engineer a hopelessly outdated computer for graphics-heavy work, and he answers with deadpan sarcasm about how long it will take.

file: 1995/1995-06-14_reengineered job_more fulfilled_value chain_stages of prodcution_fired secretaries_credenza.gif
title: Reengineered Job Means Doing Secretaries' Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great news! I've reengineered your job to make you more fulfilled!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll no longer be limited to one little part of the value chain. You'll be involved in all stages of production!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh Lord, you fired all the secretaries!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dust my credenza.

situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Dilbert that he has reengineered Dilbert's job so he will be more fulfilled and involved in all stages of production. Dilbert realizes the reorganization means the secretaries were fired and their duties have been dumped on him. The Boss then orders him to dust his credenza.
punchline: The 'reengineering' and 'fulfilling' job enrichment is really just a cost-cutting layoff that makes the engineer do menial secretarial chores like dusting the boss's furniture.
summary: A manager spins the elimination of the support staff as a chance for an engineer's personal growth, then hands him a feather duster.

file: 1995/1995-09-11_employee benefits_eyegalsses_support new vision_radila keratotomy_squinting.gif
title: Squinting Replaces Eyeglasses Benefit

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: As Director of Human Resources I've been asked to reduce the cost of employee benefits.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company will no longer pay for eyeglasses. But we WILL support a new vision-correction procedure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Radial keratotomy?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Squinting.

situation: Catbert, as Director of Human Resources, tells employees at a conference table that benefit costs are being cut. He announces the company will stop paying for eyeglasses but will support a new vision-correction procedure. Dilbert guesses it is surgery, but Catbert reveals it is simply squinting.
punchline: The company's supposed support for vision correction is just telling employees to squint, a cynical way to save money while pretending to offer a benefit.
summary: A feline HR director swaps the eyeglasses benefit for the cheapest imaginable fix: making staff squint.

file: 1995/1995-01-09_individual cubicles_new system_public schools_hoteling_getting tips_cubicle_computer_chair_roll of note_technology.gif
title: Hoteling: Cubicles Like Public Restrooms

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're taking away your individual cubicles. In the new system you'll sign up for whatever cube is open that day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's based on the model of public restrooms. But I call it "hoteling" because it increases my chances of getting tips.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each cubicle will have a computer, a chair, and a roll of note paper ... Take one and pass it around.

setting: Conference room during a presentation to employees
situation: The Boss presents a new office plan using an overhead projector, announcing that employees will lose their assigned cubicles and instead sign up for whatever cube is free each day. He admits the idea is modeled on public restrooms and jokes about the name 'hoteling.' He then explains each cube will have only a computer, chair and a roll of note paper, which he hands out to be passed around while Dilbert and coworkers listen.
punchline: The Boss's new 'hoteling' workspace policy is openly modeled on public restrooms, and he even pitches the name as a way to get tips, showing both his lack of tact and how little the plan respects employees.
summary: A manager unveils a hot-desking scheme he cheerfully compares to a public toilet, complete with a roll of paper to pass around.

file: 1995/1995-07-13_start documenting_market requirements_design skills_rewarding_work_doo hickey.gif
title: Customer Wants Design Menu First

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, let's start by documenting your market requirements.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, let's start by you telling me all the things you can design. Then I'll tell you which one I like.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Work can be very rewarding. You should try it.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What's that doohickey you have there?

situation: Dilbert sits at a table with his laptop and tries to start by documenting a customer's market requirements. The customer refuses and asks Dilbert to list everything he can design so the customer can simply pick one. Dilbert snipes that work can be rewarding, and the customer, unfazed, asks about the laptop.
punchline: The customer wants to choose from a menu of finished ideas instead of doing the work of defining requirements, and he is so detached from real work that he doesn't even recognise a laptop.
summary: A client who won't state what he needs expects an engineer to pitch designs for him to choose from, and he gets mocked for never having done any actual work.

file: 1995/1995-02-18_bad news_no raises_making worse_own reward_rewarded_twice as much.gif
title: No Raises, Work Is Its Reward

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bad news

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're not giving any raises.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Making it worse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we think work is its own reward.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Making it much worse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Expect to get rewarded about twice as much next year.

setting: Boss's office, seen from the employee's side of the desk
situation: The Boss sits in his chair and delivers an announcement in three escalating stages, each under a caption. First he says there will be no raises, then that work is its own reward, then that next year's reward will be twice as large. The panels are nearly identical, with only the captions and his cheerful grin tracking the worsening news.
punchline: Since the 'reward' is just the work itself, doubling it next year means no pay increase and twice the workload, delivered with a smile.
summary: A manager cheerfully breaks the news that pay raises are cancelled and compensates with more of what he calls a reward, which is simply more work.

file: 1995/1995-01-15_avoid completing_do it right_does anything_fear of mistakes_higher quality_inspire_morale low_new philosophy_paralyzed_punish anybody_realize mistakes_value opinion_victims.gif
title: Do It Right the First Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new philosophy is "We do it right the first time."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This will inspire you to higher quality because you'll realize mistakes are not tolerated.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Since mistakes are inevitable, wouldn't your philosophy inspire us to avoid completing anything?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll be paralyzed by the fear of mistakes, victims of our own unrealistic philosophy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You might as well have a philosophy that says "We punish anybody who does anything."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I value your opinion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to make some posters that say "We do it right the first time."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wally's paralyzed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next item: Why is employee morale so low?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces a new quality philosophy of doing everything right the first time, saying mistakes won't be tolerated. Dilbert and Wally point out that this will only make employees afraid to finish anything. The Boss claims to value their opinion, then assigns Wally to make posters promoting the very philosophy they criticized.
punchline: The Boss ignores the valid criticism that a zero-tolerance-for-mistakes policy paralyzes employees, then wonders why morale is low.
summary: A manager's no-mistakes policy leaves his staff frozen with fear, yet he is baffled by their sagging spirits.
keywords: do it right the first time

file: 1995/1995-11-18_more proactive_fires dilbert_doesn't know why.gif
title: Proactive Boss Fires Dilbert Preemptively

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on I'm going to be more proactive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're fired!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For what??

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know yet. That's the problem with being proactive.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and announces he will now be more proactive. He immediately fires Dilbert. When Dilbert asks what he did wrong, the Boss admits he doesn't have a reason yet.
punchline: The Boss's idea of being proactive is acting before any problem exists, so he fires Dilbert before he can even identify a reason, showing how management buzzwords get applied absurdly.
summary: A manager vows to act before problems arise and promptly dismisses an employee without any cause, admitting the reason will have to come later.

file: 1995/1995-10-09_succeed_competitors_salary increases_external competition_idiot boy.gif
title: Competing With Your Own Coworkers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll succeed if we understand who our competitors really are!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My competition is Dilbert and Alice, with whom I compete for salary increases and rare promotion opportunities.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I meant our external competition.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Tell me again what we make.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No raise for you, idiot boy.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team they will succeed if they understand who their competitors really are. Wally answers literally that his competitors are Dilbert and Alice, since they compete for raises and promotions. The Boss clarifies he meant outside competitors, and Wally asks what the company makes, which gets him a denied raise.
punchline: Wally's honest answer exposes that internal competition for scarce raises is the real contest, and the Boss punishes him for it while also revealing Wally doesn't even know what the company makes.
summary: A manager's pep talk about rivals is derailed when an employee names his teammates as the real competition for pay and promotions.

file: 1995/1995-07-19_teds baby shower_gift_hand crafted items_three holes_paper bag_lovely baby dress_cheap.gif
title: Cheap Baby Shower Gift Ideas

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know what kind of gift to buy for Ted's baby shower.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Hand-crafted items are good. Cut three holes in a paper bag and you've got a lovely baby dress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He might think I'm cheap.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Do you think the kid has a salt shaker yet?

setting: Office cafeteria, at a lunch table
situation: Dilbert and a bald coworker eat lunch in the cafeteria while Dilbert wonders what to buy for Ted's baby shower. The coworker suggests a homemade gift, a baby dress made from a paper bag with three holes cut in it. When Dilbert worries about seeming cheap, the coworker asks if the baby has a salt shaker yet, implying he'd give that as a gift too.
punchline: The coworker's advice to be cheap gets even cheaper when he suggests a salt shaker, probably swiped from the cafeteria table, as a gift, ignoring Dilbert's concern about looking stingy.
summary: A frugal lunch companion advises a gift-shopping colleague to hand over a paper-bag outfit, then shrugs off worries about stinginess by proposing a cafeteria condiment too.

file: 1995/1995-06-06_renewed psychologist_peak performance_relative_dysfunctional team_realistic goals_postpone canibalsim.gif
title: Dogbert Postpones Team Cannibalism

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired renowned psychologist Dogbert to help us achieve peak performance in teamwork.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Peak performance is somewhat relative. You're a highly dysfunctional team, so we must set realistic goals.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What would be a realistic goal for us?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I can postpone cannibalism.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss introduces Dogbert, whom he has hired as a renowned psychologist, to improve the team's teamwork. Dogbert explains that because the team is highly dysfunctional, they need realistic goals. When the Boss asks what a realistic goal would be, Dogbert suggests he might be able to delay the team's descent into cannibalism.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of a realistic goal for this dysfunctional team is merely delaying them from eating each other, implying they are hopelessly bad at teamwork.
summary: A consultant brought in to boost team performance sets the bar so low that his best hope is staving off cannibalism.

file: 1995/1995-08-14_dehumanization_weekly status_doubt exostence_invisible_pager buzzing_batteries.gif
title: Dilbert's Existential Status Report

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My status for the week is that the ongoing dehumanization from my job has caused me to doubt my existence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is reason to believe I am becoming invisible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do I hear your pager buzzing, Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I doubt it; I don't keep batteries in it.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Plink

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: At a weekly status meeting, Dilbert reports that job dehumanization is making him doubt his own existence and that he may be becoming invisible. Wally sits beside him reading his notes and ignoring him. Meanwhile the Boss, oblivious to Dilbert's report, asks Wally about a buzzing pager, and Wally says he keeps no batteries in it.
punchline: Dilbert's cry about becoming invisible proves true as everyone ignores him, while Wally reveals he deliberately disables his pager so nobody can reach him.
summary: A staffer's despairing weekly update goes unheard while his coworker brags about keeping his pager dead to avoid being contacted.

file: 1995/1995-09-21_tech support_bob_newest manuver_turban wedgie_regular wedgie.gif
title: Bob the Dinosaur's Turban Wedgie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been on hold for tech support since Tuesday. Get Bob and meet me in the car.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I can't wait to try my newest maneuver, the "turban wedgie."

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It starts like a regular wedgie then I wrap it around his head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question...

situation: Dilbert has been on hold with tech support since Tuesday, so he tells his friend Bob, a green dinosaur, to join him in the car. On the drive Bob gleefully announces his new wedgie maneuver, and in the final panel he demonstrates it on a hapless man in a turban-wrapped underwear getup while Dilbert, still holding the phone, asks a question.
punchline: After days stuck on hold, Dilbert is taking Bob to physically assault a tech support person, an absurd and violent escalation of customer frustration.
summary: Fed up with endless waiting for help, a man brings his wedgie-obsessed dinosaur friend along to settle things in person.

file: 1995/1995-04-20_new offcie_volunteered_coordinate_move_cubicle assignment_existence_lord wally_puppet master_cubicle.gif
title: Wally, Lord of Cubicle Assignments

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We're moving to a new office across town. I volunteered to coordinate the move.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I control your cubicle assignment. Nay, your very existence. From now on you will refer to me as "Lord Wally the Puppet Master."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think it's legal to enjoy your work this much.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I banish you to the cubicle closest to your boss!!

situation: Wally tells Dilbert that the company is moving offices and that he has volunteered to coordinate the move. He then gleefully declares that he controls Dilbert's cubicle assignment and demands to be called 'Lord Wally the Puppet Master.' Dilbert remarks that it can't be legal to enjoy work this much, and Wally responds by banishing him to the cubicle nearest the boss.
punchline: Wally, who normally does as little work as possible, finally enjoys a task, and he is so thrilled by the petty power over cubicle assignments that he abuses it dramatically.
summary: Handed a tiny shred of authority over office-move logistics, the notoriously lazy Wally turns into a gloating tyrant who threatens a coworker with a dreaded desk location.

file: 1995/1995-03-26_photocopier_access code_proprietary information_same comapny_ask question_who's on first.gif
title: Copier Access Code Catch-22

transcript.speaker: Photocopier
transcript.text: Please enter photocopier access code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the code for this machine?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That's proprietary information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We work for the same company. My cubicle is down the hall.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I have no way of verifying your claim. Anybody could come in here and say that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask me a question that only an employee of this company could answer.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: What is the access code for this copier?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I just have one...

situation: Dilbert needs the access code for the photocopier and asks a coworker, who refuses to share it as proprietary information. When he offers to prove he is an employee by answering a question only an employee could answer, she asks for the copier's access code, which is the very thing he is trying to find out. Dilbert ends up sobbing in frustration.
punchline: The coworker's security verification question is the very thing Dilbert doesn't know, so her 'proof of employment' test guarantees he can never pass it.
summary: A guarded coworker demands proof that Dilbert works there, then picks a test question he cannot possibly answer, leaving him in tears.

file: 1995/1995-10-15_dogbert_long range planner_impossible evaluation_flex-time_supposed to work_internet connection n_telecommute_not pollute_give a hoot_losers_demanded relocation_no budget_poodle graohics_big raise.gif
title: Dogbert Negotiates Long Range Planner Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do you want to be our new "Long Range Planner," Mister Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because "long range" is very far away . . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...therefore it will be impossible to evaluate my performance.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If it's not too much to ask, I'd like to be on flex-time so you'll never know if I'm supposed to be at work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll need an Internet connection at home so I can telecommute and not pollute.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because I give a hoot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Also, I'd like to be in a group with lots of losers. That way I'll get the biggest raise when we're ranked.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired. All of the other applicants demanded relocation expenses and I have no budget for that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do I have to work while you just look for poodle graphics on the Internet?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't work too hard; I'd like a big raise.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Dogbert interviews with the Boss for a Long Range Planner position and lists self-serving conditions: unmeasurable performance, flex-time, and telecommuting from home. The Boss hires him because the other applicants wanted relocation expenses he can't afford. Afterward Dilbert complains that Dogbert just surfs for poodle pictures while Dilbert works.
punchline: Dogbert exploits every management blind spot, landing a do-nothing job with a raise tied to the hard work of Dilbert's group of 'losers'.
summary: A canine job applicant sells his boss on a role whose very nature makes him unaccountable, then cheerfully coasts while a colleague's efforts pad his pay.

file: 1995/1995-04-23_turning est_artificial software_repsonse_on screen_computer_staretgy_visonize_enhance earnings_motivate emplyees_improve focus_opportunity_opinions_redefine_technology.gif
title: Turing Test Exposes Management Gibberish

transcript.speaker: Technician
transcript.text: You'll be performing a "Turing test" on our new artificial intelligence software.

transcript.speaker: Technician
transcript.text: Try to determine if the responses on your screen come from our computer or a human in the next room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll ask it to write a strategy for our company.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: "Our strategy is to visionize quality resources that enhance earnings."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll ask it how to motivate employees.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: "Reorganize often to improve focus. Redefine work as 'opportunity' and increase it daily. Take time to ask for opinions then explain why they're wrong."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be a computer because there's no human intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Technician
transcript.text: Unless...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nice try, Boss.

setting: Office cubicle, plus a small room next door
situation: Dilbert is asked by a technician to run a Turing test on new AI software, judging whether on-screen answers come from a computer or a person in the next room. He asks for a company strategy and employee motivation advice and gets buzzword-laden managerial nonsense. He concludes it must be a computer, then opens the next-room door and finds the Boss typing the answers.
punchline: The responses are so full of empty, counterproductive management jargon that Dilbert assumes no human could have written them, only to find the Boss was the one typing.
summary: A machine-intelligence experiment turns out to be powered by the Boss, whose vapid management-speak was mistaken for genuine computing.

file: 1995/1995-11-30_dating for a year_needs can't fulfill_internet been broken.gif
title: Dilbert's Needs: Home Internet Access

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've been dating for a year now, Liz. There's something I'd like to do tonight...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are some needs that I can't fulfill at work.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: I understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes! Yes!

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: How long has your internet connection at work been broken?

setting: Liz's living room couch, then at her computer desk
situation: Dilbert tells his girlfriend Liz of a year that there is something he wants to do tonight, hinting at a need he can't satisfy at work. Liz sympathetically says she understands and takes his hands. In the last panel Dilbert is happily surfing the internet on her computer while she reads a book and wryly asks how long his work connection has been broken.
punchline: Dilbert's romantic buildup was really a ploy to get access to her internet connection, and Liz sees through it, implying he's only after her computer, not her.
summary: A man's tender talk about unmet needs turns out to be nothing more than a bid to use his girlfriend's computer to get online.
themes: work life spilling into personal life

file: 1995/1995-03-22_new org chart_changed mind_sore but free.gif
title: Catbert's Reorg Throws Employees Around

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Come see the new org chart.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Oops, changed my mind!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: WHAM!!

transcript.speaker: Woman employee
transcript.text: Ouchie.

transcript.speaker: Man employee
transcript.text: I'm sore, but I've never felt so free.

characters: Employee (man in glasses and green tie)
setting: Office meeting area with a raised platform and a gray floor
situation: Catbert stands on a ledge holding a pointer to a new org chart and invites two employees to come see it. The employees rush forward, but Catbert changes his mind and whips the chart away, so they slam into the wall or platform. Bruised afterward, one employee says he is sore but feels liberated.
punchline: The reorganization literally hits employees hard, yet the dazed victim spins the painful, capricious change as a feeling of freedom.
summary: A malicious cat executive lures staff toward a freshly drawn org chart and yanks it away at the last second, leaving them battered but oddly cheerful.

file: 1995/1995-12-23_additional funindg_porject_meeting_spectacular failure_any advice_breath mints_business.gif
title: Spectacular Failure Guarantees Everyone Promotions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the advice of my dog, I'm asking for an additional ten million dollars for my project.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That will make a more spectacular failure, thus guaranteeing a promotion for me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As your boss, I'd get recognition too... Okay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow! Do you have any advice for me?!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Breath mints.

situation: Dilbert tells a meeting that, on his dog's advice, he is requesting another ten million dollars for his project. Dogbert explains this will make the project fail more spectacularly, which will earn him a promotion, and the Boss approves because he would get recognition too. A bald coworker then eagerly asks Dogbert for advice and gets a curt, unhelpful answer.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is openly cynical, since inflating a doomed project into a bigger failure gets everyone promoted, and the eager coworker who asks for similar wisdom gets only a dismissive tip about breath mints.
summary: A dog's scheme to bankroll a bigger flop for career gain wins over the boss, and an envious coworker who asks for similar tips is brushed off.

file: 1995/1995-12-04_engineers_field support people_inferior technology_most attractive feamle_prodcuts.gif
title: Attractive Saleswoman Beats Inferior Technology

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: On one hand, my company does use inferior technology in our products...

transcript.speaker: Saleswoman
transcript.text: But on the other hand, I'm the most attractive female who has paid attention to you this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What kind of engineers do you think we are??!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have pictures of your field support people?

setting: Conference room during a vendor sales meeting
situation: A female vendor sales rep pitches her company's products to Dilbert and Wally, openly admitting the technology is inferior. She then argues they should buy anyway because she is the most attractive woman who has paid attention to them this year. Dilbert indignantly protests the stereotype, while Wally eagerly asks to see pictures of her field support staff.
punchline: The saleswoman's pitch plays on the stereotype of lonely engineers, and Dilbert's indignant denial is undercut by Wally immediately proving her right by asking about her colleagues.
summary: A vendor admits her product is second-rate but bets that flattery and her looks will win over a pair of socially starved engineers.

file: 1995/1995-09-28_sitting for boss_prodcutivity_efficiency_queen alice.gif
title: Alice Becomes Queen Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Alice is sitting in for the Boss!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Productivity at last!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Efficiency! Yes!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As long as she doesn't get an attitude...

situation: A coworker announces that Alice is filling in for the Boss, and Dilbert and another coworker cheer the prospect of finally getting productivity and efficiency. In the last panel Alice appears wearing a crown and holding a scepter-like mallet while a coworker bows down before her.
punchline: The hopeful coworkers' worry about Alice getting an attitude is instantly proven right, as the temporary power has turned her into a tyrannical queen demanding groveling.
summary: Colleagues celebrate having a competent stand-in manager, only to find her ruling the office like an imperious monarch.

file: 1995/1995-07-01_dogbert the consultant_took adice_formed buisness_compmay_spend time fighting_guarantee future business_expired.gif
title: Consultant's Contract Conveniently Expires

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We took your advice and formed business units within the company...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now we spend all of our time fighting with each other about who does what.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What exactly did you mean when you said it would "guarantee future business"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh look - my contract just expired.

situation: The Boss tells consultant Dogbert that the company followed his advice and split into business units, but now employees spend all their time fighting over who does what. In the background, two employees are physically brawling. When the Boss asks what Dogbert meant by guaranteeing future business, Dogbert pretends his contract has just expired and escapes.
punchline: Dogbert's advice was designed to create chaos that would guarantee him future consulting work, and he dodges accountability by claiming his contract has ended.
summary: A consultant's reorganization advice turns the company into a battleground, and when questioned he slips away citing a convenient end to his contract.

file: 1995/1995-09-01_tina brittlke tech_dysfunctional_opinions_email_women portrayed_lawyers_startship captains_art class.gif
title: Dogbert Solicits Reader Opinions on Tina

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This week we introduced Tina the brittle tech writer to the strip. Tina is dysfunctional like everybody here except me.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: RRRR

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Send your opinions by e-mail to scottadams@aol.com

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's the only way we can learn.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: RRRR

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pick one

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A. Women should only be portrayed as lawyers and starship captains.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: B. I don't have e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: C. Tina should be treated with the same dignity as Dilbert and Wally.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: D. Take an art class.

situation: Dogbert, seated at a conference table beside the growling Tina, addresses the reader about the newly introduced character Tina, calling her dysfunctional, and asks for feedback by e-mail. The last panel presents a multiple-choice 'Pick One' survey of possible reader reactions.
punchline: The strip lampoons the feedback it expects from readers, listing the typical complaints about a female character's portrayal and ending with the dismissive suggestion that critics should just take an art class.
summary: The cartoonist uses Dogbert to invite reader reactions to a new character and then jokingly lists the predictable responses he anticipates.

file: 1995/1995-12-17_taken vacation_use vacation days_work 7 days a week_year end review_artificial project_vacation target_mutually exclusive goal_frustration.gif
title: Mutually Exclusive Project and Vacation Targets

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, our records show that you haven't taken a vacation all year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Company policy requires you to use your vacation days.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How?? You told me to work seven days a week to prepare the project for your boss's year-end review.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you want me to meet the artificial project target or the artificial vacation target?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hello!!! These are mutually exclusive goals!!! Hello!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ooh... Sorry. I usually just think that last part in silent frustration.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Moving right along... Kudos to Wally for using all of his vacation days ahead of schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get over it, Alice. We can't all be superstars.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss tells Alice she must take her unused vacation days under company policy. Alice points out that he ordered her to work seven days a week to prepare for a year-end review, so the two demands conflict. After she vents, he ignores the problem, praises Wally for using up his vacation early, and tells Alice to get over it.
punchline: The Boss praises lazy Wally as a superstar for burning through his vacation days while dismissing Alice, whose overwork was caused by the Boss's own contradictory demands.
summary: A manager imposes two incompatible requirements on a hard-working employee, then brushes off her complaint and rewards the slacker instead.

file: 1995/1995-06-05_transfer_department_dysfunctional organization_love and support_long distant_fax room_resume_complete jerk.gif
title: Wally's Transfer Interview With Jerk Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do you want to transfer to my department, Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm in a dysfunctional organization. I'm not getting the love and support I need. That's why I've been making long-distance personal calls from the fax room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your résumé says every boss you've had was a complete jerk.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So, when do I start?

setting: Manager's office, during an internal transfer interview
situation: Wally interviews with a manager for a transfer to the manager's department. He explains that he wants to leave his dysfunctional group and admits to making personal long-distance calls from the fax room. The manager points out that Wally's résumé calls every previous boss a jerk, and Wally cheerfully asks when he can start.
punchline: Wally treats the manager's accusation that all his past bosses were jerks as a qualification, assuming the hiring manager is a jerk too, or simply not caring that his own résumé describes him as a complainer.
summary: A man seeking a job transfer cheerfully admits to wasting company phone resources, then responds to a damning note on his résumé as if it were an offer.

file: 1995/1995-01-19_left engineering_acme manger_sexy_liz_decrease sex appeal_planning number_ham radio licence_compensate loss_goose bumps.gif
title: Manager Sex Appeal Planning Number

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I left engineering and became a manager would I be as sexy as I am now, Liz?

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: I think it would decrease your sex appeal by 17%. But that's just a planning number.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I got my ham radio license to compensate for the loss?

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Look at my arm: goose bumps.

setting: Outdoor walking path in a park
situation: Dilbert walks with Liz and asks how becoming a manager would affect his sex appeal. She gives a precise-sounding estimate of a 17% decrease, calling it a planning number. Dilbert suggests getting a ham radio license to offset the loss, and she shows him the goose bumps on her arm.
punchline: Liz's goose bumps are ambiguous sarcasm: they imply she is repelled by the ham radio idea, while Dilbert's earnest question treats his sex appeal like a quantifiable business metric.
summary: A man asks a woman to quantify how a career change would hurt his attractiveness and then proposes a nerdy hobby to make up for it, with predictably unflattering results.

file: 1995/1995-11-05_worked all night_presentation package_date on page_color transparencies_no reason to date_clutter page_dumb idea by boss_no calendars_brain exploded_february 30th.gif
title: Boss Demands Pointless Presentation Dates

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked all night but I finished the presentation package you wanted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put the presentation date on each page.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those are color transparencies. It would take hours and cost hundreds of dollars to reprint them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no reason to date them. In fact, it would limit future use and clutter the page.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But since you're incapable of admitting error...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I eagerly await your bizarre, other-worldly explanation for putting the date on each page.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some people might not have calendars. And we have to make sure it's not a holiday.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BAM!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch. My brain exploded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first presentation is February 30th...

situation: Dilbert delivers a presentation package he stayed up all night finishing, and the Boss orders him to date every page even though they are costly color transparencies. Dilbert explains why it's a bad idea, then taunts the Boss to come up with a justification. The Boss offers a nonsensical reason, and Dilbert's head slams the desk in disbelief.
punchline: The Boss's absurd excuse for the date requirement is so illogical that Dilbert's brain 'explodes', and the strip ends by noting that the first presentation date is February 30th, a date that doesn't exist, proving the Boss's dates would be useless anyway.
summary: An employee sarcastically challenges his stubborn manager to justify a pointless and expensive formatting order, only to be floored by a ridiculous rationale.

file: 1995/1995-10-23_revoke angel status_bad name_healing_ugly people look attractive_too late_old look_beautiful.gif
title: Angel Dogbert Beautifies Ugly People

transcript.speaker: Voice from above
transcript.text: We've decided to revoke your angel status. You're giving us all a bad name.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your problem is that you define "healing" too narrowly. I'm making ugly people look attractive, and that's important, too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it too late to go back to my old look?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why? You're beautiful!

setting: Dogbert's desk in an office, with a voice speaking from above
situation: Dogbert, wearing a halo, is told by a heavenly voice that his angel status is being revoked for giving angels a bad name. Dogbert defends himself by saying he heals people by making ugly people look attractive. A transformed Dilbert then asks if he can go back to his old look, and Dogbert insists he is now beautiful.
punchline: Dogbert's cosmetic 'healing' has left Dilbert looking so different that he wants his old face back, while Dogbert blithely insists the unwanted makeover is an improvement.
summary: A self-styled angel redefines healing as cosmetic makeovers, and his unhappy patient begs to be changed back.

file: 1995/1995-12-08_critical system_all the power_essential upgardes_simple fool_next emplyee_vendor issues_compatibility.gif
title: Vendor Lock-In Gloats at Customer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's funny - before your company bought that critical system from me, YOU had all the power...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But now, only I can provide essential upgrades!! I call the shots, you simple fool!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Send in the next employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least we don't have any multi-vendor compatibility issues.

setting: The Boss's office and the cubicle area
situation: Dogbert, a vendor, stands on the Boss's desk and gloats that since the company bought his critical system, only he can supply essential upgrades and so he holds all the power. The Boss, unfazed, calls for the next employee in line. Dilbert, waiting with a numbered ticket, comments that at least the company has no multi-vendor compatibility issues.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically puts a positive spin on being locked in to a single vendor, noting that the only upside of having no alternatives is that there are no compatibility problems.
summary: After selling a system that only he can upgrade, a smug vendor taunts his customer, while an employee wryly finds a silver lining in being stuck with one supplier.

file: 1995/1995-10-28_using binders_illeagl_size of cubicle_staus_raise.gif
title: Binder Wall Cubicle Expansion Scheme

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It looks like somebody is using binders to illegally increase the size of his cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You think your status will increase with your cubicle size, don't you! Well, it won't work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's a raise. I don't know why.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Pssst. Is he seeing anybody?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Rrrr

situation: Dilbert happily stacks binders along his cubicle wall to make it bigger, and Wally, whistling nearby, accuses him of cheating to gain status and insists it won't work. The Boss then arrives and hands Dilbert a raise for no clear reason, while Alice whispers to ask if Dilbert is dating anyone, leaving a fuming Wally behind.
punchline: Wally's insistence that a bigger cubicle won't raise status is immediately disproved when Dilbert gets a raise and sudden romantic interest because of the binder-built walls.
summary: A coworker scolds a man for padding his cubicle with binders, only to watch that very trick earn him a raise and admirers.

file: 1995/1995-01-18_stay engineer_career in mangement_engineer_dark side_found probelm_engineering.gif
title: Dark Side Calling Is Literal

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't decide if I should stay with engineering or pursue a career in management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my heart I'm an engineer but I hear a voice calling me to the dark side.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I found your problem.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Boy is my face red.

setting: Dogbert's office, with Dilbert on a couch
situation: Dilbert lies on a couch talking to Dogbert, who plays a therapist, about whether to stay an engineer or move into management. He says he hears a voice calling him to the dark side. Dogbert looks over the back of the couch and discovers a devil in a red costume crouching behind it, whispering to Dilbert.
punchline: The voice tempting Dilbert toward management is literally a devil hiding behind the couch, implying that management is the path of evil.
summary: A therapy session about a career choice reveals that the tempting inner voice belongs to an actual devil lurking behind the sofa.

file: 1995/1995-07-31_i think_therefore i am_philosophical question_you're not me_you're irrelevant.gif
title: Micromanaged, Therefore I Am Not

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think, therefore I am.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'm micromanaged, therefore I am not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a philosophical question for you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not me, therefore you're irrelevant.

setting: Office cubicle, then Dogbert's reading spot
situation: Dilbert sits in his cubicle musing on Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am.' The Boss then hovers over his shoulder, prompting Dilbert to conclude that being micromanaged means he doesn't really exist. He then brings his philosophical question to Dogbert, who dismisses him outright.
punchline: Dogbert's self-centered logic mirrors Descartes' format to dismiss Dilbert, topping the joke that micromanagement erases a worker's sense of self.
summary: A cubicle worker twists a famous philosophical maxim to lament his overbearing supervisor, then gets brushed off by a self-absorbed dog.

file: 1995/1995-04-06_attractive incentives_elbonia_zero taxes_cheerful_leave labor_environmental regulations_best you can do_lawn ornament.gif
title: Elbonia's Desperate Incentives for Relocating Companies

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We're offering attractive incentives to companies that move to Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Zero taxes, cheerful slave labor, amnesty from any inconvenient laws, and absolutely no environmental regulations!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that the best you can do?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Here, use my firstborn son as a lawn ornament.

situation: An Elbonian representative pitches the benefits of relocating a company to Elbonia to the Boss, listing zero taxes, slave labor, legal amnesty and no environmental rules. The Boss is unimpressed and asks if that is the best he can offer, so the Elbonian sweetens the deal by offering his own young son as a lawn ornament.
punchline: The Boss's greed is so insatiable that even an offer of slave labor and no laws isn't enough, so the Elbonian escalates to offering his own child as a decoration.
summary: A foreign delegate lists shamelessly exploitative perks to lure a business, then offers his own son when the greedy manager demands more.

file: 1995/1995-09-26_hired_audit_perfect job_give money_call dolts_alice_engineer_makes slides_eat donuts_engineering.gif
title: Dogbert's Perfect ISO Audit Job

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been hired by your company to perform an ISO 9000 audit.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Basically, you give me money and I tell you that you're a bunch of dolts. It's the perfect job for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell me what you do here, Alice, if that's your real name.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm an engineer. I make slides that people can't read. Sometimes I eat donuts.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, tells Alice he has been hired to perform an ISO 9000 audit at her company. He describes his job as taking money to call the client a bunch of dolts, then asks Alice to explain what she does. She answers with a bleak description of her engineering work.
punchline: Alice's deadpan summary of her job as making unreadable slides and eating donuts suggests the consultant's insult may be fair, and that the audit will find nothing productive.
summary: A consultant dog openly admits his audit work is just collecting fees to insult clients, then asks an engineer to justify her role and gets a cynical answer.

file: 1995/1995-08-06_boss evil_entity from another dimension_synergies_win win solution_delight every customer_new internet access_tour of cubicles.gif
title: Boss Hijacks Customer Meeting With Jargon

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: When did you start believing that your boss was an evil entity from another dimension?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to sit in on your customer meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me share the high level strategic view.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here we go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Life began in the primordial stew literally hundreds of years ago...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we are the only company who ever found synergies in our win-win solutions!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And we won't stop until we delight every customer!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'd be delighted if you just told me about your new internet access product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I cancelled the funding yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who's up for a tour of our cubicles?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gotta go.

setting: A therapist's office, then a conference room during a customer meeting
situation: Dilbert, lying on a therapist's couch, explains how he came to see his boss as an evil alien. He recalls the boss crashing a customer meeting, rambling about primordial stew and synergies for two hours while the customer sits bored. When the customer only wants information about an internet access product, the boss admits he cancelled its funding the day before, then offers a cubicle tour.
punchline: The boss talks for two hours about delighting customers, yet the one product the customer actually wants has already been defunded, proving his rhetoric is empty.
summary: A meandering executive monologue full of buzzwords wastes a customer's time, only to reveal the product they came to hear about no longer exists.

file: 1995/1995-10-14_catbert_hr director_too stressful_company counselor_re engineered_counseling process_cover sand.gif
title: Catbert Buries Stressed Employee in Sand

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert the H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My job is too stressful. Can I see a company counselor?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I re-engineered our counseling process. Now we put you in a big hole and cover you with sand.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If this is my only benefit I'd better get a lot of sand!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Just keep your mouth open.

situation: A stressed employee asks Catbert, the H.R. Director, if he can see a company counselor. Catbert announces that he has re-engineered the counseling process into putting employees in a hole and covering them with sand. In the final panel the employee is buried in the hole, and Catbert shovels sand onto him, advising him to keep his mouth open.
punchline: The company's re-engineered counseling is really just burying the employee alive, with Catbert cheerfully telling him to keep his mouth open so he can still breathe.
summary: A worn-out worker seeking help from the cruel H.R. cat discovers that the new counseling program amounts to being interred in a pit of sand.

file: 1995/1995-01-26_form a vidion_concept for requirements_startman_mission critical_functions_quality vectors_fine line_participation_and mockery.gif
title: Mocking Meeting Buzzwords With Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we could form a vision statement of our concepts for requirements.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or maybe we can bound our straw-man by the mission-critical functions of our quality vector!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're shameless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's a fine line between participation and mockery.

situation: In a meeting, the Boss proposes a vague, jargon-filled idea about a vision statement for requirements. Wally responds by spouting even more nonsensical buzzwords, appearing to contribute. Dilbert calls him shameless, and Wally admits he is blurring participation and mockery.
punchline: Wally mimics meaningless corporate jargon so convincingly that his mockery passes as genuine participation in the meeting.
summary: A coworker answers the manager's empty buzzword suggestion with an even more absurd string of jargon and gets away with it.

file: 1995/1995-06-12_two week retreat_mountains_management retreat_four star hotle_no room_brag_employees_glib_business.gif
title: Management Retreat Brag Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have fun working. I'm off to the two-week management retreat in the mountains.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's so sad you can't come. I guess there isn't room at the four-star hotel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I know why it's called a retreat.

situation: The Boss gloats to his employees that he is leaving for a two-week management retreat at a four-star mountain hotel while they stay behind and work. He smugly adds that there isn't room for them. In the last panel, books and objects are hurled at him and he flees, thinking about the word 'retreat'.
punchline: The Boss's tactless bragging provokes his employees into pelting him with objects, forcing him to literally retreat, which he glibly connects to the name of the event.
summary: A boss rubs in his luxurious mountain getaway to his overworked staff and gets chased off by a hail of flying books.

file: 1995/1995-04-13_blame the media_blow out proportion_dispappear_human nature_third wife_wally_free replacements.gif
title: Blame the Media for Missing Q

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You could offer free replacements for all the keyboards you sold without a "Q," or you could blame the media for blowing it out of proportion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's blame the media. They'll admit they were wrong and the whole thing will disappear.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have a brilliant grasp of human nature, Wally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know. My third wife always said the same thing.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss on how to handle the fallout from selling keyboards that lack a "Q" key. He offers two options: costly free replacements or blaming the media. The Boss picks blaming the media, expecting the press to admit fault, and Dogbert flatters him.
punchline: The Boss's absurd belief that the media will simply admit they were wrong shows he understands human nature poorly, and his reply about his third wife hints that his flaws have wrecked several marriages.
summary: A consultant dog talks a clueless executive into dodging a defective-product mess by pinning it on the press, then flatters him with a compliment that gets an ironic reply.

file: 1995/1995-08-19_neuter work_uninformed managers_no work_all week_work concept thing.gif
title: Skipping Work Before Meaningless Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know where you're going.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're going to a meeting where equally uninformed managers will make decisions that neuter the work I did all week.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You didn't do any work this week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I've got this whole "work" concept figured out.

situation: Dilbert confronts the Boss as he heads to a meeting, predicting that uninformed managers will make decisions that gut the work Dilbert did all week. Alice then points out that Dilbert didn't actually do any work this week.
punchline: Dilbert preemptively complains about management ruining his work, but since he did no work, he sarcastically claims to have mastered the concept of work, which is to avoid doing any so it can't be ruined.
summary: An employee grumbles that clueless managers will wreck his week of effort, only for a coworker to reveal he did nothing, which he treats as a clever strategy.

file: 1995/1995-06-26_saint dogbert_mediate_dispute_computers_desert and seek_enlightenment_path of computing_plan springs_endorsement_contract_end of line.gif
title: Saint Dogbert Sells Computing Enlightenment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked Saint Dogbert to mediate our dispute over what kind of computers are allowed here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I shall go to the desert and seek enlightenment. When I return I will reveal the true path of computing.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Palm Springs

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You call this an endorsement contract?! Go to the end of the line!

setting: Office, then a Palm Springs desert resort
situation: The Boss explains that he has asked Saint Dogbert, wearing a mitre and holding a bone staff, to settle a dispute over which computers the company should allow. Dogbert announces he will go to the desert to seek enlightenment about computing. In Palm Springs he is seen sitting at a table while vendor representatives with bags of money and cash line up to offer endorsement contracts, and he haughtily rejects one.
punchline: Dogbert's holy quest for the true path of computing is really a pretext to be bribed by competing vendors, and he treats the offers like an auction.
summary: A self-appointed saint is hired to judge a hardware dispute and promptly turns his spiritual retreat into a bidding war for paid endorsements.

file: 1995/1995-07-05_reprogrammed dna_marketing guys_heavens sake_thank you_power of suggestion.gif
title: Marketing Guy Overhears Alice's Insult

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe you shouldn't have told Stan you reprogrammed his DNA through the LAN.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Those marketing guys believe anything. They even believe market research, for heaven's sake.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's no telling what the power of suggestion might do.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Well, thank you very much.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert he shouldn't have convinced Stan, a marketing employee, that he had reprogrammed Stan's DNA over the network. She goes on to mock marketing people as gullible, even believing market research. In the last panel a marketing man has been standing nearby and overheard her.
punchline: Alice insults marketing people as gullible fools, only to discover a marketing guy has been listening and is offended.
summary: A coworker's scornful remarks about marketing staff being easily fooled are interrupted when one of them turns up and hears everything.
themes: getting caught talking behind someone's back

file: 1995/1995-03-02_new employee programs_new dignity enhancement program_drug testing_clue meter_reading zero_handsome coffee mug.gif
title: Dignity Program Meets Drug Testing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're announcing two new programs for employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first is a new dignity enhancement program and the second is our new random drug testing initiative.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The clue meter is reading zero.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You each get a handsome coffee mug as part of the kick-off.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces two new employee programs at a meeting: a dignity enhancement program and random drug testing. Alice, holding a clue meter, notes that it reads zero. The Boss carries on, promising everyone a coffee mug as a kick-off gift.
punchline: Management pairs a program about employee dignity with degrading drug testing without noticing the contradiction, and tries to smooth it over with a free coffee mug.
summary: A manager cheerfully unveils a dignity program alongside mandatory drug screening, oblivious to the irony, and sweetens it with swag.

file: 1995/1995-08-10_feels good_fester and grwo_micromanage_plan_self directed team_team meetings_full blown loathing.gif
title: Self-Directed Team Breeds Micromanagement Begging

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to make you a self-directed team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: After a few team meetings, the disrespect you have for each other will fester and grow into full-blown loathing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll beg me to micro-manage you!! Ha ha ha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It actually feels good to have a plan.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss stands at a projector screen and announces his plan to turn the group into a self-directed team. He gleefully explains that team meetings will make the members grow to loathe each other, so they will eventually beg him to micromanage them. Dilbert, seated with his coworkers, remarks that it feels good to finally have a plan.
punchline: The Boss's 'plan' is to deliberately make his team miserable so they will beg for micromanagement, and Dilbert is so starved for any plan from management that he finds it comforting anyway.
summary: A manager reveals a scheme to sour his team's relationships so they will plead for his close supervision, and an employee oddly appreciates having any plan at all.

file: 1995/1995-03-06_week behind_poor leadership_drained_parents_accept some resposibility_creating you_parents drunk.gif
title: Blaming the Boss's Parents

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you explain why you're a week behind schedule?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your poor leadership has drained me of the enthusiasm that is necessary to succeed. But it's not completely your fault.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Frankly, your parents have to accept some responsibility for creating you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Even if they were drunk?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why his project is a week behind schedule. Dilbert blames the Boss's poor leadership for killing his enthusiasm, then extends the blame to the Boss's parents for creating him. The Boss, apparently missing the insult, asks whether that still applies if his parents were drunk.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss by blaming his parents for producing such a leader, and the clueless Boss responds by wondering whether drunkenness excuses them, implicitly admitting he's a product of a bad decision.
summary: A worker answers a schedule complaint by faulting his manager's leadership and then his manager's upbringing, and the manager takes it as a serious question about mitigating circumstances.

file: 1995/1995-06-02_wally hat_safety rule_email_human resources_short ep_lyees_visibilty_aluminum foil pants_business.gif
title: Short Employees Wear Flag Hats

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the hat for, Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a new safety rule. I think it's stupid.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The e-mail from Human Resources said all short employees must wear these to improve visibility while in the cubicle aisles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: HR should change their password once in a while.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll bet we can make him wear aluminum foil pants.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally why he is wearing a hat topped with a small red flag. Wally explains that an e-mail from Human Resources ordered all short employees to wear them for visibility in the cubicle aisles. Dilbert and Alice suspect the e-mail was a hoax sent by someone who hacked HR's account.
punchline: Wally has obeyed an obviously bogus e-mail from a hacked HR account, so Dilbert and Alice joke that they could trick him into wearing anything, even aluminum foil pants.
summary: A gullible coworker obeys a dubious company e-mail by wearing a flagged hat, and his colleagues realize the message was probably forged and could be used to manipulate him further.

file: 1995/1995-01-08_floor warden_fire_leadership_leader_uniformed decisions_huge stock options_risking death_high rise inferno_fallen co workers_stock options_cpr.gif
title: Floor Warden Fire Duty Gets Mocked

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Congratulations!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've been named "floor warden."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In the event of a fire we'll rely on your leadership to get us out safely.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me see if I understand this...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: YOU'RE the leader when it involves uninformed decisions in return for huge stock options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'M the leader when it comes to risking death in a highrise inferno while you scramble over the ashen backs of fallen co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What makes you think your life is worth more than mine?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got stock options and you're a floor warden.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't expect any CPR.

situation: The Boss cheerfully informs Dilbert that he has been named floor warden and will be relied on to lead everyone to safety in a fire. Dilbert points out the unfairness of the arrangement: the Boss gets stock options for uninformed decisions while Dilbert would risk his life. The Boss coldly answers that his stock options make his life more valuable.
punchline: The Boss openly admits that his stock options make his life worth more than Dilbert's, so Dilbert shouldn't expect to be rescued or revived.
summary: A manager hands out a dangerous safety title as if it were an honor, then bluntly admits that his own financial perks put his life above his employee's.

file: 1995/1995-01-13_dogbert venture capitalist_word processing_windows_interesting concept_french bread.gif
title: Venture Capitalist Dogbert Hires Bread Beating

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert, Venture Capitalist

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: My idea is to develop a word processing program for Windows.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's an interesting concept. I wonder if twenty dollars would be enough.

transcript.speaker: Man
