transcript.text: To start a software company?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, to pay our waitress to beat you with a loaf of French bread.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a venture capitalist, meets over a meal with a man pitching a startup idea for a Windows word processor. Dogbert feigns interest and asks whether twenty dollars would be enough, which the man assumes is seed funding. Dogbert reveals the money is to pay the waitress to hit him with a French bread loaf.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the pitch as so unoriginal that it deserves a physical beating rather than funding, mocking the crowded market for word processors.
summary: A dog posing as an investor listens to a software pitch and offers a tiny sum that turns out to be a bounty for a bread-based assault.

file: 1995/1995-03-19_meeting_wouldn't conclude_pregnant pauses_window of opportunity_reinterating_hake hand_awkward pause_business.gif
title: The Meeting That Never Ends

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... okay, great...

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Alright then...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trapped in the meeting that would not conclude!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm too polite to say "We're done. Please leave."

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Like I said before...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh no! I missed the window - he's reiterating!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... okay, great...

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Alright then...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe if I shake his hand he'll leave.

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: But like I said before...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Noooo oooo!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Then there was sort of a long awkward pause...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So... okay, great...

setting: Dilbert's cubicle or small office with a conference table
situation: Dilbert tries to end a meeting with a visitor who keeps repeating himself. Dilbert is too polite to ask him to leave, misses his chance to wrap up, and even a handshake fails to end it. Later he tells Dogbert about the long awkward pause, and Dogbert falls into the same "So... okay, great" routine.
punchline: The endless-meeting dilemma is so contagious that even Dogbert, listening to the story, gets stuck in the same unable-to-conclude loop.
summary: A painfully polite engineer cannot get a rambling visitor to leave, and the awkward stalling phrases spread to everyone who hears about it.

file: 1995/1995-04-03_laptop computer_upside down_reboot_etch -a - sketch.gif
title: Rebooting an Etch-A-Sketch Laptop

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My laptop computer is locked up. Can you help?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remember you have to hold it upside down and shake it to reboot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, that's right.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I wonder if he'll ever realize we gave him an "Etch-A-Sketch."

situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert and Wally, complaining that his laptop is locked up. Dilbert tells him to hold it upside down and shake it to reboot, and the Boss obediently does so. Afterward Wally wonders whether the Boss will ever realize the 'laptop' they gave him is actually a toy.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless about technology that he doesn't notice his laptop is really an Etch-A-Sketch, and shaking it to 'reboot' is just how that toy clears its screen.
summary: Two employees hand their technologically ignorant manager a children's drawing toy in place of a computer and convince him that shaking it is a legitimate reboot.

file: 1995/1995-06-29_dogbert the consultant_nobody likes prodcuts_ix that_internal business units_don't like boss.gif
title: Dogbert Recommends Bickering Business Units

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One way to look at your problem is that nobody likes your products.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But I don't know how to fix that. So I recommend forming internal business units to bicker with each other.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would you recommend that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, I'd be lying if I said I liked you.

setting: Executive office or conference room with a large desk
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, tells the Boss that the company's problem is that nobody likes its products. Admitting he cannot fix that, he recommends creating internal business units that bicker with each other. When the Boss asks why, Dogbert reveals he simply dislikes the Boss.
punchline: Dogbert's useless consulting advice is motivated by personal dislike, so he deliberately recommends a dysfunctional reorganization to make the Boss's company suffer.
summary: A consultant dog offers a deliberately unhelpful restructuring plan and cheerfully admits it's because he can't stand his client.

file: 1995/1995-03-16_ban all meetings_dress code_casual staus_mission statements_have fun_satisfy customers_make money_fit five more_cucbicle_chair_stock options.gif
title: Dilbert's Dream of Benevolent Management

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As new owner of this company I hereby ban all meetings over one hour. The dress code is casual. Status reports are optional!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No more mission statements or "visions." Our motto is "Have fun, satisfy customers, make money."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And stock options for all.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can fit five more in this cubicle if we remove the chair.

setting: Company meeting room, then a cubicle
situation: Dogbert, standing on a podium as the company's new owner, announces a series of employee-friendly reforms: shorter meetings, casual dress, optional status reports and no more mission statements. The employees listen in delight, but it turns out to be Dilbert's dream. He wakes slumped at his desk to find the Boss proposing to cram five more people into his cubicle by removing the chair.
punchline: The utopian workplace was just a dream, and the real management response is to make conditions even more cramped and miserable.
summary: A sleeping engineer imagines a perfect company run by his dog, only to be jolted back to a boss planning to squeeze more workers into his tiny cubicle.

file: 1995/1995-08-05_ratbert the temo worker_demand respect_eye contact_peripheral vision.gif
title: Ratbert Demands Eye Contact From Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the temp worker

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm only a temp, but I demand respect!!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Okay, maybe that's too much to ask. But I demand that somebody make eye contact with me!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's this?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That's peripheral vision!!!

setting: Office, with Ratbert sitting in a cardboard box
situation: Ratbert, a lowly temp worker sitting in a cardboard box, demands respect, then scales his demand back to simply asking that someone make eye contact with him. The Boss picks Ratbert up by the tie and looks off to the side, claiming to oblige.
punchline: The Boss technically grants the request by looking at Ratbert only out of the corner of his eye, showing he's still unwilling to genuinely acknowledge a temp.
summary: A tiny temp worker lowers his expectations to a bare minimum of acknowledgment, and management still manages to give him less than that.

file: 1995/1995-05-17_need approval_business case_wedge_claim_feel prodcutive_when doomed.gif
title: Burying the Business Case Approval

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your approval on my business case, Tom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll wedge it in here so you can claim you never saw it when I ask about it next week.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The weird part is that I can feel productive even when I'm doomed.

setting: Office, in front of Tom's overflowing pile of paperwork
situation: Dilbert asks Tom, a coworker buried under a towering stack of papers, to approve his business case. Knowing it will never be read, Dilbert simply wedges it into the pile and Tom thanks him. Dilbert walks away humming, reflecting that he feels productive even though his project is doomed.
punchline: Dilbert knows the approval process is hopeless, so he cheerfully goes through the motions and still gets a sense of accomplishment from a task he knows is futile.
summary: A resigned engineer stuffs his proposal into a colleague's mountain of paperwork and walks off satisfied despite knowing it will vanish.

file: 1995/1995-07-03_engineers_charge time_marketing_reprogram_compuetr_radiation_alter dna_possible_business.gif
title: Dilbert Threatens Marketing Guy's DNA

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Ha ha! Now that the engineers must charge their time to marketing, we own you!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just reprogram your computer through the LAN so its radiation will alter your DNA.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Is that possible??!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As far as you know.

situation: A smug marketing employee gloats that engineers now have to bill their time to the marketing department, so marketing owns them. Dilbert calmly replies that he will reprogram the man's computer over the network so its radiation alters his DNA. The worried marketer asks if that is possible, and Dilbert gives a deliberately ambiguous answer.
punchline: Dilbert exploits the marketer's technical ignorance, bluffing a ridiculous threat that the man cannot disprove, which turns the power dynamic back around.
summary: When a gloating salesman claims ownership of the engineers, Dilbert scares him with a made-up threat that only sounds plausible to someone who doesn't understand technology.

file: 1995/1995-03-17_destroying prodcutivity_hire contract employees_constractors_humilaition.gif
title: Preferring Rumors to Certain Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The rumors are destroying our productivity. We can't work with all this uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to buy proven technology and hire contract employees. You'll be gophers for the contractors until you resign in disgust and humiliation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there any way to get back to uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll see what I can do.

setting: Executive office with an armchair and a wooden cabinet
situation: Carol complains to Dogbert, who is sitting in a chair as the decision maker, that office rumors are wrecking productivity. Dogbert reveals his plan to replace the technology and staff with contractors, reducing the current employees to errand runners until they quit. Dilbert, now alarmed, asks whether the uncertainty can be restored.
punchline: The certainty Carol demanded turns out to be far worse than the rumors, so Dilbert begs to go back to being uncertain.
summary: A worker's plea for clarity backfires when the answer is a plan to push the staff out with contractors.
keywords: be careful what you wish for

file: 1995/1995-08-09_alice_casual friday_tan pants_business casual_unattractive_unorofessional_fashion opinion_engineer matters.gif
title: Alice Rebuts Casual Friday Fashion Critique

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, it wouldn't be Friday if I didn't see Alice wearing her one pair of tan pants.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I love the "business casual" look for the way it combines unattractive with unprofessional while diminishing neither.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you think the fashion opinion of a male engineer matters to me??

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Twins!

situation: Wally, leaning back in his chair, mocks Alice's tan pants and then the whole business casual dress code. Alice turns on him and asks why a male engineer's fashion opinion would matter to her. Dilbert walks up wearing the same polka-dot shirt as Alice and happily points out they match.
punchline: Alice dismisses engineers' fashion sense, while Dilbert, oblivious, proudly notes that he and Alice are dressed in identical polka-dot shirts.
summary: Wally sneers at casual Friday outfits until Alice shoots down his fashion judgment, and Dilbert cheerfully notices he is dressed just like her.

file: 1995/1995-04-27_spare cubicles_house convicts_opinions mattered_prisoners complained.gif
title: Spare Cubicles No Longer House Convicts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Effective immediately, we will no longer use our spare cubicles to house convicts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!!! Our opinions mattered!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, it's because the prisoners complained.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder what he plans to do with the spare cubicles now.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces that spare cubicles will no longer be used to house convicts. Wally cheers, believing the employees' opinions influenced the decision, but the Boss says it was because the prisoners complained. In the last panel Dilbert and Wally walk past a spare cubicle where pigs are sitting, implying the cubicles now house livestock.
punchline: The company only listened to the convicts' complaints, not the employees' (employees' opinions count for less than prisoners'), and the spare cubicles are now being used to house pigs.
summary: Management drops a plan to lodge prisoners in empty cubicles only because the inmates objected, and the vacant space ends up holding pigs.

file: 1995/1995-03-25_most user freindly_computer_pre insatlled_software_one button_leaves factory_over my head_tech support number_technology_engineering.gif
title: The One-Button Computer Mystery

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: ... But by far, this computer is our most user-friendly.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: The pre-installed software has only one button. And we press it before it leaves the factory.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does it do?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Whoa! I'm in over my head. Let me give you their tech support number.

setting: A computer store or sales office with computers on desks
situation: A computer salesman pitches a machine to Dilbert as the most user-friendly one they sell, claiming its software has just a single button that gets pressed at the factory. When Dilbert asks what the button actually does, the salesman suddenly admits he is out of his depth and offers the tech support number instead.
punchline: The salesman touts the product's simplicity but cannot explain what it does, exposing that he knows nothing about what he is selling and is just passing the buck to tech support.
summary: A clueless salesman brags about a computer's single-button software but bails out the moment he's asked to explain it.

file: 1995/1995-06-20_fiance dept_reduce costs_short sighted ways_save money_job harder_forget.gif
title: Finance Rep Forgets His Other Side

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm from the Finance Department. I'm here to reduce costs.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It might seem like all I do is come up with short-sighted ways to save money while making your job harder. But there's another side to this story.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And that would be...?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I forget.

situation: A small creature from the Finance Department approaches a seated coworker at his computer and announces he is there to cut costs. He admits he mostly devises short-sighted money-saving schemes that make people's jobs harder, and promises there is another side to the story. When asked what that is, he says he forgot.
punchline: The finance rep admits his job is making things worse for employees, then fails to produce any redeeming side, implying there is none.
summary: A cost-cutting finance visitor concedes he only makes work harder, hints at a bright side, and then cannot remember what it was.

file: 1995/1995-01-20_dark side_engineering_technical knowledge_generlaist_easy path_suite_applications_unnatural.gif
title: Devil Tempts Dilbert With Compatible Software

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Come to the dark side, Dilbert. Renounce engineering and become a manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Never!!

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Your technical knowledge is getting stale. You're becoming a generalist... take the easy path.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: I brought you a suite of applications that all work together.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's unnatural!!! Be gone!!!

situation: A red-costumed devil carrying a giant spoon tempts Dilbert at his computer to give up engineering and become a manager. Dilbert refuses at first, even when told his technical skills are going stale. Then the devil offers a suite of applications that all work together, and Dilbert recoils in horror.
punchline: Dilbert resists the temptation of management but considers software applications that actually work together so unnatural that he treats them as the true work of the devil.
summary: Satan himself can't sway an engineer with promotion, but offering software that actually interoperates sends him running.

file: 1995/1995-03-03_dna smaple_fatal genetic problems_hurt productivity_project dealine.gif
title: Genetic Screening for Productivity, Then Deadline

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Drop your trousers and turn around. I need a DNA sample.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're scanning for any fatal genetic problems that could hurt productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh... we decided to move your project deadline up a week.

situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert holding a syringe and tells him to drop his trousers and turn around for a DNA sample. He explains the company is screening employees for fatal genetic problems that could hurt productivity. Afterward, the Boss returns with a paper and casually announces that Dilbert's project deadline has been moved up a week.
punchline: The Boss's invasive 'genetic screening' is an absurd cover for a calculation that Dilbert might not survive, so he tacks on a tighter deadline, showing management cares only about squeezing output from staff.
summary: A manager threatens an invasive genetic test to protect output, then casually shortens the schedule his employee must meet.

file: 1995/1995-05-31_little stuffed doll_looks like boss_emotional lift_likeness nearby_smacks doll.gif
title: Boss Spots Voodoo Doll Likeness

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey! That little stuffed doll looks just like me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It gives me an emotional lift to have your likeness nearby.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I never realized what he thought of me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop dropping in like that!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whack!

situation: The Boss drops by Dilbert's cubicle and notices a small stuffed doll on top of the computer monitor that resembles him. Dilbert says it gives him an emotional lift to have the likeness nearby, which the Boss takes as a compliment. In the last panel the Boss walks away pleased while Dilbert, thinking angrily, whacks the doll.
punchline: The Boss mistakes the doll for a flattering tribute when Dilbert actually keeps it as a punching bag to vent his frustration at the Boss's constant interruptions.
summary: A boss is flattered by a miniature version of himself on an employee's desk, unaware it exists to be beaten up.

file: 1995/1995-08-29_tweaking brittle_brittle people_tech wroter_forms of expression_insult gender_tina_orgs of expression_venus de milo_women_lift heavy objects.gif
title: Dogbert Tweaks Tina the Tech Writer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I feel like tweaking some brittle people. Do you know any brittle people?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try Tina the Tech Writer. She believes that all forms of expression are an insult to her gender and her profession.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The statue of "Venus de Milo" has no arms.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Oh, I get it. You're saying that women can't lift heavy objects.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and Tina's desk
situation: Dogbert announces he wants to provoke someone easily offended, so Dilbert points him to Tina the tech writer. Dogbert then makes a seemingly harmless remark about the Venus de Milo statue having no arms, and Tina immediately takes offense.
punchline: Tina reads a sexist insult into a neutral art-history fact, proving she is as hypersensitive as Dilbert claimed.
summary: A mischievous dog tests a notoriously touchy coworker with an innocent remark and she finds a way to be insulted anyway.

file: 1995/1995-05-25_greatest accomplishemnts_big raise_draft_white paper_impact of work_owls_losy woodland_habitats.gif
title: Dilbert's Accomplishment Destroys Owl Habitats

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell me your greatest accomplishments at work. I'll use that to hype you up with your boss so you get a big raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote a draft of a white paper on a strawman process to reengineer our product process.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And what was the impact of that work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think some owls lost their woodland habitats.

setting: Dilbert's office, with Dogbert typing on a laptop atop a filing cabinet
situation: Dogbert offers to promote Dilbert's achievements to the boss to win him a raise and asks what he has accomplished. Dilbert cites a draft white paper on a strawman process for reengineering the product process. When Dogbert asks about its impact, Dilbert admits the only real effect was on owls who lost their habitats, presumably because paper was wasted.
punchline: The only measurable result of Dilbert's buzzword-laden paperwork is environmental damage from the paper it consumed, showing his work had no real business value.
summary: Asked to name his proudest work achievement, Dilbert can only point to a jargon-filled draft document whose sole consequence was harming wildlife.

file: 1995/1995-10-02_posted for success_huge earnings_market share_agenda_raises difficult year_united way_two agenda items_oopsie.gif
title: No Raises, Then Charity Update

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're poised for success. We expect huge earnings and increased market share!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next on the agenda... There will be no raises because it will be a difficult year...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I thought I told you to put the "United Way" update between those two agenda items.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Oopsie.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his staff that the company expects huge earnings and market share growth. He then moves to the next agenda item and says there will be no raises because it will be a difficult year. He complains that his assistant Carol failed to schedule the United Way charity update between the two items.
punchline: The Boss wanted the charity donation pitch sandwiched between the glowing profit news and the no-raises announcement, so employees would feel guilty and be softened up before the bad news, and Carol's scheduling slip ruined his manipulation.
summary: A manager brags about record profits, then denies pay raises, and grumbles that his charity-drive pitch wasn't placed to cushion the blow.

file: 1995/1995-10-10_more involved_project_roll up sleeves_work buttons.gif
title: Boss Gets Involved, Can't Work Buttons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to get more involved with your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm just going to roll up my sleeves and pitch in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anybody know how to work these buttons?

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert and Wally that he is going to get more involved in their project, and the two privately dread it. He declares he will roll up his sleeves and pitch in, but in the last panel he asks if anyone knows how to work the buttons while Dilbert and Wally despair.
punchline: The Boss's promise to help is empty, since he is so technically clueless that he cannot operate the computer and ends up as a burden rather than a help.
summary: A manager vows to help his team with hands-on work but immediately proves he cannot even operate the equipment.

file: 1995/1995-09-10_best manager_project goosefood_hired jack_brief jack_no budget_no  support_global information network_failure certain_industry_disgarce_hired_competitors.gif
title: Goosefood: Best Managers Set Up to Fail

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We just hired Jack away from our competitor. He was their best manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Jack will be in charge of Project "Goosefood."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you two to brief Jack on the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Project "Goosefood" has no budget and no management support.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your job is to build a global information network in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Failure is certain. Soon you will leave the industry in disgrace.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... Just like the other "best managers" we hired from our competitors.

transcript.speaker: Jack
transcript.text: Just out of curiosity, how did the project get its name?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's just say that you're the goose food...

situation: The Boss announces he has poached Jack, the best manager from a competitor, to run Project Goosefood and asks Dilbert and Wally to brief him. They explain the project has no budget, no management support, and an impossible two-week deadline to build a global information network. They add that failure is certain and that previous star managers hired from competitors met the same fate.
punchline: The project is named Goosefood because the hotshot managers hired to run it are just fodder to be cooked by an impossible assignment, and everyone knows it except the new hire.
summary: A newly poached star manager is cheerfully briefed on an unfunded, unsupported, impossible project that has already chewed up his predecessors.

file: 1995/1995-12-30_correction_ant farm_milton bradley_uncle milting industries_game company_public clarification_habitat disgusting creatures_lawyers.gif
title: Ant Farm Trademark Correction Insults Lawyers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Correction

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A recent Dilbert strip used the words "ant farm" to describe a habitat for ants.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Lawyers have informed me that "ant farm" is a trademark of "Uncle Milton Industries, Inc." They demand a public clarification.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What should we call a habitat for worthless and disgusting little creatures?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Law school.

situation: Dogbert, seated at his desk, issues a formal correction stating that the phrase "ant farm" is a trademark of Uncle Milton Industries, and that lawyers demand a public clarification. Dilbert asks what a habitat for worthless and disgusting little creatures should be called instead. Dogbert answers "Law school."
punchline: The suggested replacement name for a habitat of worthless, disgusting creatures is "law school," insulting the very lawyers who forced the correction.
summary: After lawyers force a trademark correction about the term for an ant habitat, the cartoonist takes revenge by labeling law school as the proper home for vile little creatures.

file: 1995/1995-05-15_sign_business case_web server_crosses all deaportments_every director_evp_ted griffin_half eagle_half lion.gif
title: Griffin Approval for Web Server

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who needs to sign my business case to buy a web server?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm...This crosses all departments. I fear it. Get the approval of every director, every VP, every EVP, plus Griffin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mean Ted Griffin in Finance or the mythical griffin beast that's half eagle, half lion?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whichever is harder.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss who must sign off on his business case to buy a web server. The boss, fearful of the cross-departmental scope, tells him to collect approval from every director, VP and EVP, plus someone named Griffin. Dilbert asks whether that means Ted Griffin in Finance or the mythical beast, and the boss says to get whichever is harder.
punchline: The boss's approval process is so absurdly burdensome that he deliberately picks the more impossible option, a mythical creature, just to make the request harder.
summary: Seeking permission for a simple server purchase, an engineer is sent on an impossible approval quest that ends with his manager preferring the harder of two possible signers.

file: 1995/1995-02-28_singular achievement award_we are teams_check_campiagn_one thousand dollars.gif
title: Singular Achievement Award for Teamwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And Ted gets this "Singular Achievement" award for creating the "We Are Teams" campaign.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a check for a thousand dollars! Let's all give Ted a hand.

transcript.speaker: Sound effects
transcript.text: Slap! Whack! Ow!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These things never work the way you want them to.

situation: The Boss presents Ted with a check for $1,000 and a 'Singular Achievement' award for creating the 'We Are Teams' campaign. He asks everyone to give Ted a hand, and the employees respond by slapping and whacking Ted's hand. In the last panel, the Boss thinks to himself that these things never work the way you want them to.
punchline: The Boss's own award is ironic, since it rewards an individual for a teamwork campaign, and the staff take his request to 'give Ted a hand' literally by hitting Ted's hand.
summary: A manager hands out an individual prize for promoting teamwork, and his request for applause is taken literally in a painful way.

file: 1995/1995-08-23_filberts expense voucher_idiots in accounting_smart_sadistic_trolls_humanoid characteristics_right answer.gif
title: No Right Answer for Accounting

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert's expense voucher

transcript.speaker: Accounting Monster
transcript.text: What are you trying to pull?? Do you think we're idiots in accounting?!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I swear, I think you're smart but sadistic trolls with many humanoid characteristics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently there was no right answer.

setting: Accounting department office, then a cave or dungeon
situation: Dilbert submits an expense voucher and is confronted by an angry green monster from accounting who accuses him of treating them like idiots. Dilbert nervously insists he thinks they are smart but sadistic trolls. In the last panel he is hanging upside down by his feet from a rope in a pit.
punchline: Whether Dilbert insulted the accounting staff or tried to flatter them, his answer to the accusation was wrong and he ends up tortured anyway.
summary: A scary accounting clerk interrogates an employee about his expense claim, and his attempt at a safe reply still gets him strung up by his ankles.
